carriage. THE due is on the rye when a man hasn't paid his whisky bill. IF the doctor orders bark, has not the patient a right to growl? "TIME is money." Of course it is, or else how could you spend it? "THERE is no rose without a thorn." Quiz says there is—a prim-rose. WHEN you offer oats to a horse he may say neigh, but he doesn't mean it. . _ _

- - - SEVERAL years ago, when running away to get -married at Gretna Green was not an uncommon occurrence, a young man well-known in London went to consult a legal authority of Lincoln's Inn about carrying off an heiress. "You cannot do it without considerable risk," said the lawyer, "but let her mount a horse and hold the bridle and whip, do you then get up behind her, and you are rim away with by her, in which case you are safe." The next day the lawyer who gave such good advice found that his own daughter had run away in the aforesaid manner with his client. The "Daily News" must really be careful. It gravely tells its readers this morning that the 'bar- barism of the people of the Shan States manifests itself in an incapacity to steal." Are we to under- stand then, that stealing is the outcome of civilisa- tion? However, the Shan States have now been -formally "annexed." Our Indian administrators will soon enlighten the simple savage.

Mr. Froude's " Beaconsfield " does not tell us much that is new; but it contains one clever and caustic saying ot the Tory leader which has never appeared before. It was after the death of the Prince Imperial in Africa,and Lord Beaconsfield remarked: " A remarkable people the Zulus ; they defeat our generals; they convert our bishops ; and they have settled the fate of a great European dynasty."

Mr. Wm. B. Butler, Highland House, 235, Camden- road, London, publishes his thermometer readings on Monday night, showing that the lowest tempera- ture there was 27 deg. Faht. in the shade and 17 deg. on grass, or 5 and 15 deg. reapectively below freez- ing point. These, he says, are the lowest October readings in his 17 years' record. Fifteen deg. of frost on the grass is seldom exceeded there, even in mid-winter.

In Prague apiece of clerical intolerance is much commented upon. The wife of a deputy to both Reichsrath and Diet, Dr. Brauner, died in Paris some time ago, and was cremated by her express wish, communicated by writing before her death. The ashes were placed in a metal coffin and taken to Prague to be interred in the family vault. The Mayor made a speech at the tomb, commenting upon the fact that the clergy refused their services to a man who had spent large sums in building churches.

We trust that the Education Department will endorse the proposal of the London School Board to introduce the decimal system into schools. The decimal system has been applied to money in almost every country, and the metric system of measurement and weight has taken the place of more antiquated methods. Sooner or later we must follow. Nothing can be said in favour of our pre- sent complicated system, although many object to change. The change will be more easily effected if children are taught the decimal and metric systems at schools.

The Eiffel Tower in the Isle of Man, the founda- tion stone of which was laid by the Earl of Lathom in pouring rain last week, will, like its namesake, be a stupendous undertaking. The estimated cost is about £BO,OOO, and it is expected that the struc- ture will be completed by midsummer 1892. Origi- nally the tower was designed solely as an approach; but according to the plan on which it is now being worked out by the engineer, Mr. Floyd, of West- minster, it is to comprise six floors, to be used severally as a theatre, a dancing saloon, a concert- hall, a bazaar, shops, and the topmost as an observa- tory. When complete the tower will be as high as the dome of St. Paul's Cathedral.

"The sad story of the rear column," it seems has yet to be told. Mr. Stanley said some things about the unfortunate Major Barttelot in his book, which some people thought ungenerous, andwhich Bartte- lot's relatives thought unjust. In Major Barttelot's " Diaries and Letters" grave charges are made against Stanley, who now threatens to lift the veil from the mystery connected with the rear guard and Barttelot's death, and who hitherto has with- held the facts, because he did not wish to blacken the memory of a mistaken and valiant officer " Barttelot to wit. Mr. Stanley insists that Bartte- lot was "killed, not murdered," and hints at inter- ference with a chief's wife, over the drum beating of which we have heard ; but he has suppressed the facts in his book. Unless Ward, Bonny, or Troup reveal the facts, Stanley threatens to divulge them.

What fools the Tories are Here they are in ecstasies because Mr. Balfour has gone to the west of Ireland and been well received by the peasantry. That is to say, Mr. Balfour has given .the most sub- stantial proof he can possibly afford of the folly of his own policy. The Irish Secretary has been preaching for three years that the Irish are a set of irremediable rascals who can only be kept down by Coercion. He goes among thera unattended by his bodyguard of batons and rifles, and though every one of the peasants whom he interviewed believes him to be responsible for the death of John Mande- ville, for the Mitchelstown massacre, and for all the miseries and cruelties of the Coercion regime, he is received by them with a touching kindness, sim- plicity, and good nature which every visitor to Ire- land knows to be characteristic of the people. All we can say is, that if Mr. Balfoues cheek is not hot with shame when he looks back on the history of the last three years, he is a worse man than we took him to be.

In July last it was mentioned here that Lord Hartington would probably be married in the course of next year. This was then the talk of his friends, and ever since that statement the rumour has grown stronger, until at last several journals now state that the marriage will take place next Easter. There is no disparity in years between the lady whose name is mentioned and Lord Hartington and when "this grave, sober, judicial man," as Mr. Gladstone described Lord Hartington, is pleased to sanction the report of his approaching marriage, there will be a universal expression of rejoicing and good wishes. It would not surprise some of Lord Hartington's most intimate friends if in future he takes rather less than more interest in polities. Since his attack of serious illness his health has been less robust than before, and he has shown much i liking for the family residence at Eastbourne. He enjoys the mild air of that seaside place, of which his father is literally the ground landlord, and his most pleasant days are passed at Eastbourne and at Newmarket. A great and honoured figure in the State Lord Hartington will always be, but for the conflict of politics he has not even, the moderate zeal of former times.

div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

The heaviest salmon killed this season by a lady was killed by Mrs. Audley Kmgdon at Castle Con- nell on Monday last, after a tremendous struggle, in which the rod got broken; the fish weighed 4011 b.

We are informed that the City and South London Railway, the first electric railway in England—ex- perimental and what may be called toy railways of course excepted—will be opened by the Prince of Wales this day week.

Every one is very much struck with the diminu- tion in size of the Prince of Wales since he went to Homburg. He was looking so much thinner and better at Saturday's wedding, that it was a general subject of conversation.

The London correspondent of the "Western Daily Mercury" has the best reason for believing that an Eight Hours Biil for Miners will be sup- ported from the front Opposition Bench. Mr. Schnadhorst is also personally in favour of it.

It has been decided by the Indian Government that pensioned native soldiers may continue to draw their allowances after the acceptance of other situa- tions in subordinate posts in Government depart- ments. This permission is expected greatly to im- prove the recruition of native soldiers.

Mr. Jackson, Financial Secretary to the Treasury, left London on Tuesday, on his third visit to Ireland since the Recess commenced. He will further con- sider the light railways under construction or about to be commenced, and will probably meet Mr. Bal- four before his return to the Treasury.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1,18f30

Mr. Gladstone has suffered many things of the Tories, but the last is the unkindest cut of all. They have actually put up Mr. Ashmead Bartlett to reply to the Midlothian speeches. Stay—perhaps we are wrong. Perhaps it was Ashmead who put himself up.

Ministers come and go between the country and their departments like men anxious to make the best of both worlds, but giving a preference to rural earth, and not seeking more of the Heaven of public life than is necessary to prevent themselves from be- ing shut out. Lord Knutsford is off again to the coun- try to the place from which he takes his title,where his host will be Lord Egerton of Tatton. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach came to the Board of Trade for a few hours and fled again forthwith to Salisbury. Lord Lothian has left the Scotch office for his seat in , Scotland.

About five years ago Count von Moltke missed his carriage at the door of the Reichstag, and took a cab to go home. On arriving he took out his purse to pay the driver; but, whipping up his horse, the man drove rapidly off, calling out, " It was a great honour to drive you, Sir Field-Marshal! " Count von Moltke could only look after the man in aston- ishment ; but as he had taken a cab-ticket when he engaged the vehicle, he was able to find out the name of the patriotic cabman, to whom next day he sent his photograph, with the autographic inscrip- tion," Moltke to his cabman."

A French Deputy has struck on an ingenious plan to increase the revenue. He proposes a tax on titles. There is to be a graduated scale from £2O for the prefix " de," up to £50,000 for duke or count. The tax might very well be applied in this country. In France, titles have no legal standing, while here they have a great deal. A tax might not diminish the number, but those who want to enjoy such luxuries as titles are well able to pay for them. In taxing a title one is on sound economic ground. A title is not the result of industry, and it is not pro- ductive. Moreover, there is a precedent for such taxation, Armorial bearings are liable to taxation. Why not the title of which they are often the ym- bol??

While Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien are sailing across the Atlantic unmolested with R.M.'s or shadows, the trial against them and their colleagues drag slowly on at Tipperary. A recent development of the case is that the magistrates refuse to allow witnesses to give straight answers. When Father Humphreys insisted on having a direct affirmative or negative from a witness, Mr. Shannon said, "We will close the deposition it you insist on this class of argument." When Mr. Sheehy pressed for a straight answer from another witness he was promptly told that the Bench considered the wit- ness conscientious." It is clearly in the interests of the Bench to receive elastic answers. They will be all the easier interpreted when sentence has to be pronounced.

across one unawares; it discharged some of its vile secretion on him, and he had to go home and bury his clothes—and clothes cost something here I can tell you. The skunk has a beautiful black and white fur, but he would be a good man -who would attempt to skin it. The other day John shot a hawk that came after the chickens, and the following day Walter shot a pheasant. It made a nice supper, and was nice picking I can tell you. The rain started on the Ist of October. Except a passing summer shower or two we had had no rain since the Ist of April. To-day it is bright and fine and the atmosphere is clear and fresh, and already everything is looking green again. Truly this is a wonderful land. Kind remembrances to all old friends. Sorry poor Whitham has such bad luck."

of the Free Library. In acknowledging the presentation of the freedom of the city, Mr. Gladstone discussed the effect on British commerce of the M'Kinley tariff. Be was convinced that though it might injure us inci- dentally, upon the whole it would have no injurious effect. America had things to sell us, and she must take in payment our manufactures. The effect upon the American people would be most injurious. It would raise prices there, and decrease their power of competing ' with us in the rest of the markets of the world. Be deprecated retaliation on our part, and urged our manu- facturers to uncomplainingly leave the American people to discuss the evil they were doing themselves, because friendship with America was more important than com- merce with it. He considered protection a misnomer ; it should be called oppression, delusion, fraud. England should not enter into what was called a war of tariffs. Any injury to us from the M'Kinley Bill would be only tractional. After lunching with the Lord Provost, he left Dundee by special train for Fasque.

div.head: WARRINGTOMANS IN AMERICA.
div.p: WARRINGTOMANS IN AMERICA.
LETTERS FROM MR. JAMES WINSTANLEY. (Concluded.)

In addition to those published in our last issue, this week we give two more interesting letters which have been received by Mr. John Gandy, of Church-st., from Mr. Winstanley, now of Salem, Oregon, but formerly of Warrington. On Sept. 21st, Mr. Winstanley writes:—"l am re- minded that it is the Sunday for writing you again, although I only wrote you last Sunday. We are still having the most lovely weather you can imagine, beautiful ruby red sunsets, with cool morn- ings, and bright warm days. Since the first day of April we have not had twelve hours rain. I wonder how you would stand that in the old country? I guess the water works would be doleing out a very I limited supply of its aqua pure—or not quite pure, according to Mr. Diggle—with its warning notices not to be extravagant, or the result would be some- thing frightful. The people in Salem use their hose pipes and irrigate their front gardens just as lima], and they are repaid for their trouble by having the most beautiful roses and other flowering shrubs, dahlias and asters in the most beautiful colours, sunflowers loft, high and more than a foot across. The water is got from our beautiful river Mlle- mette. Although it is now as low as it has been for some years, still there is no scarcity in town, and on our place the well continues to yield its stream of cool refreshing beverage. Thus you see the flood in the early part of the year has not been all loss to us, the earth having taken in sufficient water to supply all our wants during this long dry season. Some of our late corn is still green and growing, and will continue until the first frost, also the melon and squash; and vines, in spite of the exceed- ing dryness of the earth, continue to grow. During the past week we have had the State fair held at Salem. When you consider this State is larger than England, you will know that people come a long way to attend it. Hundreds of them bring their tents along with them and camp in the woods along side the fair grounds, which includes a splen- did race track, and when I tell you we have horses which do the mile in 2mln 30sec and 2min 35sec you will know we have some smart ones,as the Americans say. There are races every day, and these attract the usual pickpockets, &c., attending such places. The gamblers sell fools, and there are still some fools in Oregon, who lose their dollars and dimes which go to swell the coffers of those already bloated gamesters. Besides these attractions there are the merry-go-rounds, with pea nut and candy stalls, and all kinds of iced drinks forming no sraall share of the wares for sale, being both agreeable and pleasant in the hot dusty place. The display of ag- ricultural implements and farm products and stock, are very good, some fine English and French horses being exhibited; also some fine cows and sheep which are grown principally for the wool. Amongst other things exhibited, such as paintings, and all manner of local industry, are ladies' knitting and fancy work, and my daughter Edith took a skirt she knit at the People's College School and she obtained the first premium for that class of work, which .I think is very creditable, considering she was only ili years old when she did the work, and I tell you on the quiet she was a little proud when I drove her round to the bank in town to get her cheque cashed_ She intends trying for more another year. The oat and wheat crop has been only very moderate in this part of the valley, the flood doing considerable damage to the full grain, and many farmers not being able to get all their land in crop again before the dry weather commenced. The grapes and hops—oh! my! happy man who has fflor 30 acres in hops—the crops have been good and the. demand equally good, consequently the price has been high, and has made many a poor farmer com- paratively rich. The kay crop has been short owing to the dryness of the season. lam happy to say we are all in the enjoyment of good health. The winter term of school starts neat Monday, after three months' vacation. Edith and Harry will attend the district school." In the second letter, which is dated October sth, Mr. Winstanley says:—"! have received your letter. You want to make believe that if you came over on a visit, we should have to go hunting, fishing, and shootingin orderto entertain you. Just let meunde- ceive you. I guess we could supply your wants with- out that trouble. My wife was saying a few minutes ago that her pantry was like a. grand grocery store. It contains over a hundred cans and jars of pre- served fruits and vegetables. We have canned straw- berries, blackberries, raspberries, apricbts, peaches, plums, prunes, &c., &c., to say nothing of tomatoes; and all our own growing and canning. We have also home cured hams and bacon in galore—our own feeding and curing, also a barrel of flour and a bar- rel of sugar, and other goods in the grocery and feeding line sufficient to resist 3 our attacks for a longer time than you would be likely to stay. The trouble here is that we have such a poormarket for many of the good things we produce. My nephew ' took two bushels of the finest tomatoes you ever saw to the cannery and he only got 45 cents, for them—not a shilling a bushel—so that they are not really worth the trouble of gathering for sale. lam very well satisfied with my place. We are doing very well, I think, notwithstanding the poor crops this year, and I have faith to believe, that if Sales 3, grows as it has done during the last two years, in. three or four years more my place will be worth 400 dollars an acre split up into lots, which it un- doubtedly will be some day. I wish it was now. I would have a run over to the old country and see my old friends once more, but we must hope on un- til the day does come.

_ We do not get much shooting round here—but I what we have is varied. Last week we shot a skunk, about as big as a Scotch collie dog, and oh dear, don't they stink? If you got a sniff of them once it would last you a life-time—and the very thought of it afterwards would be enough to turn your stomach inside out. Some dogs worried one down the road here and it made them all vomit. One of our parsons going to church on the Sunday came

div.head: MIL GLADSTONE IN MIDLOTHIAN.
div.p: MIL GLADSTONE IN MIDLOTHIAN.
AT DALKIETII.

At the meeting which was held in the Dalkieth Corn Exchange on Monday afternoon,Provost Gray was voted to the chair, and he was supported by Mr. Childers, M.P., Mr. Marjoribanks, M.P., Mr. J. B. Balfour, M.P., Mr. Asher, M.P., Mr. T. R. Buchanan, M P., Mr. Munro Ferguson, M.P.' Dr. Cameron, M.P., Mr. Donald Craw- ford, M.P., Mr. John Leng, M.P. Mr. M.Ewan, M.P., Mr. Barbour, M.P., Mr. C. S. Parker, M.P., and Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P. Many Liberal candidates were also present. The Chairman, in opening the proceed- ings, announced letters of apology from the Earl of Rose- bery, the Marquis of Breadalbane, the Earl of Elgin, Lord Grey, Lord Houghton, Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, MP., and. others.

Mr. Gladstone, was received with loud cheers. Speaking of Home Rule for Scotland, he said that the feeling in favour of it, though undeveloped, was strong. Scotland had no doubt obtained immeasurable advan- tages by her union with the more powerful kingdom of England, but, on the other hand, the operation of the union had done something towards withdrawing from the centres of national life in Scotland some powerful social influences which it would have been most desirable to retain. It was true that they had not in Scotland had their feelings trampled under foot as had been the case with Ireland, but provision at Westminster for the consultation of the Scottish people's interests had been feeble and insufficient. Scotland however, he was sure, was perfectly competent to arrive at a proper conclusion on the subject of Home Rule, and when her attention had been thoroughly aroused on the question it would not be withdrawn until the whole root of the matter had been gone into. Further.he believed that whatever Scot- land deliberately asked from the Parliament at Westmins- ter would be consistent with the traditions of Imperial unity, and that her just and reasonable demands would be met with a free and willing acquiescence. Discussing the question of the condition of the Scotch crOfters, he deprecated the idea of emigration as a remedy for distress as being the last and lowest mode of meeting the grievances of a people. With regard to the question of Disestablishment, it would be enormously to the advan- tage of Scotland and to the cause of religious belief at large if the three Presbyterian Churches of Scotland could be made one. He adhered to the principle of Lord Hartington, that when the people of Scotland declared for disestablkishment the Church a Scotland ought to be disestablishel. As for the idea of making the question "a separate issue," as had been suggested to him, the notion was absurd if it meant that they should appeal. to the country upon it. Such a course would be totalily impossible with the many weighty subjects now demand- ing the attention of Parliament. fn the remainder of his speech Mr. Gladstone referred to questions affecting Ireland, and attributed to the Government's neglect to act when distress threatened that country a portion of the responsibility for the introduction of the Plan of Campaign.

div.head: AT EDINBURGH.
div.p: AT EDINBURGH.

The fourth of Mr. Gladstone's series of addresses to his constituents was delivered on Monday,in the Music Hall, ' Edinburgh. This hall, which usually holds about two thousand persons, was made by crowding, to hold two or three hundred more than this number. When Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone appeared, the right hon. gentleman ac— knowledged the loud cheering by coming forward to the front of the platform and smiling, and bowing to the people. Mr. John Cowan, of Beeslack, presided ; and he was supported by Mr. J. B. Balfour, M.P.,Lord Beay, Sir James Carmichael, Lord Elgin, Mr. Childers, M.P., Mr. Asher, M.P., Mr. A. L. Brown, M.P., Mr. D. Craw- ford, M.P., Mr. Buchanan, M.P., Principal Cairns, Sir Charles Tennant, Dr. Walter Smith, several members of the Corporation, and many ministers. There were also on the platform Lady Elgin, Lady Fanny Majoribanks, and Mrs. Childers.

The Chairman, in the name of the meeting, expressed thankfulness that the cloud that had hung over Dalmeny was dispersing. (Cheers.) They were honoured to-day by the presence of their distinguished representative. He questioned if they considered how much honoured they were by being represented by such amen. (Loud cheers.) Who was there that was endowed with such powers, and had served his country so well ? (Cheers.) They hailed with great satisfaction another opportunity of hearing from him the plans which he had formed for thewelfare of man, for Mr. Gladstone was not merely a lover of his own country, but of all mankind. (Loud cheers.) Mr. Grindstone, on rising, met with a most enthusiastic reception, the vast audience cheering and waving hand. kerchiefs He said when the work of Scotch Disestablish- ment was entered upon it would have to be done equit- ably and' even tenderly, with respeet for every life in- terest of a legal character. Then, dealing with certain questions put to him at Dalkeith with the object of• de- coying him into revealing his methods with regard to Home Rule, he said he had pledged himself to the prin- ciple of it, but as to the mode in which it was to be dena he wished to know for what purpose such questions-were asked, and he appealed to the meeting to consider the depth of the astuteness of these gentlemen, who sought to practice on his well-knowa simplicity. There would,. according to these gentlemen, be no opportunity of deal- ing with the question until 1194, yet they modestly asked hinvto bind himself to the method of tackling Home Rule, leaving his opponents absolutely free. What he desired was to get by continued discussion a ripened' public opinion both with regard to the principle and the manner of proceeding, and he gave. a - general warning to the Liberal party not to divide their ranks by what were called' test questions, such aathe question of Temperance, the Eight Hours Bill, Disestablishment for Scotland, and other projects,atid to remember his warning when the time came for pronouncing the great and solemn judgment which the country would have to give on the present great controversy. He touched upon public economy, and, referring to the increasing expenditure on the army and navy and the desire of the Government to conceal its real extent, likened them to Ananias and ' Sapphire, who kept back part of the money they received. He. asked and answered the question" How has Parliament done its duty ?" pointing out that five good measures had been passed with the support of the Liberal party in the House ; but he showed that the Government had wasted a vast amount of time, and that ita -withdrawal' of the Public-house Compensation Bill through fear of. defeat, was a triumph far the Liberal opposition and a matter ot congratulation to the temperance reformer. ridiculed the Government excuse of "obstruction,"' dealt with their foreign- policy, and afterwards pointed to the improved condition of Bulgaria, saying that here they had a striking example of a country that was allowed to manage its•own affairs, a cournry that instead of a weakness had become a strength„ a buffer between Turkey and Russia, and he urged the meeting to go for-1 ward towards the consummation of the good and sacred I work of giving Home Rule to Ireland..

WISIT TO OIL WORK& Mr. Gladstone left the residence of hit host, Balfour, on Tuesday at 12.30, for a drive to Calder-Hill, the residence of M. M‘Lagan, Bra': The righY hon. gentleman had airanged to make an 'inspection of the rumpherston Oil Works during his -temporary stay in the locality. Mt. Gladstone drove in an open carriage4,l and was accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, a second carri- age being occupied by Mr. and Lail? Fanny Marjoribanks and Mr. Campbell (election agent): Calder IMP we, reached a few minutes before two o'clock. The inspection' ended, the party proceeded to Jne of' the paraffin shedts. in which a, platform had been placed, and where. the majority of the work-mem,. several hundred' di', number, had assembled. Mt.- M‘Lagan took the I chair, and after a few introdoetory wort% expres,-1 sive of gratification at Mr. Gladstone's 'presence. in that part of the constituency, introduced Mr. W.. Fraser, managiing director, who ?ormally presented' to Mr. Gladstone a case containing samples of the raw material and several productions derived ttiereftorn, namely,,orucie oil, ammonia mater, sulphace,of ammonia oils, and.candies made 2rorn paraffin. Ile also gave a brief sketch of the history, of the works. Mr. Aochiitald Fraser, secretary and general manager, then presented Mrs. GladSOone with two busts in paraffin wax of Mr. Gladstone, and a case of,speoltnens of lanthine.—Mrs. Gladstone in a few words acknowledged the giift.—Mr. J. King, one of the engineers,,next came fOrward, and on behalf of the workmen presented a brief address to Mr.' Gladstoree.—Mr. Gladstone, in reply, after congratulating his audience of Scottish workmen upon a privilege un- known to their anasstors—the possession of the suffrage, addressed himself to, the consideration of the great pros- perity of the shale oil trade, and proceeded to take a retrospective view-of the reform which the productive' system of this country has undergone during the past half century. The result of the last 50 years' legislation had been that the trades of the country had been multi- plied five times and the population had been doubled In numbers, and enormously raised in social, political, and moral conditions. The hon. gent/eman's remarks. -were enthusiastically received. The party then drove to the Oakland Oil Works. On arriving at the offices of the company, Mr. Gladstone delivered a short speech to the workmen whcrhad assembled in the neighbourhood. party afterwards returned to Edinburgh. AT DUNDEE.

Mr. Gladstone left Edinburgh by special train on Wed- nesday, and travelled to Dundee, where he was received by great crowds ot people, and most enthusiastically cheered as he drove through the streets to the Kin- naird Rail. There the freedom of the city was px.e- seated to him, and subsequently he opened a new wing

div.head: NON MOLTKE'S -NINETIETH BIRTHDAY.
div.p: NON MOLTKE'S -NINETIETH BIRTHDAY.
SPEECH OF THE EMPEROR WILLIAM.

POTAIDAM, MONDAY.-A special edition of the " Reichs- zanzeiger," published this morning, states that the Em- peror, in addressing Count von Moltke, on Monday, on the occasion of the gathering of officers of the general staff, spoke as follows : "I thank you in the name of those who have fought together with you, and whose faithful and devoted servant you have been. I thank you for all you have done for my house, and for the greatness of the Fatherland. We greet in you not only a Prussian leader who has created the Army of In- vincibleness, but one of the founders of the German Empire. The presence of the King of Saxony, who has made a point of personally congratulating you, recalls the time when he and you fought for Germany's greatness. The distinctions conferred upon you by my grandfather leave nothing in which I can personally show my thanks to you, but I beg you to accept the only evidence of my profound regard which I can bring you. It is with special pride in to-day's proceedings that I allow myself the privilege of a Monarch, viz.—to have the flags of the Army standing in his ante-chamber, and I beg you to take possession of the flags of the Guard, which have waved over you in many battles,as a personal memento. I ask you to take the Field Marshall's baton, which you have already won before the enemy, as a symbol of my regard, devotion, and gratitude. I call upon those present to express their feelings of gratitude that Field Marshal von Moltke had known how to stand alone in his greatness, and to form a school of leaders of the Army for future generations, by giving cheers for his Excel- lency.

div.head: ST. MARY'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, WARRINGTON.
div.p: ST. MARY'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, WARRINGTON.

Several improvements and additions have been made towards the completion of the sanctuary, and its altars of the above church. The corbels of the arches leading to the side chapels have been carved in a very artistic and workmanlike manner by Mr. Essenhigh. This was found necessary in prepara- tion for the elegant choir screens surmounted by angels in Caen stone, which together with a new altar dedicated to the Sacred Heart, are in course of erection. A window in honour of the five wounds has been put in, whilst a large crucifix, in memory of Oberammergau' now forms a conspicuous object of devotion near the doors of the church. As the church is dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary,, an attempt has been made in the sculptures of the high altar and the figures in the window above to represent her as the great woman of pro- phecy, the mother of God. In the window she is shown as prefigured in her chief prerogatives, in the characters of Eve, Rachael Ruth, Esther, Judith. and Bethesda-,.the mother of Soloman. In the smaller lights, are heremblems' the lily, the star, the pomegranate, whilst she herself as "Mystical Rose" fittingly occupies the centre light of the rose window. Itninediately be- neath are statues of the Marian doctors, who in their writings or by their preaching have been instrumental in developing doctrine; or spreading devotion to her, as- mother of God. In, the frescoes, ancl in the carved panels immediately to the right and left of the tabernacle are represented the four great events of her life as mother of God, viz., the Annunciation, the Visitation. Bethlehem,. and Epiphany, proclaiming her mother of God to the Jews, and mother of God to the Gentiles; that is to the whole world. lathe reredos of the Sacred Heart Chapel our Lord is represented with arms extended as on the cross, and kneeling close at His feet are the figures of Margaret Mary, the foundress of the devotion to the Sacred Heart, and St. Gertrude,. Abbess 0.5.8., and in the outer panels are the figures of the prodigal son and St. Mary Magdelene. In the window above are depicted the Five Adorable Wounds,. and the instruments-of the passion, sublime proof to all men of the love of the sacred heart. In the altar and reredos of the Lady Chapel, the Virgin is represented in sorrows,,and in glory. In the panel beneath the altar is a very faithful copy of the famous picture of the "Three Marys "' by Annibale Carracei, representing the dead Christ in the lap of His mother, who has swooned away in the arms of the'other women. In the reredos the Vir— gin Is crowned in glory, standing on the clouds of heaven, with angels at her feet and above her head, whilst on the other side stand the statues of her parents, St. Joachim and St. Anne: The whole of the work of the three altar pieces and the screens have been executed by Messrs. Boulton and Sons, of Cheltenham, from designs • furnishelby Messrs. Pugin and Pugin, of London.

div.head: BY SYLVINUB COBBf JR..
div.p: BY SYLVINUB COBBf JR..

CHAPTER 11. , A STRANGE PROCEEDENG. When Runic Caine down in the morninglie found the monk already there, and breakfast nearly.ready. But little was said during the meal time, for the monk seemed busy with thoughts of his own... and Runic was too much engaged, in studying the strange man's features, and pondering upon, the various doubts and surmises that had enteredi his mind. After the meal was over the monk accom- panied the gun-maker to his shop, and there he spent some time in examining the (plaint articles of machinery that were used in , the manufacture of arms.

Runic was engaged in finishing.a pair of pistols, and for some minutes the monk stood silentiy by his side watching his movements: At length the youth stopped in his work and laid the pistol down. "Excuse me, good father," he said, rather nerv- ously, at the same time gazing his visitor in the face ; " but I must ask you a question. Where have I seen you before?"
"Ho w should I know ?" the monk returned with a smile.

" Why," resumed Runic, with some hesitano.y, "I knew not but that you might enlighten me.. I. have surely seen you somewhere." "And are there not hundred whom you have seen in this great city—aye, thousands—whom yonanight recognize as you recognize me ?" " Ah—it may be so : but not like this. There may be a thousand faces I would recollect to have seen, but not one of them woula excite even a passing emotion in my soul. But your face calls up. some powerful emotion—some startling memory of the past—which bothers me. Who are you, good father? What are you? Where have we met be- fore? Was it in Spain e "No:' said Valdunir, with a shake of the head.. And then with a more serious shade upon his face,. he added : "Let this pass now. I ,will not deny to you that there may be some grounds for your strange fancies but I assure you most sacredly that until last night I never came in direct companionship with you before—at any rate, not to my knowledge You, have acted the good Samaritan towards me,. and I hope I may at some time return the favour." 'No. no," quickly responded the youth:l." if return it then it will be a favour no more. I have only done for you what every man should do to his, neighbour, and so far from needing thanks for my services, I would rather give them for the,occaeion,. for I know of no source of joy so pure and pleasur- able as that feeling in the soul which tells us we have done a good act." The dark monk reached forth and took the youth- ful artisan's hand, and with more ,• than ordinary einotioa he said:

" You touch the harp-strings of the souk with a noble.hand, my son, and if any deed of kindness-cart give Ise joy it will be a deed for you' We may meet again, and until then I can only say" God blese and prosper thee."

. . --- With these words the monk turned away, and ere, Ruric could command presence of mind enough to• follow him he had gone from the house, . The youth. wished to say something, but amid the varied emo- tion& that went leaping through his,mind he could'l gatherno connected thoughts. After the monk was gone Runic returned to his bench and resumed his work. Re asked his boy if he had ever seen the strange man before, but Paul only shook his head, and answered dubiously. "'What do you mean ?" the gun-maker asked; gaz- ing the boy in the face. "Do you think; you, have seen him before ?"
"I cannot tell, my master. I may have seen him before, and I may not. But surely you would not suppose that my memory would serve- you better than your own."

Ram was not fully assured by this -answer,. He gazed into Paul's face, and he fancied he detected some show of intelligence there which had not been spoken. But he resolved to ask no mere • questions at present. He had asked enough', he thought, upon such &subject, and he made up his mind to bother himself no more about it, feeling sure that if his boy knew anything which would be for, his -master's interest to know it would be commnnicated in due season. So he applied himself anew, to his work, and at noon the pistols were limahed. • Towards the middle of the afternoon, . jpat as Rurie•had finished tempering some parts of • a gun- locki.the back door of his shop was opened, and two men entered. They were young men, . dressed in costl* furs, and both of them stout. and good-look- ing. The gun-maker recognized there as the Count Conrad Damonoff and his friend Stephen Urn. "I think I speak with Rurien Nevel•P said the Count, moving forward. "You do." returned Runic, not at all 'surprised by the visit, since people of all 'classes were in the habit of calling at his place ta order arms, • The Count turned a shade paler than•lbesiore, and his nether lip trembled; but Raric • thought that mighe be the result of coming from the cold into a warm place. ..lowever, he wee soon • mrleceived, for the.C.Junt's next remark was. signifidant : "You are acquainted with the Ladp Rosalind Yaldair be said.
"I am," returned Marie, now baginning to wonder.

"Well, sir," returned Thitnonoff',! with much 'haughtiness, "perhaps irAy business can, be quickly and satisfactorily settled. . It•is my,desire to make the Lady Rosalind my wife."' Buric Navel started czthesa words,,and he clasped hishands to hide their tremulousness. But he was- not 3ong debating uporsan answer. '‘.And why have you. coir-e to maw-kb this inforl- ' mation, sir ?".he askee,
"'You should know at already..Dayou not loro., the lady?'
"UpOn my soul, Si:.-Ctiunt,: yotiq ask me a strange question. What right, have yout to qyzestion me xp- on such a theme ?"

" The right that envy man,. ha.s.to pave the way for his own right c;,* replieetJ Dansonoff sharply. "But if you choose not to ,anawer, let it pas 0,.. know you do love ti!k•lady. And; now I ask ycia to renounce all claims tor her hazd."'

"By St. Paul, Sirt•Counti :your tongue rinp,into strange moods of speech. I renounce all claims to Rosalind Yaldai's Land ?Wias% SiD you meant " Aye, sir—precisely so."' " Perhaps you wiltinformarne what claircl. I may have upon the lean" Runic returned, with some tremulousness in tone, for the very sub;ect was one that moved him deeply; " Ruric Neve], you r shall, not say that Ddid not make myself fully.understood, and hence S will ex- plain." The Coust,sptko-this as speaks rman who feels that he is doing a. very condescending thing, and in the same•toue he proceeded: "The Lady Rosalind is of noble.. parentage and ve7y wealthy. My own station,and wealth are equtlo with hers.. My station, at afleveuin, She may possess the un- divided right to more-property than I do. But thatz matters not. Illone lior and must 113.7,5 e her for my wife. I have beam to see the noble Duke, hen guardian, andlhe oMects not to my suit. But he informed me.that there was one impediment, and that was her-love fur you. He knows full well— as I know, and ask all must knowr--that she could :never become.yonzwife; but yet he is anxious.not ,to interfere too much against bur inclinations., So a simple denial fmm you, to the .eftlect that ymaz can never claim her hand, is all thatis necessary. WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening for the purpose 'of corn- pleting the business of the municipal year. The MAYOR said he bad received the .following letter t from Mr. John Crosfield Dear sir, 1 wish to retire ' from the Town Council and therefore beg to resign my " seat as an alderman of the borough d Warrington. In the case of the "Clio" parents were coropelled to contribute, Lsot the money, he believed, went to the treasury. The minutes were then confirmed. THE LIRRAMY AND MUSELTM. Report of the knowing gifts for will& the thanks of the Com- mittee were ordered to be sent to the donors :—Parcel of fossils from Guilden Morden from Mr. Reuben Seddon ; herbarium of plants collected in the lake district by Miss Martha Guest, from Robert Davies ; " Transactions of the Liverpool Engineering Society," vol. 11, from the the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society. And for the corresporuting period last Year :—Adults, 39 .; minors, 74 ; stillboin and premature 11. The receipts for the past four weeks were £7l Is. 20d. and for the-corresponding period last year £lO3 1.5.5. 11d. Adopted on the motion of Alderman HARRISON, eec.ouded by Councitim• TAYLOR. 'ISLE BATHS. From the report of the bath-keeper to the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee it appeared that the income from the Baths during the past four weeks was £lB 53. 84., and for the corresponding period last year £5 gd. The Committee also proposed that the Borough surveyor be instructed to erect a wood partition across the centre ef the gymnasium so as to separate the part used by boys from that used by girls ; and that the gymnasium be enclosed with an unclimablo iron Palisade. Also that the gymnasium be closed on sun- dam The MAYOR moved Councillor 33ourofir seconded the adoption of these minutes. Councillor PIERPOINT asked if it were the intenticn of the Committee that the borough arms should form a Part of the design of the tesselated pavement to be put ,down in the vestibule of the Town Halt. If that were so ne thought it would be a very great mistake. Councillor BOLTON : It is finished. Councillor PIRRPOINT : Councillor 13O1tegs Rys it is 4nished• i that NT, 744 pr ?

The MAYOR,. It is not begun yet. Councillor PLERPOINT : Then Councillor Bolton is wrcng. COUneßiOr FLEMING : As usual. (Laughter.) Councillor PIERPOINT said he could quite understand that the proper place for a coat-of-arms was upon a wall or forming part of the design of a stained glass window, but,in all his experience he had never noticed such a flagrant departure from the canons of art taste as in the scheme the Committee proposed to adopt. Here they had a. coat-of-arms of ,an ancient borough, and they were.going tomake that coat-of-arms part of a pave- ment overwhich the ,dirty feet of everybody would be allowed towalk. He shmlcl like Alderman Chandley, who hacts, long and practical knowledge of decoration, to givean opinion onthe subject. .Alderman CMANDLEY said he must decline offering opinions on matters of taste, but at the time the design of the borough arms was placed before the Committee lee was not one of those,who voted in its favour. Councillor PLATT.: That is quite sufficient to condemn

it. The MAYOR said they were going to put bees on the floor; but Mr. Pierpoint objected to walking over bees. and in deference to his opinion, they changed from that to a little flower. Councillor PIERPOINT : Which is a great improvement. Tmon the suggestion of Councillor Flood, some designs for-the ;pavement were placed before the members of the Council. Councillor PLATT., Councillor VOISEY, and Alderman Hammon supported Councillor Pierpoint's objection to the coat of arms, mid on being put to the vote' the coat of arms was unanimously rejected, and another design substituted. 'file minutes of the Committee were then adopted. ' THE MARKETS. The total incomoof the Markets Committee from all sources was reported to be £284 4s. 10d. • On the motion of Councillor HUTCHINSON, seconded by Councillor TAYLOR,the minutes were adopted. THE GAS. 'Tle Has Committee reported that the illuminating, power of the gas during the past fortnight was equal to 1811 candles at both works. 'At a meeting held on the 24th October it was resolved that the report and comparative statement for the year: Marcie2sth, submitted by the gas engineer (Mr. Had-; dohk), be approved. The report stated that the gas: manufacturing plant had been kept in a good state of:, repair, and the alterations made at the works had been very beneficial. The ;largest quantity of gas made in 24; hours was 528,000 cubic feet at Longford, on December! ' 6th, and 401.900 cubic feet at the Mersey-et. works on, December 21st. The largest quantity made in one day•; was-T00;700 cubic feet,, on December 21st. The largest; quantity sent out in one week was 6,013,300, for the weel3: ending ;Decentber 22nd. The smallest quantity! sent out in , one week was 1,500,403 cubic feet,' for the; week ending :fund 30th. Owing to the Manches- ter -;Ehip'Canals severing the mains in Chester-road, , Northwich-road, Grappenhall-road. Knuesford-road, it had been necessary to make an entire change in the mode: of suipplying the Cheshire suburban districts which was! being carried out at the-expense of the Ship Canal Com- pany. • When the proposed alterations were completed there +would be two subways under the canal, one on the Knutkiord-road, the otaer at Twenty Step Bridge on the, Isiatthwich-road. The supply of gas fer Latchford be- ' yend Sim canal woulelipass by the Knutstord-road sub- way arid along the new road running alongside the canal • from linutsford-road to Grappenhall-road. The supply of gas ler Lower Walton, .beyond the canal, would be conveyed by Stockton likath and Walton New-road. The new roams in Cheshireshad been laid during the past year, • and were completed with the exception of the mains through the subways, which were not yet con- structed. The reductioiv in the pressure had had the desired ',effect of reducing the unaccounted for gas, it having fallen to 5564 percent., which was almost as low as it waspossible tosalstala it. This reduction in the percentage of unaccounted for gas was a direct saving of about-TWO for raw material, and also £560 which it would have cost in wsges, as compared with 1888. The reduced pressure had repented in an adverse manner, the sales ;of gas being about 3 ;per cent. less than last year, which he regretted. and hoped to overcome by increasing ;;the size of the mains and services in the districts most affected by the low pressure. lin all cases which had,been reported at the dice, the oupply had teen made satisfastory except in a few in- stances, where the house fittings had been inadequate. 'During the.past year there had been a large number of s inferior sburners sold to customers by some initerant dealers who -charged enormous prices for their wares, mid represented them as consuraine- about one-fourth of the actual quantity. The Gas CcZmuitte offered their customers the +very hest burners at almost cost Trice, anSI were always willing to asss.st them in the choice of bet ners. Any; information sista the quantity of gas butssed, or the fluty obtained by any burner, vsoadd he given at the setice without charge. The wages in gas works having advanced allover the country, strikers aSked for an increased wagevith a reduction in the hours of labour, and after carefiel consideration it w4s decided to makea concession to the men, which willn- crease the cost Of manutacture. about one-third Of .r penny-per thousand. The price Of coal had advanced to.sueis an extent ;during the past year that it would have been difficult to supply gas at a profit, except ; for the fact of having bought at -the best tinae and ;under the most favourable citr.umstances. The outlook for the coming year was net promising, the, present market price being about 16 to 40 per cent., more than were now being paid. If the present prices for coal were maintained they would require to makeats increase in the price of gas. Alderman Hos.angs moved the confirmation of the minutes., and slid he wished to emphatk.e very strongly, " a sentence in Mr. Haddock's report that cases of court plaint with reference to the gas were attended to at once. He heard informally of many complaints. For instance, a gentleman said his shop was badly lighted, and when the ease was enquired into it was found that he had only ; ten-ligirt meter, although he had 18 Belts burning downstairs and some upstMrs. It was utterly impossible to have sufficient light under those circumstances, but when they put in a 30 light meter a good supply ef gas was afforded. He noticed in going along the streets that some of the shoos were well lighted and others kadlythe reason generally being that the fittings were good in one case and had in the other. If people who complained of the insufficient supply of gas would have their fittings and burners adjusted the complaints now made would be very much reduced in number. (Hear, hear.) All com- plaints should be made to the gas office. Alderman CHANDLEY seconded the motion for the pass- ing of the minutes. Councillor HEATON said that at half-past five that after- noon he was in Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' office, and his attention was drawn to the 'poor quality of the gas. Although there were nearly 40 lights in the room one could scarcely see the clerks at the far end. He should have pleasure in telling Messrs. Pearson and Knowles what Alderman Holmes said. Alderman HARRISON said that on Sunday night no- thing could exceed the supply of gas he had in his house, but on Monday night the gas was so absolutely miserable, that it made the darkness visible. Some said the pressure was taken off to prevent a leakage. Ile pro- tested against this being done, as he did not think the public had a right to be tortured with an insufficient supply of gas. They ought to have good gas, and plenty of it. (Hear, hear.) Alderman CHANDLEY supported what had been said by Alderman Holmes as to its being very important that all complaints should be lodged at the Gas Works. Alderman SUTTON said there was no doubt that the gas was good some nights and bad at others, and this showed a want of pressure. Councillor SHAW-GREEN said he saw from the report that there was a possibility of an increase in the price of gas. He hoped that was only put in to frighten them, and not with the de'iberate intention of raising the price of the gas. There was a feeling in town that the price , • paid was already a high price. (Hear, hear.) The Com- mittee should decrease rather than increase the price. (Hear, hear.) Councillor VOISEY said the poor gas was attributable in a great measure to the want of pressure. There should be a better pressure, even if the leakage went on and ; prevented them from accumulating profits. Alderman Boum said that £l,OOO a year was saved by reducing the pressure, and that sum was not to be thrown away lightly. The minutes were adopted. THE COUNCIL AND THE SHIP CANAL. The Rivers Committee's minutes contained the follow- ing :—That the Borough Surveyor laid before the Com- mittee a plan submitted by the Manchester Ship Canal Cos of the bridge proposed to be constructed over the river at Walton. After carefully considering the same, it was resolved that Councillors R. T. Fairelough and Heaton, and the Borough Surveyor be requested to see • Mr. Leader Williams with a view of obtaining a headway of at least 26 feet above low water, and ascertain the width and position of the locks to be constructed in the river at Walton. Also, that permission be given to Mr. Aaron Whitby to place a properly constructed stage on, and to moor pleasure boats to land belonging to the Cor- poration, near the end of Wharf-st., upon payment of an annual charge of £1 per annum. 'Councillor R. T. Fainctorron moved the confirmatien of ths minutes, and said the negotiations with reference to the Ship Canal bridge had not yet been completed. The report of the Borough Surveyor would be entered on the minutes, and fifty or a hundred years hence it would show the quantity of water which flowed down the river in the year 1890. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PIRATON seconded, and the minutes were adopted.

The Board direct me to refer to the interview which Mr. Alderman Davies had with one of the officials of the Board upon this subject on the 9th inst., and to the memorandum left by him in which the Board observes that it is stated that the 'inn- tees of the Infirmary would be prepared to purchase the land ,for such a sum as might be deemed to be reasonable; and to state that the Board would not object to consider a proposal on the part of the Corporation to sell the piece of laud in question. Should the Town Council propose toadopt this course the proposal should be embodied in a memorial under the seal of the Corporation, which should be accompanied by a valuation of the land pro- posed to be sold, by a valuer independent of the Corpor- ation:" Ths Committee has passed the following resolu- tions—That Mr. Percy Silcock, A.R.1.8.A.. be called in to-make the valuation ; also, that the Town Clerk be in- -strueted to prepare and forward a memorial under the seal of the Corporation to the Local Government Board to carry out the proposal contained in the above com- munication. The MAroamoved the passing of the minutes of the Committee. Alderman Surron seconded, and said he hoped when -the new Council met that the General Purposes Com- miittee would take into consideration the advisability of approaching-the London and North-Western 'Railway 'Company with a view of getting the Wilderspool level crossing done away with. (Hear, hear.) CouncillorT LEMING : I hope the Council willgo a step 'further and remove the railway altogether and take it -overhead. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR said that Mr. Morley and himself attended a meeting of the Council of the Association of Municipal 'Corporations in London, and it was decided to recom- mend to the boroughs the expediency of adopting a uni- 'form scale Of superannuation for the police. 'A maximum -scale shcrultrbe adopted, and no limit of age imposed. ' The minutes were agreed' t. THANKING THE MAYOR.

. Alderman SUTTON moved"' That the best thanks of this Council 'be presented to Richard Walker 'Trancomb, 'Esq., alderman of this borough, kr the satisfactory manner, in vehich he has discharged the responsible duties devolving upon him as Mayor and chief magistrate of this borough during his year of office, and for the un- varying-courtesy and impartiality displayed by him when presiding over the deliberations of the Council and in his intercourse with its members." The office of Mayor, he aid, was attended with many responsibilities. and the performance of the duties required considerablettisne and Attention. lie thought no one would deny that the Mayor ha:dscquitted himself well as the head of the Council andef the Corporation, and had performed his duties in a- manner alike creditable to himself and to the Corporation. (Applause.) Alderman GRINDLEY seconded the motion, and said it was a pleasure to him to corroborate what had been said by Alderman dutton and by other gentlemen on a previ- ous occasion. The Mayor's year of office had been nmelred byseveral important events. The purchase ot the'Waterworks and the extension of the borough were very important matters in the annals of the borough. He Wished to empress to the Mayor his conviction, and that of the members of the Council generally, that he had dis- charged the duties of the office with the greatest credit andtthe greatest impartiality. 'if he had a fault it had been an over indulgence to the Council. In his anxiety to give everyone fair play he was afraid that sometimes the reins of government had got under the horse's tail as it were. He hoped the Mayor might long look back with pleaerre upon his year of office. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PLATT wished to add his testimony to the excellent,manner in which the Mayor had conducted the business of the Council during Ids year of office. At the outset, he l(Countillor Platt) thought it was his duty to oppose the election of Alderman thought as Mayor. However, that was an event of the,past, and he hayed they had been none the less friends on that account, as he felltit tc be his duty to support a gentleman who hud been a lonter time a member of the Council. He must say that Alderman Fra.ncomb had filled the chair to the satisfaction of all of them and certainly • they had newer had a better tempered Mayor. (Hear, hear.) Counciller'Bovroir added his testimony to the excellent manner in which the Mayor had acquitted himself He thought the general bulk of them would say that the Mayer had Med the port better than they had expected. t The Maroa,in reply, said he was greatly obliged to 1 them for the very hearty vote of thanksthey had given him and he could assure them that although he felt he had had many shortcomings, he had the satisfaction of knowing that 'he had tried to do his best. If he had failed in any particular pint, he must ask them to put it down to want of ability, mut not to anything 'else. The past year had been a very anxious one to every member of the Council, and he must say that he felt heartily ,thankful to all ctf them for the attention they had given to their duties -during the year. Had it not been iLY the extraordinary help he had received, he did not hrow what he should have done when they were passing tli.s Bill through the Lords. Only that day his natural curiosity led him to read some of the elec- tioneering addresses, and he thought many promises were made which, if carried out, meant a lot of expense. He thought when the new Council met that the greatest friends of the town would be those who tried to reduce the rates. If they wanted to make Warrington a great manufacturing centre, they must attract people witk capital, and they must do it by having low rates. He did not mean to say they must not make any progress, but economy must be their watchword for some years to come, if Warrington was to benefit by the introduction of the Ship Canal. (Applause-) The Waterworks would be a great blessing,and Una Councilwould have in their power a great means of helping the manufacturers, because if they acted with wisdom and sold the water cheaply they should soon be able to help manufacturers very considerably indeed. (Applause.) The meeting then ended.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1890
THE HAMPSTEAD TRAGEDY.

MURDER OF A WOMAN AND HER CHILD. STARTLING REVELATIONS. Inquiries made by the police on Saturday have con- firmed the identification of the woman who was found murdered near Eton-avenue, Hampstead, as Stirs. Phoebe Hogg, wife of a furniture porter, 141, Prince of Wales's- road, Kentish Town, and the supposed murderer has been arrested. The body of the murdered woman's baby was found on Sunday morning, at half-past six, in a field near West End-lane, Finchley, by a gipsy. The police were immediately informed, and Mr. Hogg subsequently identified the body as that of his child. The clothes were saturated with rain, but no external marks of violence were visible. The gipsy saw the body of the infant lying amongst some furze bushes just off Finchley- road. He at once called the police, and Dr. Briggs, of Child's Hill was summoned to examine the body, which was eventually removed to Hamstead Mortuary, and placed beside its mother. Dr. Briggs was unable to say , whether the child had been strangled, smothered, or , poisoned. The murdered woman is said to have borne a good character, and the suggestion that the miscreant, whose name has acquired such terrible notoriety in another part of London, has made his appearance in the West, may ,be said to be entirely discredited. It was ascer- tained that the murdered woman left her home in Kentish Town about three o'clock on Friday afternoon, taking her baby, Phcebe Hogg, aged eighteen months, I with ber.M a bassinette. She then visited a friend, a Mrs. Piercey (since arrested) living in apartments at 2, Priory-street, in the adjoining neighbourhood. From this point all trace of the mother and child was lost, until the finding of the woman's body as already described. Her husband, Frank Hogg, who is employed by his brother in his business of furniture moving, had left home as usual early in the morning, and returned in the ' evening. His mother and sister, who reside in the same house, informed him that his wife had gone out. Al- though she had said she would not be long away, no alarm was felt at her non-appearance, the 'belief being that she had gone to see her father at Ricksmanworth, as she was said to be unwell. It was supposed that she had decided to remain for the night at her father's house. Mr. Hogg sat up until two o'clock, but no information was given to the police. It was the custom of the house for certain tablots to be hung in the hall when inmates had not returned home, in order to prevent the door being locked. The landlord asserts that when he re- turned from the Brewers' Exhibition, about half-past eleven, Mr. Hogg's tablet was hanging on his bell, indi- cating that he was out. Miss Hogg, however, is certain that her brother had been at home for some time before that hour. Next morning Mr. Hogg left home soon after six o'ciock, and returned as usual to break- fast. Miss Hogg afterwards induced Mrs. Piercey to accom- pany her to the mortuary to see the body. It is asserted that Mrs. Piercey said she could not recognize the body, and on Mica Hogg attempting to touch it, Mrs. Piercey screamed, "Oh, don't touch her." It next became necessary to see the bassinette found in Hamilton-terrace, and this was at once recognised by I Miss Hogg as the one her sister-in-law had taken out with the child. a had apparently experienced very rough usage. The porcelain handle was broken, and the cprings I seemed to have had to bear a heavy load. There were marks on oneside as if it had been tilted over .on the ground, and a nut was missing. Returning home, the two women saw Mr. Hogg, who appeared terrified at what they told him. The party I then accompanied the detectives back to the polite sta- tion. From this period Mrs. Piercey was virtually under arrest. The police had meanwhile paid a visit tober heine at 2, Priony-st., which consisted of the ground floor, I containing a parlour, a bedroom, and kitchen. Them are two other floors in the house, occupied by several framilies. The oficers found in Mrs. Piercey's kitchen many signs of blood. The window was smashed, and the room disarranged, whilst some knives were found, , stained with blood, and what apparently was human hair sticking to them. The police theory is that the murder was committed in this room between four and five o'clock, and that the body was removed in the perambulator to the place where it was discovered. When formally charged with the wilful murder of Plicebe Hogg, and on suspicion of having also killed the baby, the accused is stated to have treated the matter with indifference. Some scratches are said to have been observed on her hands, which she accounted for by say- ing that she had been killing mice. At the divisional

div.head: PEASANT RISING IN RUSSIA.
div.p: PEASANT RISING IN RUSSIA.
ALARMING OUTLOOK.

A St. Petersburg correspondent says the private telegram received by the Minister of the Interior, gave an alarming account of the politico-economical disturbances in the governments of Kharkoff and Yeka- terinaslay. In the former place tranquility has not been restored. In the Bogodooksov district the peasants had refused to return to their homes, and 6,000 soldiers had been sent out against them, and the general in command had telegraphed for further reinforcements. At present there is a force of 9,000 men operating against the in- habitants of that one district alone, the people refusing stubbornly to give up their ringleaders and accept a full pardon. The peasants are prowling about in armed bands, attacking the houses of landowners and firing buildings, and pilaging and ravaging the country. The Minister has despatched a telegram abolishing all the rights of the peasants in the disturbed districts, and dis- solving all their institutions, such as the Mir.

div.head: BEN WELL MURDER.
div.p: THE BEN WELL MURDER.

THE LETTER FROM "THE COLONEL." MONTREAL, WEDNESDAY.—Renewed interest is being shown in the Benwell murder case, in consequence of the mysterious letter received by Birchall from Michi- gan, in which "the Colonel," as the writer signs him- self, confesses to having committed the crime. Mr. Stevens, a prominent citizen of this city, again recalls the fact of his meeting Birchall and Mr. Benwell with an American, whom they called "Colonel" at Morley's Hotel, in London, in December last, when the Colonel said he was Using Birchall as a moans of obtaining an end he had in view. Mr. Stevens does not know the Colonel's name, but believes it will be found in the register at Morley's Hotel, as he occupied one of the bast rboms and had plenty of money. Mr. Stevens declares he is con- vinced "the Colonel" will prove tt) be the murderer, and he has made an affidavit as to the truth of his story, par- ticulars of which he has submitted to the Minister of Justice in an endeavour to secure a respite for Birchall.

The " Colonel's " letter f:om Jackson, Michigan, is regarded as the clumsiest fabrication that Birchall has yet put forth. An examination of the handwriting, and comparison with the samples of Birchall's show a very general resemblance between the two, and in some cases, a very striking likeness.
