div.p: the levying of large sums under the head of Secret Service Money. MT. GLADSTONE reproachfully remarked,on Saturday, that the country had ceased to pay due regard to the growth of national ex- penditure ; and it is not too much to say that sope of this indifference is due to the fact that thlp has been no successor in the House of Commons to Mr. PETER RYLANDS. And yet he did not by any means confine himself to this important ques- tion. Speeches and correspondence alike testify to the wide range of his outlook, and to his inces- • sant activity. He had at all times some- thing useful to say on Temperance, Education, and Foreign Affairs, whilst he was a host in himself in exposing anything in the shape of "family arrangements" and departmental jobbery. The letters which he received from all kinds of people upon all kinds of subjects show how highly his aid was valued. He worked hard —too hard in the end—and the worry of two con- tested elections within a short time of each other, and when he had ceased to be in harmony with many of his former colleagues, undoubtedly, as his son says, hastened his death. Nearly four years have elapsed since that sad event—an event which was sincerely mourned by all classes irres- pective of party. The loss is still felt, for it was more than a local loss; and we therefore welcome the memorial of him which his son has furnished in this publication of his Correspondence and Speeches.

Mr. Gladstone THE fifth Midlothian campaign has i n this week been brought to a close Scotland. under circumstances which leave everybody marvelling at Mr. GLADSTONE'S un- exhaustible energy both of body and of mind. Ten years ago, when the ex-Premier had reached what is commonly called the allotted span, it was the Tory custom to speak of him as an old man, with a weakening mind, who had seen the best of his days. But they soon found that the old man was in every way too many in the House of Commons for all the young men they could pro- duce ; the absurdity of their cry forced itself even upon them, and they dropped it, never again, it would seem, to return to it, for to-day they are constrained to acknowledge that Mr. GLADSTONE at eighty is like an eagle that has renewed his strength. It is impossible of course that he can be physically as strong as he was fifty years; but there is every reason to believe that mentally he is stronger. Let critical readers study the addresses he has delivered within the past ten days, and if they are capable and candid they will be com- pelled to acknowledge that they reveal the fullest evidence of wide range, firm grasp, felicity of ex- pression, an unrivalled vocabulary, and easy strength in dealing with his opponents. The speech at Dalkeith, on Saturday, was devoted in the main to dealing with Scotch questions. Our friends across the border are a pugnacious people, and they are clever at what is called " heckling" a candidate. They have " heckled " Mr. GLADSTONE, but the process has simply acted as an intellectual stimulant, and enabled him to give satisfactory answers to objections which might not otherwise have occurred to him. The cry for Disestablish- ment in Scotland does not trouble him in the least. He takes his stand upon the statement of Lord HARTINGTON, made some years ago, to the effect that when the people of Scotland declare for Disestablishment the Church must be Disestablished. He believes that Scotland has through her representatives pronounced judgment ; and the fate of the Scotch church as an establish- ment, as well as that of the Welsh church, may be said to be sealed. As to the cry of Home Rule for Scotland, the Liberal leader remarks that the feeling is strong, but it is as yet an initial, un- formed and undeveloped feeling. He sees no unsur- mountable difficulty in the way; and regards it as an issue which, in the first instance, it is for the people of Scotland themselves to decide. The pressing question—the one question which over- shadows every other—is of course the Irish ques- tion; and Mr. GLADSTONE makes short work of the suggestion that there is any prospect of a settle- ment, except upon the basis of giving Home Rule to Ireland.

Monday's speech was delivered at Edinburgh, and may be said to have been addressed to the Liberal party as a whole. It contains a timely entreaty to Liberals who are apt to raise " test " questions, " and a protest against our rapidly growing expendi- ture upon the army and navy in a time of profound peace. Following on this, the proceedings of the present Parliament were reviewed in a style which is alike masterly and merciless ; masterly because it covers the whole field and leaves nothing un- touched; merciless because the indictment is sup- ported at every point by an array of facts which cannot be gainsaid. Mr. GLADSTONE shows that the Tories have had the cordial support of the Liberals in all the good measures they have brought forward, and that it is their own bung- ling and incapacity in introducing such stumbling blocks as the Parnell Commission, and the Publi- cans' Compensation Bill which have resulted in bar- renness and enormous waste of the time of Parlia- ment. In 1889, fifteen measures were promised in the QUEEN'S speech. "They passed five of them, and failed in ten." In 1890, ten bills were pro- mised, and two only have found a place on the Statute book. The record is lamentable, for it is a record of failure which is Karcely paralleled in the annals of Parliament. It is not to be denied that every bye-election testifies to the un- popularity of the Government, or that Tories out- side the House of Commons are themselves complaining of the mismanagement of their leaders. But what then ? Toryism is Toryism. Men do not gather figs from thorns nor grapes from thistles. The remedy will be in the hands of the people at the next election. Let them see to it that the block is removed by returning Mr. GLAD- STONE to power with such a majority behind him as will speedily clear the way.

AUTOMATIC GAS PURVICYORS. The Newton Commissioners at the last meeting of the Committee decided to adopt the system of supplying gas to those who wish to be 90 supplied, by.means of the new automatic meters, by which with the aid of a penny dropped into a slot, a suffi- cient quantity of gas can be turned on to last for two or three hours. There are many people in Earlestown who do not use gas, and no doubt the introduction of this system, will be an inducement for them to do. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. Sc W. DUTTON'S Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. DETERMINED SUICIDE BY A CHESHIRE FARMER. On Monday morning James Stanway, farmer, Middlewich, committed suicide by jumping into a brook. Deceased, who had been attended by several medical men tor some months, owing to injuries he had received by being run over,retired to rest about ten o'clock on Sunday evening. At half-past two in the morning his mother went into his bedroom for the purpose of giving him some medicine, but found that lie had left the house. A search was at once instituted, the immediate neighbourhood was scoured, and ultimately deceased was found lying dead in a brook containing some two feet of water, and which is situated about a mile from the farm. DAMPS, choice designs.—Garland's Lamp Shops, Earlestown and Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

-- It will be seen from the proceedings of the War- rington Town Council that the extension of the borough necessitates an increase of the Police force. There is plenty of work for the new brooms, and it is to be hoped that they will sweep clean.

It is stated that Professor Koch,!of Berlin, has at last succeeded in finding a cure for consumption. Good news, if true, for humanity,abd especially for Professor Koch ; he will be "the cock of the walk amongst medical men.

"More light, my lords, more light" is still the cry at Warrington. It is stated that the cause of this "effect defective is lack of pressure on the mains; but there is a growing impression that it wouldn't be amiss to put a little pressure on the Gas Committee.

Ryder Haggard had a good deal to say about "She ;" and there are expectations now of not a little being said before long about O'Shea. There is always a " she "in these cases, and as to the "0," was it not Byron who said : Both "Oh," and " Ah " alas! to her belong?

Canon Eyre seems to be in luck's way. He has been four years only at the Parish Church, St. Helens, and now he is promoted to the Rectory of Tiverton, Devonshire. There was a farewell gather- ing in the Parish Church Schools, on Monday, and the Canon was presented with a cheque for £l.OO. It must ba nice for a canon to "go off" loaded with gold.

The judges have decided that Mr. Conybeare, M.P., is to lose his seat on the London School Board through having been convicted in Ireland under the Crimes Act. It may be law, but it is not justice. Mr. Conybeare has fo,ught a battle for liberty in Ireland, and the ratepayers of Fins- bury should now be prepared to fight one in Eng- land. They ought to insist on re-electing the man of their choice.

"Truth" says :—A grim stroke of humour is being attributed to the Marquis of Ailesbury in Wiltshire. A large supply of hand-grenades for extinguishing fire had been ordered for the mansion at Savernake. After all the corridors had been sufficiently supplied there were still six of the grenades over. A servant asked the Marquis What should be done with them. His lordship reflected for a moment, and then replied : "I think you had better put them in my coffin !"

-- The remark of the Marquis reminds us of a recent conversation between a lady and a gentle- man concerning a wealthy old man in Warrington, who, although he is said to be coining money, is as reluctant to part with the "spondulucks" as though they were drops of blood. "Why," said the gentle- man, "should he be anxious to make pile upon pile at his time of life? He cannot take his money with him ?" "Just so," answered the lady, "and if he did it would melt."

The Home Rule idea is spreading; it has reached Australia, where our colonists enjoy some but not enough of Home Rule. It is proposed to divide Queensland into three provinces, each having a separate Parliament, with one central Parliament. The new movement is supported by the ex-Premier of the colony, and a considerable number of mem- bers of the Legislature. We must hurry up in this slow-going country, or we shall be left a long way behind.

There appears to be some casting about as to who should be the next Mayor of Warrington. But why shoald this be the case? Amongst those who have served the public well, and have not yet held the office, there is none whose claims are greater than those of Mr. Frederick Monks. The Tories themselves admit this. What then is the difficulty ? Is it that he is not a Tory? He is a Unionist, however; and we should like to know if the order has at last gone forth that " the union of the Unionists" is not to be maintained ?

"Snow, snow, beautiful snow," is something to be sung about, but it is impossible to appreciate it when it comes in October close on the heels of a spell of really warm weather. It helps, certainly to preserve the average—no coat one week, and two coats next; but, coming without warning, it is hard on those who never know what it is to have an overcoat. There was little snow to be seen in this part of the country, but in parts of Cheshire it fell, on Sunday, to the depth of several inches.

--- The quarrel between Mr.'H. M. Stanley and the brother of the late Major Barttelot seems to he anything but" a very pretty quarrel as it stands." There is something yet to be told about the doings of the explorers "in darkest Africa." It is now stated that Barttelot was not murdered but killed —shot by a chief because of his interfering with the Chief's wife. It is not stated that the inter- ference was of a shameful kind; but what was it that it should have been " kept dark ? " It must come out; and the sooner the better.

It is not unlikely that Miss Gladys Knowles will get a portion, at any rate, of the £lO,OOO awarded to her for breach of promise on the part of the editor of the " Matrimonial News." On Wed- nesday, Mr. Duncan disclosed the fact that a sum of £6,000 lies in the National Safe Deposit Com- pany's office, and this sum will accordingly be at- tached by the Official Receiver. It transpires that the tales told as to gifts of over £6,000 to two ladies were "utterly and entirely false."

An eight-hours bill for miners will be brought before Parliament, and, in due time, passed, for the , occupation of the miner is exceptionally arduous ' and dangerous; but working-men are not them- selves agreed upon an eight-hours bill for all trades. Mr. Howell, M.P., has resigned as a mem- ber of the London Liberal and Radical Union rather be party to the policy which the Union has adopted upon the subject; but the Executive have asked him to withdraw his resignation, as the resolution of the Union does not go beyond a "declaration in favour of the Government and Municir alities setting a good example as, employers by adopting, where practicable, a normal eight- hours days, paying standard wages, and permitting combination."

In Warrington the Trades Council is trying to influence the municipal elections; but a small meeting of a dozen members is not justified in speaking in the name of all the Trades Unionists of the town. It is too suggestive of "the three tailors of Tooley-street," who spoke in the name of "the people of England." There is evidence, too, that they have shown favour to some candi- dates for reasons other than the answers to their questions. This won't do; it is neither fair nor consistent. The Tory members who have been pulling the strings for the Tory candidates have their reward, however. Let them read the report of the Tory meeting in St. Austin's Ward, and they will see that Mr. llepherd, the candidate, and his chairman, Alderman Sutton, both characterise the questions as an insult to common-sense.
mas'

Working-men must be very:short-sighted if they think they have anything to gain by supporting the party of class exclusiveness and class privilege. It is the Liberals who have sustained the agita- tion for freeing the Library, and it is the Liberals who have put forward the proposal for obtaining new baths. It was the Liberals in the London County Council who passed the motion which strikes at " sweating " prices; but the Tory mem- bers of the Warrington Town Council, instead of supporting the same motion, walked out of the Council Chamber to prevent its being discussed even. It will never be discussed if Tories are returned to the Town Council. Let working-men have this in mind, and watch their own interests by voting for the Liberal candidates, who are all pledged to support the recognised wages in connec- tion with Corporation contracts, and the payment of Corporation servants.

On Tuesday Mrs. H. M. Stanley, who was accompanied by her husband, opened the new buildings ot the Boys' and Girls' Refuge, Strangeways, Manchester. The in- stitution has for twenty years past accommodated chil- dren rescued from the street. GENERAL Satisfaction commands the vast army of people who use "SUNLIGHT SOAP."—Advt.
LOCAL NEWS.
POOR RATE FOR CLIFTON. The Runcorn magistrates on 'Monday, sanctioned the levying of a poor rate of 10d. in the £ for the township of Clifton.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. His Honour Judge Ffoulkes held a sitting of this Court on Tuesday, when the business included one adjourned plaint, 209 original plaints, and three adjourned sum- monses. SHIP CANAL MISSION, RUNCORN. At this missien on Wednesday evening, the Hon. and Rev. R. Grimston, M.A., gave a magic lantern exhibi- tion, showing views of the Ship Canal Works. There was a good audience. FIRE AT WIDNES. A wooden stage, in the revolver shed, at Messrs. Mort, Liddell, and Co.'s works, took fire on Sunday, but there was a plentiful supply of water at hand and the flames were quickly extinguished. The damage is about £5O, covered by insurance. BILLIARD MATCH AT RTJNCORN LIBERAL CLUB. On Wednesday a number of the members of Wins- ford Liberal Club paid a visit to the Runcorn Club and a match at billiards, eight aside was played. The Runcorn players won by over one hundred points. The visitors were entertained to tea and appeared well pleased with their reception. IN MEMORY OF MR. J. B. IMISON. OF WIDNES. The sum of upwards'of £lOO has been subscribed for the purpose of erecting a memorial to the late Mr. J. B. Imison of Widnes, and it has been decided to place a stain glass window in the centre of the chancel window of St. Paul's Church, in which the deceased gentleman took a deep 4,nd active interest. The window has been ordered from an eminent London firm, and the subject will be "St. Paul." The necessary faculty has been obtained.

WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS AT RUNCORN. As well be seen from our announcement column the annual missionary services will be held to-morrow (Sun- day) in St. Paul's Chapel, and on Monday evening the annual missionary meeting will be held. The principal preachers and speakers will be the Rev. James Lewis, one of the selected preachers at the Central Hall, Manchester, and the Rev. Smith Spencer, ex-president of the South African Conference. Mr. Robert Shaw, formerly of Runcorn, will preside. RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOL EVENING CLASSES. These classes, which were recently commenced, have achieved a success the most ardent promoter could nst have desired to exceed, and Mr. Moulton, the head master, and his assistants are kept busily employed attending to the students. In order to give the pupils a greater interest in their work, Mr.Moulton gave a lecture on " A voyage Round the World" on Monday evening, the subject being profusely illustrated by lime light views. Mr. Bowyer manipulated the magic lantern, and the entertainment was highly appreciated.

WIDNES WELSH PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH. The members of the Welsh Presbyterian Church Milton- st., Widnes, who have been without a pastor for three years, have decided to ask Mr. J. D. Jones, of Llitlifaen, Carnarvonshire, to become their minister, and there is good reason to hope that the call will be accepted. Mr. Jones is a young man' not yet ordained, but he is a powerful preacher and one likely to be very acceptable to the congregation. The Church is in a flourishing con- dition. There are over 100 members, there is no burden- some debt, the coffers are not empty, and the attendance at the services is very good.

SONS OF TEMPEUANCE. At the usual fortnightly meeting of the above order, on Saturday night, a paper was read by Mr. Ed. Key on "Temperance Work." The writer dwelt on the necessity of more aggressive work on the part of the temperance party, all along the line, so as to arouse a healthy public opinion on this great question. Mr. Key made a strong point of their responsibility, and showed how much good might be done to the cause by individual effort. There was an interesting discussion after, in which the follow- ing members took part—Messrs. Daniel Bisbrown, Thos. Heesom, Thos. Cooke, and John Jones. Mr.Jas. Johnson occupied the chair.

SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN MUSICIAN. Mr. John Holford, conductor to the Runcorn Tonic Sol-Fa Choir, and musical instuctor to Widnes School Board, has just succeeded in passing the examination for the Advanced Certificate of the Tonic Sol-Fa College. This is the highest certificate attainable for practical work, and is highly esteemed in the musical world. In order to achieve this success, Mr. Holford had to display a high standard of proficiency in reading music at first sight, in writing harmony from ear, in the cultivation of the voice, in the elements of musicalcomposition,musical and verbal expression, the analysis of classic harmonies, and the use of the staff notation—a list of musical accomplishments which reflect upon him the highest credit. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sailkey-St., Warrington.—Advt. RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY. The first concert of the season will be held on Tuesday evening, in Runcorn Public Hall. It was originally an- nounced to be held in the Drill Hall, but owing to the illness of the wife of Sergeant-Instructor Player, this arrangement had to be abandoned, and the Public Ball engaged. An excellent programme has been issued, and the concert bids fair to be of a most enjoyable character. The principal vocalists are Madame Clara Sam aell, and Mr. Edward Grime, and the chorus and orchestra will number over 150 performers. The orchestral music will be a feature of the concert. In order that persons from Warrington and Manchester may reach home, a special train has been arranged to leave Runcorn at 10.40, to catch the 11.6 express from Widnes. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. Henry Beacham, an inspector in the employ of the Cheshire Lines at Widnes, met with a terrible accident on Pridav night. He was crossing the lines at the time the 9.30 Liverpool was arriving in the station, and when mounting on to the platform, his foot slipped and he fell back on to the metals. The engine and several carriages passed over him and he was terribly mutilated. Dr. Saul was quickly on the spot and rendered every assistance, and Mr. Beacham was immediately removed by train to Liverpool and conveyed to the Northern Hospital where he died at two o'clock on Saturday morning. Mr. C. Aspinall. the County Coroner for Liverpool, on Monday, held an inquest on the body and the jury returned a ver- dict of " Accidental Death." The deceased who was well known in Widnes was highly respected. He leaves a widow and four children. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey.st., Warrington.—Advt.

- FIRST Am To THE INJTJMID. Sincethe branch of the St. John's Ambulance Associa- tion was formed at Runcorn, the members have rendered valuable service to injured persons, and on Saturday last a human life was in all probability saved by a know- ledge of "first aid." A woman named Sarah Ann Bate, of Zion Place, was cleaning the floor of her house when her wrist came in contact with some broken glass, and one of the small arteries was severed. Blood flowed most copiously, and the woman was taken to the shop of Mr. Speakman, chemist, where she became unconscious through loss of blood. Superintendent Large who hap- pened to be passing at the time Wok the case in hand and by means of a cork and a bandage stopped the flow of blood, and then had the woman conveyed to Dr. Mc Dougall's surgery. The doctor expressed the opinion that but for the prompt aid rendered by Superintendent Large, the woman's life might have been sacrificed. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. 14 W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt.

SALE OF WORK AT RUNCORN. On Thursday afternoon the annual Sale of Work in aid of the Home and Foreign Missions, was held in Holy Trinity SchooLand there was displayed a large variety of useful and ornamental articles. The sale was promoted several years ago by Mrs. Preston, wife of the vicar of Holy Trinity Church, and has since been carried on by her with much success. That lady assisted by the ladies of the sewing meeting, presided over the principal stall, and the refreshment stall was in charge of Mrs. Cun- ningham, Mrs. Brigley and the Misses Stubbs and Tyris. The flower stall was provided by Mrs. Moon, of London. Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., had consented to open the pro- ceedings, but an important business engagement pre- vented him from attending or fulfilling that duty. Accompanying the latter of apology was a cheque for £5. In his absence the Rev. Dr. Preston delivered a speech, and declared the sale open. In the evening an enter- tainment arranged by Mi:s Preston was a groat success. EWBANIC. CARPET SWEEPERS,—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-St-., Warrington.—Adid. MORE WOUNDING CASES AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Benjamin Davies, 13, Midwocd-St., was charged with causing grievous bodily harm to Michael Brennan on the 25th. Dr. O'Keeffe said he was called to Brennan's house on Satur- day night and found him in a state of utter prostration from loss of blood. There was a wound on the right side of the head which penetrated to the bone caused by the mouthpiece of a brass instrument. The wound was a very dangerous one and it might cause deafness during the whole of the man's life .—The prisoner was remanded for a week.—Thomas O'Neil, Marsh-st., was charged with unlawfully wounding his son James, aged seven years. Mary Walsh said the prisoner and his two child- ren lodged with her, and on Sunday night after they had gone to bed she heard him threaten to cut them to pieces. She went upstairs and found the bedclothes covered with blood. Dr. Hutchinson deposed that the boy had two wounds on the head penetrating to the bone and his body was literally covered with bruises, showing that he had been violently assaulted. The prisoner was re- manded for a week. Now OPEN FOR THE SEASON.—Smart and Co.'s private Writing and Commercial Academy for ladies and gentlemen, at the Literary Institution, George-st., Altrincham. Open on Tuesdays only from sto 9 p.m. Writing : Gentlemen are taught a fine, bold, rapid business hand, and ladies an elegant and flowing style. Terms for complete course, One Guinea. Book-keeping : Pupils are taught how to open, keep, balance, and close a complete set of books by double entry ; and our certificate for protieency is given to each pupil. Arithmetic and mental calculation taught practically. Shorthand, Pit- man's system. Pupils will oe received on Tuesday next, at any hour from sto 9 p.m. No classes, the Instruction is individual. Card of terms and full particulars may be had at the Literary Institution. George-st., Altrincham. or post free from our Head Academy, 2, Brown.at,.. Market-st., Man- elsester.—Advt4

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1890.

UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH,WIDNES. On Thursday afternoon in this place of worship the Rev. M. T. Myers, of Rochdale, president of the United Methodist Conference preached an eloquent sermon to a good congngation. In the evening the rev, gentleman delivered a lecture on" Stanley and Africa." Mr. T. S. Swale presided, and Mr. T. snape, C.C., was present. Collections were made in aid of the Chapel Fund.

RUNCORN MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN. The proposed Seamen's Church and Institute for Run- corn, which has been under consideration for some time past, is a step nearer accomplishment. A site in Station-road has been purchased from Major Orred, at a cost of £4OO, and plans of the building and specifica- tions have been submitted to the committee and approved, and a start will be made as soon as ' practicable. UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURE AT RUNCORN. The third of the course of lectures on "'rue Problems of Wealth and Industry," was delivered in Bethesda schoolroom, on Thursday evening, by Mr. H. Llewellyn Smith, 8.A., B.Sc. There was a fair attendance. The spf &al subject for die evening was "Law Custom and Competition." with which the Lecturer dealt in an ex- haustive manner, and the usual class for discussion after- wards took place. There are a large number of books in the Free Library,bearing, upon the subject of the lectures, and every facility will be afforded to borrowers. THEFT EROM A BUNCOMq CLOTHIER'S SHOP. Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. Brim- drit and Major Hazlehurst, a labourer, named Peter Jones; of Rock Savage, was charged with having, on Saturday, stolen a boy's overcoat worth 18s. 61. from the shop of Mr. John Yates, clothier, Church-st. 'The pi- soner was seen by a boy to take the overcoat from inside the shop door and Mr. Yates being informed, went in pursuit, captured the man and recovered tlig overcoat. He however allowed the prisoner to depart. Afterwards P.C. Woodrow apprehended the prisoner as he was leav- ing the Barley Mow Hotel. Mr. Knowles defended and called witnesses to prove an alibi, but the Bench considered the evidence conclusive and fined the prisoner 10s. -

Mn. LEADAM'S CANDIDATURE. A public meeting was held at Sale on Thursday evening in furtherance of the candidature of Mr. I. S. Leadam for the representation of the Altrincham division in Parliament. Addresses were given by Mr. Leadam and Mr. Duncan, M.P. for Barrow, and a resolution condemning the present methods of governing Ireland was passed. SHIP CANAL MYSTERY AT RUNCORN. On Thursday, the body of a sailor, was found by a boatman floating in one of the locks of the Man- chester Ship Canal (Bridgewater undertaking) at Runcorn. The body, which was very much decom- posed, and which had been in the water for about two weeks, was conYeyed to the mortuary awaiting an inquest. From papers, found on deceased he is supposed to be Uharles Martin, a sailor from Guernsey.

NEW POLICE SUPERINTENDENT. It is stated that Mr. II igginbothom, of Rossendale, has been appointed superintendent of police for the Leigh and Warrington County Petty Sessional Division, and he is to take the position which was rendered vacant by the unexpected death of Mr. Superintendent Weir, which took place about three weeks ago after a very short illness. Mr. Iliggin- bothom is exp.ctad to commence his duties in the course of a few days. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston, Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New ZPaland, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner " 011 ice, by Cunard, GUIOII, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, "Examiner ' °NW. newsev-st.. Warrington.—Advt. _

BANKRUPTCY OF A WARRINGTON MAN. Mr. Registrar Giffard, sitting on Thursday, at the London Bankruptcy Court, heard an application for an order of discharge made on behalf of William Halford, iron founder, late of Warrington and St. Helens, and recently managing director of the South- wark Foundry Company, London. Two things were proved, imperfect bookkeeping, and a previous composition, and the discharge on those grounds was suspended for nine months.

EMPLOYERS LIABILITY. In the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Hawkins and Mr. Justice Lawrance, the case of M'Shane v. Baxter and Sons came on for hearing. This was an appeal from a decision at St. Helens. M'Shane brought an action for damages, under the litn- ployers' Liability Act, against the defendants, his masters, and was awarded £75. After considerable argument the court reserved judgment. SEE OUR ALMANACK, entitled " Heavenly Light."— Imperial Tea Co.—. Advt. PRESENTATION TO Mn. SALMON, OF WARRINGTON. The other evening the employs of the Singer Manufacturing Company in the Warrington district, at the kind invitation of Mr. Salmon, their late manager, met at his residence, Froghall-lane, War- rington, and partook of an eicellent repast. After the tables were cleared, Mr. Jones, of the Runcorn office, was elected to the chair and addressed the company.—Mr. Henshaw said he had great pleasure in presenting Mr. Salmon with a gentleman's smok- ing companion, on behalf of the friends present. as a token of their esteem.—Mr. Salmon suitably returned thanks. After a vote of thanks to the Chairman, the rest of the evening was spent in a social manner.

FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS. On Saturday night, a woman named Elizabeth Gornall. wife of John Gornall, living at 59 Judfield- st., Haydock, ;died under circumstances which necessitated the case being reported to the Coroner. The woman had been in failing health for about two years, and for most of thot time had been at- tended by Dr. Hayward. About 9 o'clock on the 9th inst. she was going upstairs to bed, when she fell backwards down three stairs on to her head, and inflicted a slight scalp wound. Medical aid was called in, and she was attended to but a few days afterwards she had a paralytic stroke, and died as stated, In view of the facts, the coroner did not deem an inquest necessary. GAS FITTINGS.—GarIand, Gas Fitter, 51, Bridge-st., War- rington.--.Acist. THE STOPPAGE OF A. ST. HELENS GLASS-BOTTLE

div.head: WORKS.
div.p: WORKS.

A private meeting of of Lyon Brothers, Limited, Peasley Glass Bottle Works, St. Helens, has been held and the decision of the directors to voluntarily wind up the company was confirmed, and Mr. Spencer, of the firm of Banner, Spencer, and Co., accountants, Liverpool, was appointed offi- cial liquidator. The works were stopped last Satur- day and the furnace fires are now out. Only a few hands are kept on to pack the stock and finish up. The old hands on receiving wages for the last time were considerably affected,and seemed scarcely able te realise the blow which has come upon the firm. Some of them have obtained situations at other bottle works in the district, but a large majority of the 250 men and boys have still to find work. CISIDRELLAS Rg-COVERED at the shortest notice.---J. & W DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt.

DEATIC OF A CITESTEIt CELEBUITY. Information reached Chester on Wednesday morning of the death of Mr. Enoch Gibbon Salis- bury, which took place in London. Deceased who for many years had resided at Glan Aber, Chester, was a Parliamentary barrister, and had represented Chester in Parliament as a Liberal for a short time. Ile sat as repr3sentative for Trinity Ward in the City Council from 1873 to 1882, during which time he became well known for his advocacy of questions affecting the velfare of the citizens. Deceased was seventy-two years of age, and a few years ago left Glan Aber,where he possessed one of the finest Welsh libraries in the country, to reside in the metropolis, in order to carry on his profession. Ile was a staunch supporter of Liberalism, and was well known in Cheshire and various other places in Eng- land. Mr. Salisbnry frequently corresponded with the late Mr. Peter Rylands and acted in conjunc- tion with him in political matters. In the sick room, as a disinfectant, use" SUNLIGHT SOAP: Advt.

the docks, deposed that as far as practicable vessels were I discharged in the order in which they were booked. They had no men at liberty until the 15th June, to discharge the Queen of the Clippers, whether the vessel had been berthed or not.—Timothy Mannion, gaffer of the gang who discharged the ship, said the gang worked proper hours and did their duty by the ship.—His Honour held the opinion that the vessel was not discharged in its turn, and gave a verdict for £25.

div.head: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE LATE MR. TIMMINS.
div.p: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE LATE MR. TIMMINS.

-- - A meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners was held on Wednesday night for the pur- pose of passing a vote of condolence with the family of the late Mr. E. Timmins, and of appointing his successor. Mr. J. W. Lightburn presided, and there were present Messrs. F: Speakman, C. C. Grice, Ran- kinson, Pritchard, Imison, Meadowcroft, Wiswall, Humphreys, Mellor, and Abel, W. Marshall (secretary), Lake (law clerk) and Barker (surveyor).—The Chairman in moving the vote of condolence, said in the death of Mr. Timmins the Board and the town had lost one whose sound practical experience had been of great advantage to them. As a townsman he had conferred a boon upon his fellow inhabitants by securing contracts in all parts of England, and providing labour for them, and the Bridgewater Foundry was a monument to his intelligence energy, and skill. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Timmins) was beloved by all his workmen, and he trusted that the sons he had left behind would continue to do for the town what their father had done.—Mr. Speakman seconded the motion, and remarked that Mr. Timmins had ever used his varied talents to the interest of the town.—Mr. Meadowcroft, Mr. Pritchard, Mr. Once, and Mr. Wiswall, also spoke of the character and ability 64t the deceased gentleman, and the motion was carried unan- imously. On the proposition of Mr. Speakman, seconded by Mr. Grice, and supported by Mr. Wiswall, Mr. flankinson, Mr. Humphreys, and Mr. Meadowcroft, the vacant seat was filled by Mr. Walter Timmins, whom Mr. Speakman described as the worthy sou of a worthy sire, and all spoke of him in eulogistic terms.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Brock and Mr. H. Gaskell, jun. VAGRANCY.—John Kelly was sentenced to seven days hard labour, for begging. DRUNKENNESS.—WiIIiam Kite, John Mitchell and Thomas Burns, were each fined ss. and costs for this offence. Sarah Jervis who made her 25th appearance was sent to gaol for a month.—John Dunbery, of San- key, for being drunk while in charge of a horse at Bain- hill was fined 10s. and costs. ASSAULT ON A CONSTABLE.--ChriStOpher Daley, Caro- line-street, was charged with having on Saturday night been drunk and assaulted P.C. Davies. The prisoner was abusing his sister, and the officer interposed and took him into custody. On the way to the police office the prisoner kicked him savagely on the legs. For being drunk the prisoner was fined es. and costs, and 40s. and costs for the assault. A GUILTY THlEF.—Alexander Crompton, Deacon-rd., pleaded guilty to stealinc, a cap worth 40. from the shop of George Louis Merkel, Widnes-rd., and he was fined 20s. including cpsts. ROBBERY FROM A FLAT.—Albert Newton, of no fixed abode was charged with stealing several articles of wearing apparel, worth 10s. from the flat Gertrude, whilst lying in West Bank Dock on the 30th September. He was also charged with stealing a number of articles worth 185. belonging to Owen Atherton of Winsford, from a fiat in Widnes Dock on the 6th October. The prisoner pleaded guilty to both charges and he was com- mitted to prison for three months.

PAWNBROKER'S CERTIFIC-ATETLHORTy Dodd, New Eger- ton-st., was granted the renewal of his certificate to act as a pawnbroker. STRAY lionsys.—William Wilkinson, farmer, Aston, was summoned for allowing six horses to stray on the highway at Halton. The defendant said a number of boys had caused the colts to jump out of the field. A fine of 6d. and costs was imposed. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. George Hines, Joseph Clarke, and James Jessamine, young men, were charged with being drunk and disorderly, and were each fined ss. and costs.—Mary Ann Glover, a middle-aged woman, was summoned for being drunk, and on promising to sign the pledge, she was discharged.—Matthew Schofield, a rough looking fellow, was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and disorderly.—For a like offence an old raan named John Ireland was fined ss. and costs ss. Bd.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY. —Before Mr, F. H. Gossage and Mr. E. K.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY. —Before Mr, F. H. Gossage and Mr. E. K.

Muspratt. DOGS AT LARGE.—For this offence a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed upon George Morris, of Ditton. STREET OBSTRUCTION.—Two youths named John Murphy and Thomas Gately, were charged with obstruct- ing the footpath in Albert-road, and were discharged on promising not to offend again. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—William Hewitt, Travis-st., was summoned for causing a horse to be worked in an unfit state,and Martin Connor, a youth, was charged with working the animal. It was proved by P.C. Radcliffe and Inspector Wilson that the horse was lame on every one of its legs and that it was with diffi- culty it could move along the road.—Hewitt, who said the animal had been destroyed, was fined 40s. and costs; the summons against Connor was discharged.
A DRUNKEN MOTHER OVEPZLIES HER CHILD.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, the Coroner, on Tuesday, held an inquest at Runcorn on the body of the infant child of Ann Boden, wife of Thomas Boden, who is living apart from her husband at 7, Nelson-st. The mother said she went to bed with the child on Saturday afternoon, and when she got up at seven p.m. the child was dead. When she went to bed she gave the child the breast, and it was lying on the breast when she (witness) went to sleep. She was not drunk, but she had told the off cers she was drunk. —Mary Nash, 11, Nelson-st., said the mother had had some drink, but she (witness) was sober.—lnspector Bowyer said he went to the house about 11 p.m. and found the child wrapped in some cloth and lying on the top of the dresser. He found no marks of violence on the body, but saw that the right side of the face and the ar were flat as if pressed down by being laid upon. The mother was suffering from the effects of drink and she told him she was drunk when she went to bed. Mrs. Nash was as drunk as she could be.—The Coroner said this was a very sad and disgraceful case. There could be no question at all that the child had been overlain by its mother, who was drunk. lie had on previous occasions impressed upon parents the necessity of put- ting their children outside the bed, in a cot. The practice of putting children upon the breast, when going to sleep was full of danger, but when the mother was drunken and unable to take care of the child, the danger was greatly increased. It was not in the province of the jury to return a verdict of man- slaughter, because the poor woman was probably very sorry for what had occurred, but it was a case of gross carelessness and disclosed a very horrible state of things.—A juryman : (Mr. Boyle) I 'think the child has been smothered.—The Coroner : Decidedly so.—A Juryman said Mrs. Boden was a woman of very drunken habits and on Saturday beer was being carried into the house all day. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidentally overlain" and requested the coroner to severely censure the mother, who was called into the room and the coroner told her that her drunken- ness and drunken habits had cost her child its life, and he hoped it would be a severe lesson to

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—A paper was given at a meeting of this class held last Friday week by Mr. Stanley Carter, of Overton, on the "Cost of Roy- alty." The essayist gave a full and descriptive account of the several seemingly exorbitant and needless sums (in some instances) paid to the Royal Family and to officers connected therewith, and then briefly referred to the costs of other Governments. At the close of the paper the following gentlemen discussed the question :—The President, Messrs. Dawson, Rhodes, and Robinson. A vote of thanks was ultimately passed to Mr. Carter.

div.p: PENKETII.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. At the usual weekly meeting held on Wednesday, the evening was devoted to elocution. There was a good muster of members, Mr. Snoddy presided.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

BAND OF HOPE.—A meeting of the Wesleyan Band of Hope was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Harry Brown. Recitations were given by the junior members, and Miss Brown also sang. Boy IN THE CANAL—The son of Mr. Alfred Leather, of Lymm, narrowly escaped being drowned the other after- noon. Whilst playing on the canal bank, near Lymm Bridge, he fell into the water. Fortunately, Mr. Ferris, hearing the lad's screams, went to his aid and rescued him from his perilous position. WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—The re-opening services were con- tinued in the above chapel on Sunday, when the pulpit was occupied, morning and evening, by the Rev. Alfred Freeman, one of the newly-appointed ministers to the circuit. There was a large congregation in the evening. The collections were in aid of the decorative fund. CONCERT.—On Tuesday evening a successful concert was eiven in the parochial schoolroom. There was a godattendance. The Rector (the Rev. G. W. Guest) presided. The programme, which was of a miscellane- ous nature, was much enjoyed, the various pieces being well rendered. The object of the concert was to inau- gurate a fund for the purchase of a piano for church en- tertainments. PAINFULLY SUDDEN DEATH.—A young man named Thomas Moston, of Rush Green. eldest son of the late Mr. Thomas Moston, of Whitbarrow, Lymm, died very sud- denly on Monday morning. The deceased had been in failing health for some time, but followed his occupation no later than Friday last. On Saturday, not feeling as well as usual, he went to see Dr. Williamson. The doctor attended him on Sunday, but Mos on gradually grew worse, and expired, as stated above, on Monday. The funeral took place on Tuesday afternoon, in the parish churchyard, in the presence of a large number of the villagers and relatives of the deceased, who was well- known in Lymm. The funeral service was conducted by the Rev. R. Coward. PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR.—The bazaar in connec- tion with the building of the new Primitive Methodist Chapel was continued on Saturday in the Drill Hall. At the conclusion of the days' sales the amounts realized by the various stallholders were announced as fOll @WS : Mrs. Thomason and Mrs. Jackson's stall, £5O US. I.d. ; Mrs. Evans and Miss Cross, £B2 ss. 3d. ; Mrs. Edwards and Miss Rathbone, £62 us. 3d.; Mrs. and Miss Groves (refreshment stall), £l4 14s. lld.•' the Misses Evans, Welford, and Chantler (toy stall), £l3 4s. 11d. ; receipts at door £4 9s. 3d.; do. season tickets, £8 12s. ; total, £231 Bs. 34-d. We understand that together with the amount realised by social teas during the past summer. the Committee have a total sum of £286 8s 3:1-d. in hand. The new chapel which it is propoed to build will be erected at an estimated cost of about £l,OOO. EXCITING CHASE AFTER A TRAMP.—At the Altrincham Police Court, on Friday, Robert Porter and his wife Mary Ann Porter, were charged before Messrs. Bulkeley Allen and J. Gaskarth, with begging at Bollington, on Thursday, and also with assaulting P.C. Ennion. That officer said that at half-past one on Thursday afternoon he was on duty at Bollington,when he saw the prisoners. The male prisoner had been into the shop of Mrs. Evans. He went to the shop, and Mrs. Evans said that a man had been into the shop, with no shoes or stockings on. that he was carrying a baby, and had asked for some shoes, stockings, and shirt. In sympathy she gave him a halfpenny. Witness overtook prisoner, and asked him to come back to the shoo. He replied that he would not go. He then struck witness and the female prisoner also struck him, the latter parleying with him whilst the male prisoner got away. He then gave chase, and run across some fields for about two miles. Coming to the river Bollin, the prisoner entered the stream and witness had to fetch him out.—The Bench said that they were quite satisfied that prisoners were regular tramps, and were very impudent ones, and that they were charged with' a number of offences, for resisting the constable, hawking things without a licenses and begging, and they should send them to prison for one month.

LIBERALISM IN THE ALTRINCHAM DIVISION. Last evening Mr. Duncan, member of Parliament for Barrow, addressed a meeting at Lymm, held in the Plough Hotel, in support of the candidature of Mr. I. S. Leadam for the Altrincham Division of Cheshire. The chair was occupied by Mr. John fly- lands, who was supported on the platform by a number of prominent local Liberals. On the proposition of the Rev. W. Evans, seconded by Mr. Ridyard, and supported by Mr. Duncan, the following resolution was passed I with applause :—" That this meeting heartily congratu- lates Mr. Gladstone on the success of his recent tower in Midlothian, expresses its intense satisfaction at the splendid victory achieved by Mr. Roby, at Eccles, and anticipates with confidence the result of the general election, and the grant to Ireland of power to manage for herself her own exclusive affairs, leaving Imperial mat- ters to be settled at Westminster, as at present."

div.head: INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.
div.p: THE INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.

The canvass of the inhabitants of Widnes, with regard to the question of incorporation, will not be completed until to-night. So far, however, there is a tremendous majority in favour of converting the township into a borough, and there is not the slightest doubt that the Committee having the matter in hand will recommend the Board to apply for a charter of incorporation.

div.head: CHEMICAL UNION.
div.p: THE CHEMICAL UNION.

The Chemical Union is now practically an accom- plished fact, and this week-end stock taking will be proceeded with at Runcorn and Widnes preparatory to handing them over to the Union. In order to enabre this to be done, a stoppage will have to be ccade in some of the departments. Pro- spectuses are expected to be issued in a few days, and it is stated that the capital is fixed at £6,000,000, the great bulk of which will be subscribed by the present owners of the works. Widnesians will learn with pleasure that Mr. E. Carey, of the firm of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., has been appointed general secretary to the Union. Such is the state- ment by a reliable authority.
ARTICLES OF 'ASSOCIATION BEJECTEDI
The Central News learns that the articles of asso- ciation of the company formed to work the pro- posed Chemical Union were presented at Somerset House, yesterday, for registration but were rejected.

div.p: WARRINGTON.

Sr. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH. On Sunday evening the Rev. J. Warnock occurded the pulpit at the above church and the subject of his discourse was "The Mountains and the Sea, or the two voices of liberty." .
FINEST KIEL BUTTER, one ' 1 tiling per pound.—lmperial Tea Co.—Advt.

RosEleNn CnowN Ilkunruns. The members of the above club turned out from their headquarters, the Rose and Crown Inn, on Tuesday night, 7.30. Owen and Thornton laid a splendid trail across country, and returned past the Dog and Dart back. They reached home at 8.30. Vernon acted as whip.

SPECIAL SERMON AT WYCL/FFE. The Rev. J. Young preached a special sermon in Wycliffe Church on Sunday evening, the subject being" Women's work for the world, as suggested by the life of the late Mrs. Booth, of the Salvation Army:' The discourse was an interesting one and was listened to by a large congregation. WORKING MEN'S SATURDAY EVENING CONCERTS. The second concert of the season was given in the Buttermarket-St. School on Saturday evening, the following taking part in the programme :—Miss E. M. Pigot, Miss W. Smith, and Messrs. Mills, Cook, Swindles, Whitfield, and Taylor. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. C. Nicolson. There was again a very large attendance. THE WARRINGTON HARRIERS. An inter-club run with the Bolton harriers took place on Saturday at Warrington in wet weather, over eight miles of country. A start was made at three o'clock, the result being a win for Warrington by 10 points. Bolton had the first man in G. Cliffe, but three Warrington men came next, J. Barlow being second, F. Hampson 3rd, J. Jefferson 4th. The Warringtonians thus maintained their record of never having been beaten in an inter-club run. ST. JOHN'S MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCiATION. The opening lecture for the session of this associ- tion was delivered in the schoolroom of the church, on Tuesday night, by the Rev. John Huey, M.A., 8.D., Nlanchester, his subject being " Why should the New Testament have been revised ?" There was a I very large attendance of members and friends, and the President, Rev. James Warnock, presided. In the course of an able and exceedingly interesting lecture Mr. Huey stated that among the reasons for revising the New Testament were the following : (1) Following precedent ; (2) words in course of time became obsolete and changed their meaning; (3) three centuries' study brought to light blemishes in the old version; and (4) there was now far more manuscript authority. The lecture was listened to with rapt attention, and its high appreciation was manifested in the hearty manner in which the vote of thanks, proposed by Mr. Reive and seconded by Mr. Basil Shearer, was accorded to Mr. Iluey. The coming session of the association promises to be very successful. CRITCHLEY, Practical Tailor, 13011-st.,Warrington.—Adrt.
EXIDIANITEL CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMRNT SOCIRTY.

At the weekly meeting of this society,on Monday, a paper was read by Mr. H. Landon on" Fermen- tation." In the first part of the paper he described the nature and construction of yeast cells, all that is known of their origin and power to ferment and their means of reproduction. The second part of the paper was devoted to fermentation as applied to the manufacture of alcoholic drink. with special references to beer, wines, and spirits. Messrs. Box, H. Gandy, E. Jewkes, J. Allen, and W. Parsons took part in the discussion which followed.

ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON. A man named William Appleton, 47 years of age, a fitter, employed on the London and North-Western Railway, was admitted to the Infirmary on Wednes— day evening suffering from a severe wound on his head. Appleton who lives in West-st., was follow— ing his usual employment near Dallam Forge, when it is supposed a bar of iron rolled off one of the wagons, striking him on the head. On inquiry at the infirmary last night it was found that the in— jured man was progressing favourably.

div.head: COCKIIEDGE MISSION CONCERTS.
div.p: COCKIIEDGE MISSION CONCERTS.

Another successful concert was held inthe above mission, on Saturday night. There was a large attendance, and an excellent programme was rendered. Mr. J. Willett presided. The following was the programme :—Violin solo, Miss Whittle; song, Mr. Butterfield; song, Miss Ellison ; recitation, Mr. Wilks; song, Miss Hough; reading, Mr. Butter- field; song, Miss Ellison; recitation, Mr. Wilks ; violin solo, Miss Whittle: song, Nlr. Butterfield ; recitation, Miss Hough; song Mr. Whittle ; recita- tion, Mr. Butterfield. Mr. W. Travis was the accom- panist.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.

The first meeting of the session of this Society was held on Saturday evening. The President (the Rev. S. Wilkinson, M.A.), read a paper entitled "Through the Dark Continent." After giving a brief account of the origin of Stanley's second expe- dition, the rev, gentleman dwelt at length on the explorer's journey after leaving Zanzibar, and des- cribed in a graphic manner the chief occurrences by the way. The Rev. T. Emmott, Herr Thornley, and others having spoken, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Vicar for his very interesting and instructive paper. THE OPEN AIR TOTAL ABSTINENCE MISSION.

On Saturday, though the weather was very un- favourable,there was a special meeting held in con- nection with this society, on the enclosed ground off Bewsey-st. Mr. J. Drury conducted, and was supported by Mr. Ned Lowry (Liverpool), the well- known temperance lecturer, who gave a short ad- dress. On Sunday, the usual meetings were held on the enclosed ground. In the afternoon Mr. R. Storey presided, and Mr. Lowry gave an interesting lecture, taking for his subject, "Drink and its curses." In the evening there was a very large attendance, Mr. Drury in the chair. Mr. Lowry gave another address," Will I or will I not be re- formed ?" The usual meeting was held in the Ragged School, Bewsey-st., Mr. J. Price (president) presided. Several persons took the pledge.

THE REV. PETER MACKENZIE AT WARRINGTON. The Rev. Peter Mackenzie, the celebrated Wes- leyan minister, occupied the pulpit at the Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel, morning and evening, on Sunday. Theie was a large congregation at the morning ser- vice, and in the evening the chapel was crowded. The rev, gentleman in the morning founded his discourse on Gen. xxii. 1-2, and in the evening preached from the text Philippians iii. 8. The col- lections for the day, which were in aid of the society funds, realized ..£2o.—On Monday evening, the rev, gentleman delivered his popular lecture on "The Proverbs of Sol3mon, and others," in the Bold-st. schoolroom. There was a large audience. Mr. Wm. Barlow presided, and the lecturer was supported on the platform by the three Wesleyan ministers, the Revs. J. Gunnell, Alfred Freeman, and Thomas Ross. The lecture was delivered in Mr. Mackenzie's characteristic style, and was very highly appreciated. At the close of the lecture the Rev. Thomas Ross proposed, and Mr. Starkey Smith seconded, a vote of thanks to Mr. Mackenzie. The vote was accorded with acclamation. A similar compliment to the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. Mackenzie, seconded by the Rev. J. Gunnell, and the pronouncing of the Benediction, closed the meeting. FINEST KIEL RIITTEIL one shilling per pound.—lrnperiat T,a Co.—Advt.

THE PASSION PLAY OF 1890. On l;lunday evening at Cairo-st., Chapel, the Rev. Frank K. Freeston, brought to a close the series of addresses on the Passion Play. The scene of the crucifixion was described in detail, reference being made, to the appearance of the chorus in black robes the horrible hammer strokes while Jesus was nailed to the cross ; the raising of the cross into its central position between those on which the two thieves were already extended, the agonizing group at the foot, the callous crowd around, the tearing of the scarlet mantle and the playing dice for the seamless robe, the piercing of the side with a spear, the breaking of the bones of the malefactors, who were then borne away, after which the priests, people, and executioners all departed, leaving Jesus alone with his friends. The Descent from the Cross, which followed, was a won- derfully artistic repetition of the celebrated picture by Rubens, all the various details being most carefully and tenderly reproduced. But he must ask his audience to imagine, for it was impossible to describe it, the terrible reality of such a cruci- fixion scene, the awful interest riveted on the cen- tral figure, the strained attention with which every I detail was watched and followed, and the inex— pressible solemnity which held that hushed assembly awestrucic for eighteen minutes. You forget to think of it as something acted, it was so real, so intense, so breathlessly still, save for a few words uttered at intervals. The chapel was again crowded to the doors. LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOC/ETY.

The session of 1890-91 of the Literary and Philo- sophical Society was opened on Monday evening by a lecture on" Electricity and telegraphy," which was given by the Postmaster (Mr. C. H. Kerry). The Vice-president (Rev. 11. Gibson Smith) occupied the chair, and there was a fairly large attendance of members. In introducing the lecture!, the Vice- Piesident remarked that Mr. Kerry's reputation as. an electrician preceded him to Warrington. The Hon. Secretary (Mr. J. Rymer Young) submitted the names of several candidates for election, and I mentioned that, with one exception, all the papers to be read during the coming session would be the work of members of the society. The Lecturer, who was cordially received, gave a very interesting lecture dividing his remarks under three heads, viz. :—First, the Morse alphabet, which was the universal signal by which telegraphy was carried on throughout the world; secondly, electricity; and thirdly, the telegraph as now in use. Mr. W. D. Jeans moved. and Mr. C. S. Burgess seconded, a vote of thanks to the lecturer. The vote was sup- ported by the Vice-president, who reminded the audience what an important part in the civiliza- tion of the world the invention of the telegraph had played. The great thinker, Bentham, said that In the world there was nothing great but man, and in man there was nothing great but mind ;" and it seemed as if the lecturer had given them a very clear demonstration of that famous saying. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Kerry, in replying, acknowledged his indebtedness to Messrs. Madeley, Selby, and Broad- hurst for their assistance in his experiments. NATIONAL LEAGUE MEETING. On Sunday afternoon a public meeting was held in connection with the Warrington branch of the Irish National League in the League Hall. Orford-st. There wao.a crowded attendance, Mr. F. Loughlin, president of the branch, presiding. Amongst those present were Mr. Tom Burke (Liverpool), Council- lor Flood, Messrs. Wheelan, Whitehead, Conroy, Brophy, Byrne and Donnellan, secretary. In his opening remarks the Chairman referred to the municipal elections, and urged that they, as mem- bers of the National League and Irishmen should support the Liberal candidates. That was not merely his advice, but the advice of the leaders of their party and particularly of the executive of the National League. A great deal would depend on the municipal elections and he considered them only second in importance to a Parliamentary election, which was perhaps very near at hand. He, there- fore, requested all Irishmen in Warrington to sup- port the Liberal candidates in their various wards not only with their votes but in canvassing and bringing up voters on the polling day. Councillor Flood afterwards moved, " That we heartily endorse the action of our leaders, John Dillon and William O'Brien, in the supreme contempt shown by them for Balfour and his coercionist courts, and we con- gratulate them on their escape, and their deter- mination at all costs to keep faith with our people across the Atlantic, and we wish them God speed on their errand of mercy." In moving the resolution, Councillor Flood narrated his experiences of a , journey he made a fortnight ago to the North of Ireland.—Mr. Donnellon seconded the resolution, which was enthusiastically carried. C lITCHLEY, Practical Tailor. Bold-it., Warrinzton,--Add.

div.head: IS A MIN A BAROMETER?
div.p: IS A MIN A BAROMETER?

It is stated that eighty-six per cent. of the. signal set- Vice weather predictions are accurate. This is but one of many instances which stamp the present as an age of progress. Our fathers had no indications tor foretelling weather except aching limbs, twinging pints, and pain- ful corns. These, though crude, were usually correct. The body is unquestionably an excellent barometer, and physicians often prescribe a change of air, so that the system may find an agreeable atmospheric condition. Weather changes indicates themselves by pains called rheumatism. Why bad weather should cause such pains is a mystery. Does the pain lie dormant in the system, to be made active only when the wind blows from some unfavourable quarter ? Rheumatism was at first thought to be a trouble of the joints, but all outward applica- tions left the cause unremoved. Now, however, it is universally acknowledged that "rheumatism is a fiery condition of the blood caused by an acid state of the system." This acidity of the blood which produces rheumatic pains, stiff joints, tendons, and muscles, is caused by kidney disease, which is the universal source of rheumatism. When the blood becomes surcharged with this acid, we have the acute form of rheumatism with its attendant inflammation, fever, and swelling of joints. When this acid, instead of remaining in the blood settles as a solid substance around the bone joints of the body, enlarging and impeding their free action, the result is chronic rheumatism. Rheumatism is called " Lum- bago" when in the back, " Gout "when in the joints of the feet, and when the Sciatic nerve is attacked " Sciatica." But whatever form it takes, rheumatism is the result of acids in the blood, which the kidneys, through in- action, have failed to remove, and the disease cannot be cured until the kidneys are put in a healthy condition. There is but one form of treatment, and that is to regu- late the Kidneys by Warner's " SAFE " Cure, and to "put out the fire in the blood" by Warner's' SAFE" Rheumatic Cure. These world-renowned remedies, taken by bottles in alternation, neutralize the uric acid al- ready in the blood, and prevent further accumulation. Mr. E. Routley, 8, Landseer Terrace, Battersea, London, S.W., was speedily cured of acute rheumatism by their use, and Mr. James Ferguson, 1, North Street, St. James's Street, Edinburgh, after suffering from severe attacks of sciatica, which the doctor and a course of mineral waters failed to relieve, was permanently cured by these mar- vellous medicines, 'which can be had of all chemists throughout the world.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
AN INCONSEQUENTIAL DEFENCE,

At Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, a Ship Canal navvy, named John Hookaway, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Walton on the 12th of October. After an officer had given evidence in support of the charge, the defendant, in an excited manner, said, "I admit having been to a wedding and having had a little drop of intoxicating liquor more than I ought to have had, but I was not disorderly. I met four police- men all together. and I only said to them that if they were doing their duty they would not be standihg together. I then said' Good night, officers, all.' I have characters to carry me through life—navy discharges and merchant service discharges, and I have never dis- graced myself in my life before. lam over 325 miles from the town of my birth." A fine of ss.and costs was imposed.

div.head: A. HORSE UNFIT EVEN' TO WALR.
div.p: A. HORSE UNFIT EVEN' TO WALR.

A young man named William Smith was charged at the Borough Police Court, on Saturday morning, with cruelty to a horse by allowing it to travel while it was in an unfit state. Sergeant Cheney proved the case, and said the animal was even unfit to walk. The defendant told him it was on its way to the railway station, and that it was to be sent to Liverppol to be sold.—lnspector Cox said the animal walked from Arpley Fields to the railway station. It was an act of cruelty to make the animal walk even that short distance.—Evidence having been given by Mr. Wilson, of the R.S.P.C.A., Mr Browne, who was for the defence, contended that the horse was on its way to the railway station when seen by the officers. It was to be sent to Liverpool to be slaugh- tered, and where better prices could be obtained than in Warrington.—Defendant was fined 20s. and costs.

div.head: AN OLD OFFENDER.
div.p: AN OLD OFFENDER.

At the Borough Police Court, on Saturday morning aA bef Alderman Burgess (in the chair), Councillor V ' , and Mr. Robert Garnett, a Ship Canal labourer, nThomas Farrell, was charged with the theft of a waistcoat from Messrs. Robinson and Co.'s shopdoor in Buttermarket-St. The prisoner was passing the shop- door on Saturday night, the 27th ult., when he snatched the vest from the nail upon which it was hanging. In- formation of the robbery was given to the manager of the shop, who followed the prisoner and took the vest from him. Detective-Sergeant Monaghan, who had been in search of the prisoner since the robbery, apprehended him on Friday. The prisoner said he was "as innocent as a babe."—Alderman Burgess said this was the pri- soner's 21st appearance at the Court, and it was absurd on his part to protest his innocence. He commenced his career of crime when he was only ten years of age. His first offence was theft, and for highway robbery he was subsequently committed to prison for a month and also sent to a reformatory for five years. He would now be committed for three months with hard labour.—Prisoner: It is hard, very hard.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MoNtikir.—Before Alderman Francomb, Mayor (pre- siding), Alderman Harrison and Alderman Sutton.

DRITNYNNESS AND DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—The follow- ing were dealt with as below for these offences :—John Loydon, in Farrell-st., fined ss. a.ld costs or seven days. William Prophet and Thomas Clarkson, both in Bridge- st. , on Saturday night, fined ss. each. Margaret Pearson, in Buttermarket-et., on Saturday, fined 2s. Bd. Thomas Daley, in Bridge-st., on Sunday night, fined ss. and costs or seven days. William Stokes and Annie Chester, in Orford-st. on the 19th, Chester was ordered to pay the costs, and Stokes was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days. PITCH AND Toss.—James McKean and William Beckett, two boys ,were each fined 2s. 6d. for gambling by playing pitch and toss on the 18th at Friar's-green. A ROUGH CHARACTER.—Joseph Warburton, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Turner-st., about eight o'clock on Saturday night ; also with breaking four panes of glass at the Black Horse beerhouse, doing damage to the amount of 14s.—Prisoner, who is a noted character, was committed to prison for one month with hard labour, without the option of a fine.

A GANG OF ROUGHS THROW A MAN INTO THE RIVER.— Michael Preston, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly, at 8.30 on Saturday night.—The case having been proved, the Chief Constable said the police received a report of the prisoner engaging in a fight underneath the iron bridge at Arplev. There were about half-a-dozen men at the place, and tha constable arrested the defendant. It appeared that during a squabble between themselves that one of the men was thrown into the river. At that time the police did notknow how serious the consequences of such an act might be, but the unfortunate man seemed to have got over the duck- ing. The other five who took part in the affair had been summoned and would be brought before the magistrates next Monday. At present he was unable to say who was the actual person who threw the man into the river; hut the prisoner was one who participated in it. Prisoner was fined 10s, and costs or the alternative of 14 day's imprisonment. Tnas"r OF MEAT FROM A BUTCHER'S SHOP.—A man named Thos. Mackie, was charged with stealing from the shop of Wm. Gill, butcher, Bridge-st., Ott Saturday, 612-lbs beef, value 3s. Bd. Mr. Hunt stated that the pri- soner came from North Staffordshire, and had only been in Warrington about three weeks. On Saturday, about quarter past nine, Peacock,who was Mr. Gill's assistant, saw the beef taken from the shop door, and on looking out saw the defendant walking away with the piece in his -hand. Peacock at once arrested him and took him to the Police Station. Prisoner was there charged with having stolen the meat, in reply to which he said "I am guilty of the crime." He was sent to prison for 14 day's with hard labour.

BREACH OF THE PRACE.—Peter Ward was charged on a warrant with committing a breach of the peace by fighting at Town Hill, on the 4th August last. He was bound over to keep the peace for six months on his own recognisance of £5, at d one surety for a like amount. SLEEPING OllT.—Catherine Taylor was sent to prison for 14 days' for sleeping in a shed at Howley on SundaS morning. DatTNEENNESS AND ASSAVLT.—Martin Hart was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Friar's Green on Sunday morning,also with assaulting his mother,Mary Hart, by striking her with a poker. It seems that Con- stable Wood, in company with another officer, were patrolling Bridge-st. when the defendant's mother went up to them and said she had been struck on the arm by her son. The wound, which was lin. by ho.. had been inflicted with the butt end of the poker. Prisoner was committed to prison for one month for having been drunk and disorderly, and two months fsr the assault, or three months in all.

HELPLESSLY DRIINX.-A man named F. Turner, was charged with having been drunk in Buttermarket-st., at 150 a.m. on Sunday. Defendant,. who was found by a Constable asleep in a helpless condition. on a door step, on promising not to offend again, was discharged. A SHOCKING CASE.—A very pitiful story was related to the Bench by Bridget Walsh, who was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., on Sun- day. The case having been proved, defendant said she was running after her husband because she wanted some money from him. He had sold the house up on Satur- day, and on Sunday he took the bed from under her. She had no fire to warm herself and children and no meat, and she was not drunk when the constable locked her ,213, but was upset. The Mayor said the magistrates were sorry she had such a miserable home, and they had decided to dismiss the case. Ttrusney.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (in the chair) and E. M. Crosfield. DinEinzEss.—Bamey Gandley was fined Is., for having been drunk and disorderly in flankey-st., on Xonday morning.

DRUNKENNESS AND ASSAULT.—James Jordan was charged with having been drunk in Bridge-st., on Mori- day; also with assaulting P.C. Lewis, whilst he was being taken into custody; also with having been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., on the 23rd June last.— Fined 20s. and costs, or in default one month's imprison- ment with hard labour.
A Ban CHARACTER.—Mary France was sent to prison for 14 days with hard labour, for having been tound guilty of prostitution in Butterniarket-st., on Monday night.

-A RUNAWAY APPRENTICE.—AIfred J. L. Whitman was charged with leaving the employ of Mr. John Holden, file cutter, before the expiration of his apprenticeship. An order was made for him to return to his work and pay the costs.
FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White, Alderman Harrison, and Dr. Gornall. __. .

VAGRANCY.—MichaeI Duffey, a middle-aged man, was brought up in custody, on a charge of sleeping out, the same morning. He was discharged with a caution. MAINTENANCE CASES.—David Armitage was ordered to pay 2s. ed. a week towards the maintenance of his son in a reformatory school, and Alexander Campbell was or- dered to pay is. a week towards the maintunance of each of his two sons in the same school.
OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Edward Greenall.

A TRAMP Commirrm—A youth named T. Jackson, who had tramped from Keighley, was charged with hav- ing been found on Saturday night on the premises of Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, Padgate, for an unlawful purpose, and was committed to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.

TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. Edward Greenall (in the chair), J. Charlton Parr, and W. Long. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were summoned for being drunk and disorderly : —John Dobson, Walton, 11th October, fined ss. and costs; Thomas Harrison, Appleton, 14th October, fined ss. and costs. Funions DRIVINEL—Fred Fryer was summoned for driving a horse and trap furiously at Preston Brook on the 12th October, and was fined ss. and costs.

FIRING CRACKERS,—Two lads, named Albert Massey and Wilfred Delooze, were each fined 3s. 6d. for firing crackers in the road near Wilderspool Brewery, on the 27th September. CRUELTY TO ANIMALS.—A boatman, named William Atkin, was charged with cruelly illtreating a horse, by working it in an unfit condition, at'Preston Brook, en the 15th October. Defendant was fined 20s. and costs.—Two lads, named William Haddock and Henry Britland. were charged with cruelly ill-treating a pony at Little Leigh, on the 4th October, by beating it with sticks. Each of the defendants was tined Bs.—John Summerfield, for causing the same animal to be worked in an unfit state, was fined 20s. and costs.
STRAYING Carne.—Mary Ann Carr was summoned for allowing two horses to stray on the highway, Little Leigh, on the 19th October, and was fined is. and costs for each animal.

DOG CASES —The following persons were fined for not having their dogs sufficiently muzzled :—John Buttery, fined Is. and costs ; George Kinsey, ss. and costs, and Richard Hamblett, Is. and costs. SLEEPY DRIVEIL—A carter, named Thomas Hatton, was fined 10s. and costs for riding asleep whilst in charge of two horses and a dray, at Seven Oaks, on the 18th October.

SCHOOL CASES.—William Spann was summoned for not sending his son Joseph regularly to school. Mr. Browns appeared on behalf of the Daresbury School Board, and said that the lad was twelve years of age, and had not passed a single standard, had only attended 83 times out of a possible 200 times. A fine of 55., including costs, was imposed.—John Dobson was fined a similar amount.

A SUMMONS A YEAR OLD.—A farm labourer, named John Foy, was summoned for driving a horse and cart without reins at Little Leigh, on the 7th August, 1889. The defendant said he did not know a summons was taken out against him until Thursday last —A fine of is. and costs was inflicted.

A WARRINGTON BITICHER FlNED.—Joseph Shaw, butcher, Bridge-st. was summoned for acting in con- travention of the dontagious Diseases (Animals) Act, by causing three swine to be driven through a swine fever infected area at Stretton on the 20th October. Thomas Cartwright was charged with removing the animals without an order authorizing him to do so. P.C. Bratt said he saw the defendant Cartwright driving the animals through Stretton in a shandry. He had no licence. Mr. Shaw pleaded ignorance that the order was in force at Stretton. The animals were killed the same day. Mr. Shaw was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for each pig. The case against Cartwright was dismissed. REFUSING TO QUIT.—A labourer, named William Law- son, was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and refus- ing to quit the licensed premises of William Miles, the Cat and Lion at Stretton, on tho 6th October. TILE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACT. Wright was summoned for acting in contravention of an order made under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, by causing four swine to be driven through a swine- infected area, at Stretton. John Waugh was summoned for removing the swine in the area without having an order authorizing him soto do. The defendant said that, owing to a delay in the transmission of a letter, he did not know that he was committing the offence with which he was charged. Under the circumstances each of the defendants was dismissed on payment of the costs.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

*,,* Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

WIDNES ST. MARY'S V. WEST LElGlL—Played at Widnes on Saturday, and after a splendid game ended in a draw, each side scoring 1 goal and 2 minors. RUNCORN JOCKEYS V. SIMMS CROSS ALBIONS.—PIayed at Runcorn on Saturday. Final score :—lockeys 1 goal 1 try 3 minors; Simms Cross Albions, 4 minors. SUTTON v. WIDNES A.—These teams met on Saturday, the result being a victory for the Widnesians by two goals, one try, and two minors to Sutton, one try. WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND V. WIDNES RANGERS IST. This match took place at Widnes on Saturday, and re- sulted in a victory for the home team by 1 goal, 2 tries, 1 minor, to 2 minors.

WIDNES A V. Sri-am—Played at Widnes. Craig scored for Widnes in the first five minutes, and Burgess shot the goal. Following closely upon this Harrison scored a try, which Burgess also converted; then the visitors pressed, but could not pass the homesters, who showed fine play. Mullinger got the next try, and Burgess failed at goal. Final result :—Widnes A 2 goals 1 try 2 minors, Sut- ton 1 try. WARRINGTON RANGERS v. Low GREEN WIGAN.—The Rangers journeyed to Wigan on Saturday, to play off their first fixture with the above club, but for the first time this season the Rangers found their match against the home team combination, their strong rushes over- coming the visitors' defence to the tune of 1 goal, 4 tries, 1 minor • Rangers 1 goal, 2 minors. Potts, from a free kick, landed the goal for the visitors. Ituwcons A v. WIGAN A.—At Wigan on Saturday, The ball was set in motion by the home team. Play was of anything but a scientific character for some time, and the visitors pressed their opponents, the result being that the former obtained a try. Nothing, however, resulted therefrom. Wigan then attacked the visitors' line in a somewhat determined manner and the result was an example of passing movements. At the call of half- time Runcorn had scored a try, and Wigan were without a point. No further point was scored in the second half of the game. Sr. HELENS RECS. 3RD, T.
