WARRINGTON 3nn.—The third team of, the Warrington club journeyed to the City road ground, St. Helens on Saturday, to try conclusions with the Recs. third. The home team won the toss and elected to play with the wind at their backs, whilst the visitors had to face both the wind and the incline. War- rington kicked off and the ball being returned Hurst followed up and scored a try, Rigby just failing to put the ball over the bar. From the drop out play was of an even character, neither side being able to score any- thing but a minor. When the whistle blew the score was Recs. 1 try and 2 minors, Warrington nil. At the restart the Recs. kicked off and the Warrington forwards made a combined rush to the home territory, where they suored, the place kick being successful. From the kick off Warrington again began to press and scored another try ; the place kick however failed. The Recs. now began to play better and pressed their opponents, Tur- ton at full back who was playing very, got the ball, ran a little, put his kick in and following up secured again and scored a try. The place was entrusted to Faram who made a good attempt but failed. The game thus ended in favour of Warrington score as follows :—War- rington 3rd-1 goal, 1 try, and 2 minors. Recreation 3rd,-2 tries, and three minors.

RUNCORN v. WIGAN.—It is now some four years since these teams faced each other, therefore the match was looked forward to with more than usual interest, and about 5,000 spectators were in the Runcorn enclosure, notwithstanding the wet boisterous weather. The toss having been won by the horns team, the ball was set in motion by Atkinson, but was quickly returned by Faulk- ner. It was afterwards taken to the centre of the field by Fialliwell ; but Abrams prevented any further progress being made for a time. Whilst the play reigned in the Wigan half, Crompton made an attempt to clear off with the ball, but was brought to. The Wiganers, who were decidedly the heaviest men, forced Runcorn back, the result being that a minor was conceded. Crompton kicked out, and the visitors were forced to concede a minor. The play at this juncture was stubborn, the visi- tors relying on their superior weight to overcometheir antagonists, and Mitchinson made a dash for it, but was smartly collared. Anderton received a pass from Mit- chinson, and made off; but Houghton brought him down in a clever manner. Gayter then had a look in, receiving the ball, and passing it to Abrams ; but Atkin- son prevented him from doing any mischief. A drop at goal by Crompton forced a minor, and from the kick-out Pendlebury was collared by Bullough , ere he could return. Pressure was relieved by Evans with a dribble, and a free kick for Wigan was charged down. Crompton, owing to the slippery nature of the ground, Caine to grief when he was in the act of putting in a dangerous run. At half.

div.head: TILE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1890.
div.p: TILE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1890.

time Runcorn had scored three minors, and Wigan one. Play was recommenced by Faulkner. and Pendlebury kicked into touch, thereby gaining a good deal of ground. Seddon got away, but his career was cut short, and Cromp- ton passed to Davies. By a narrow squeak Davies was only checked when near the line. After some loose play. Houghton gave a little life to the game by putting in a good run, whilst later on Crompton raised the hopes of the spectators by following suit. Halliwell was collared by Riley and Gayter, and at close of play the clubs registered 3 minors each. Runcorn kept play dangerously near the Wigan goal line for the last quarter of an hour, but the strong defence prevented a score.

Wiffeses v. ilaaeow.—Widnes journeyed to Barrow on Saturday, and met a strong team of the Barrow Foot- ball Club on the ground at Cavendish Park; but owing to the inclement weather there was only a poor attend- ance of spectators. Barrow had the same team with which they defeated Swinton last year, while Widnes were short of Plumpton, Brennan, Clarke, and Laws. Widnes won the toss, and Barrow kicked off against the wind. The Widnes forwards, from a scrimmage in their own territory, commenced a dribble to the home line, where they compelled Marsh to kick dead to save disas- ter. Widnes in turn concided a minor. Morris dropped , out with a long kick, and Marsh being unable to return, a scrimmage followed in the home quarter. Here Bar- nett, Todd, and Treweeke removed to centre, where Forster made his mark. Morris made a good attempt at goal, but the ball fell short. The return was caught by McGurl, and making his mark, Morris kicked a splendid goal from nearly the centre of the field. On re- starting the home team played up much better, and rushed the ball into the visitors' quarter, where Hartles prevented an easy try being obtained by kicking into touch. Smith next headed a dribble to the home quarter, when A. Harley . got posses- sion, but was brought down by Morris, Widnes again pressed, as did also Barrow for a few minutes later when Morris touched down. Morris dropped out to centre, where from a throw in, which was not straight by at least ten yards, A. Harley got the ball, and deposi- ted it uncharged under the Widnes posts. Milner took the kick, but failed. The try thus obtained was ack- nowledged by almost everyone to be wrong, and it is very probable that the Widnes Committee will appeal against it. The score at half-time was Widnes one goal and one minor to Barrow one try and two minors. On changing ends, Barrow being being favoured with the wind invaded the visitors' quarter, and compelled Hartles to kick dead. Widnes next transferred play to the home 25, where McGurl got injured, and had to retire from the field. Stubbs, who took his place, headed a dribble to the line, but Marsh saved just in time. Stubbs brought down Halley in a dangerous position, while Treweeke was similary treated by Hartles. Milner in the Widnes quarter got hold, and , ran in and took the place kick, a goal being the decision of the referee. The game ended with the score, Barrow one goal one try four miners to Widnes one goal and two minors. The following were the teams :—Widnes Hartles, back ; Foster, Moriss, and Peters, three-quarter backs; McGurl and Drummond, half backs; Smith, Whelan, Farmer, Hewitt, Johnson, Stubbs, Carroll, Gor- don, and Pearson, forwards. Barrow : Marsh, back; Laughton, Harley, and Milner, three-quarter backs; Barnett and Dickenson, half backs; Todd, Treweeke, Wetherall, Cowill, Leake, Jones, A. Harley, Bowker, and Garner, forwards. Referee, Mr. Thompson, Millom. WARRINGTON " A " V. ST. HELENS RECREATION " A."— The Warrington" A" team sustained their first defeat this season on Saturday. when the above clubs met at Wilderspool, before 1,500 spectators. With only a frac- tion of the regularteam available, the homesters' chances were anything but rosy, and when the teams entered the field, it was seen that not one of usual backs was present. Davies won the toss, and electing to play with the sun at his back, the Recs. started towards the pavilion goal. No return was made, and the home quarter flag was at once the scene of operations. A. Barnes relieved slightly, but it was only momentary, for some fine footwork by Matthews and Briers again harassed the Warrington de- fence. However, play did not stop here long, for a good dribble by Russell and Catterall,aided by judicious kicking I on the part of Heesom, removed the venue to the visitors' quarters. Davies, Catterall, and A. Barnes passed prettily and Isherwood made his mark in a favourable position but preferred to punt, and a possible chance was lost. Matthews and Little removed the danger, and from a bad kick by Newton the Recs, again assumed the aggressive, a minor being scored from a rush by their forwards. The drop out gave no relief, and a free kick was given Briers for offside tackling. Russell, Weisby, and Isherwood were prominent with a fine dribble ; but it was of no avail, for the visitors' forwards nearly scored immedi- ately after, a minor being conceded. A free kick to the Recs. was the next item, but the shot at goal fell short. Matthews intercepted a pass from Davies. and took the oval to the line, Heesom saving. The home team now wakened up, and Beaman and Davies were instrumental in causing the visitors to defend. Russell was nearly in after neat dribbling, and Newton kicked to the line. Deliberate offside play penalized the Recrea- tion, and Flees= had a rare chance, but failed to avail himself of it, and the danger was averted. Half- time arrived with the score standing as Recreation. 3 minors; Warrington, nil. Isherwood re-started after the usual interval, and Davies and Barnes were at once prominent. Beaman ran strongly to the quarter flag, and the forwards taking up the movement, the visitors were severely pressed. Exchange kicking by Eaves, Newton, and Mather ended advantageously for the St. Helens men, Barnes saving cleverly. Halfway was the scene of play for some time at this portion, but judicious kicking by the visitors' back division saw Warrington defending. A free kick was given Mathews, and from a rush by the homesters, Newton mulled and Little scored easily under the posts, the kick at goal striking the cross- bar. Heesom now went to full back, and Davies, Bea- man, and Welsby were prominent; but all to no purpose. Briers ran and kicked to the quarter flag, and the Recreation were still attacking when the whistle was blown for " no-side," the final score reading as St. Helens Recreation "A," 0-1-3 ; Warrington " A" nil. The following were the teams :—Warrington : Newton, full-back : A. Barnes, Heesom, and S. Beaman, three- quarter-backs; T. Davies and J. Catterall, half-backs ; Isherwood, Molyneux, Welsby, R. Barnes, W. Catterall, Russell, Creagham, Nield. and Wilkins, forwards. St. Helens Recreation : Eaves, full-back ; Mather, Briers, and Bolton, threequarter-backs, Mathews (captain) and Little, half-backs; Greenall, Naylor, Collins, Myatt, Chapman, R. Sidler, E. Sidler, Granger, and Jackson, forwards.

by Ashton, Knowles, Povey,and Jolley were each in tura applauded. A bout of passing by the Warrington backs raised a faint hope in the hearts of their admirers, but it soon collapsed when Jackson was seen to intercept, and with a judicious run and kick take the oval near to the half way flag. The two Bates again passed grandly, and Lawless, who had been comparatively idle during the greater portion of the game, had a chance afforded him, but like the rest, failed to take it. Lawless, how- ever, punted well to Jackson, but T. Jolley ever on the alert, flooredlliim in fine style. James Bate again passed finely to T. Jolley, but the Recreation forwards worked the oval to neutral ground, and although Fair Turner, Berry. Bandies, and Povey came away from a pack and rushed the leather past Jackson, the coveted point was not to be gained, Ellison coming up at the right moment and saving. James Bate crossed the line soon after, but the point was not allowed, and following this came some fluctuating play in the Warrmgton quarters, where Elli- son dodged Webster and ran in. A minor next fell to the homesters. Only two minutes were now'required to be played, and Warrington following up a long kick by Webster, carried the oval under the Recs.' posts, and Thorniley scored, Fair Turner placing a goal. Final score: St. Helens Recreation, 2-3-1 ; Warrington, 1-0-0. Teams :—Warrington: J. Boscow, back ; H Webster, T. Jolley, and P. R. Lawless, three-quarter backs; John Bate and James Bate, half backs ; H. Ashton (captain), Fair Turner, W. Povey, J. Jolley, J. Knowles, W. Ban- dies, B. Berry, J. Holmes, and J. T. Thorniley, forwards. St. Helens: T. R. Jackson, back ; J. Ellison, J. Seddon, and J. Fairclough, three-quarter backs ; J. Pilkington and J. Tudor], half backs ; W. Parr (captain,),, J. bolan, J. Pyke, P. Fildes. J. Dobie, A. Tickle, J. Mausedale, W. Dean, and J. Hankinson, forwards. Referee, Mr. Hunter, Manchester Rangers. ASSOCIATION. WESTON POINT Y. CHESHIRE ENGINEERS RESERVE.— Weston Point met a reserve temn of the Cheshire En- gineers, at Birkenhead, on Saturday, and scored five goals. the Engineers being nilled. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH ASSOCIATION v. HIIYTON QUARRY.—Tne above match was played at Huyton, on Saturday, in wreighed weather and on a poor field, the visitors winning by 6 goals to 4, and having repeatedly hard lines for scoring. Davies scored 2 goals, Meiklejohn (1), Clibborn (1), Parr (1), the home full back putting the sixth through. Ali the visitors played well with the exception of the inside right, this being the only weak spot of the team. For the losers, Whiting, Jones and Barton played best. The Parish Church have now played 6 matches, won 5, lost 1, scoring 29 goals to their oppo- nents 9.

favour of improved baths, and he thought it would be a good thing if they had an inexpensive bath at that end of the town wherein lads could go and bathe. He was in favour of corporation contracts being given as far as possible to local tradesmen, and, as for the gas, he thought it was now time that they should have it cheaper than it had been. (Applause.) Mr. Titchett having replied to one or two questions the resolution was carried with acclamation. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to aclose. ST. AUSTIN'S WARD: MR. HEPHERD'S CANDIDATURE. A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. James Hepherd, who contests this Ward in the Conservative interest, was held in the Holy Trinity Schools, Museum- st., on Wednesday evening. Alderman Sutton presided, and there was a large number who supported him on the platform, in addition to the candidate.—The Chairman read a letter which had been sent to Mr. Hepherd by the , United Trades' Council, asking if he would vote, if elected, for all work and contracts being given to those firms only who paid the recognised rate of wages to their workmen; whether he would vote tor an advance of wages to all able-bodied workmen who received less than 20s. a week, and whether he would vote in favour of the workmen of the Corporation being allowed holidays every year, arid receive wages for the same,the number of holi- days to be the same as allowed to the highest officials of the Corporation. The Chairman, in commenting on this letter, remarked that he considered it was an insult to the intelligence and commonsense of the Tory candi- dates, for he believed it had been sent to most of them. Councillor LRWIS VOISEY moved a resolution to the effect that Mr. HEPHERD was a fit and proper person to repre- sent that ward in the Town Council. Mr. HENRY FAlR- cLounn seconded, and it was carried unanimously. Mr. HEPHERD then briefly addressed the meeting. He said during the last twelve months he had endeavoured to the best of his ability to do his duty, and ifbe was again returned, he could assure them he would follow out the same programme. Referring to the letter from the Trades Council, he said he objected strongly to go into the council, with his hands tied; and he would not do it. He thought it was an insult to a candidate to have such a letter addressed to him, and his reply to it was, as he stated before, that he was determined not to go to the Council tied many way. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the chairman, on the proposition of Mr. J. Fat ncLonort, seconded by Mr. W. OWEN, brought the meeting to a close. LATCHFO RD WARD.—MEETING IN SUPPORT OF

div.head: WARRINGTON V. ST. HELENS RECREATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. ST. HELENS RECREATION.

The first meeting of these clubs this season took place on Saturday at St. Helens. That the meeting was eagerly anticipated could be evinced from the fact, despite the damp state of the weather, fully eight thous- and lined the arene, when the team entered at 3.30. St. Helens played their usual combination, not a single indi- vidual being absent, but unfortunately the same could not be said for Warrington, several of their most promi- nent players being absent. ' Losing the toss, Warrington started against the wind and sun, Fair Turner's kick off being met by Dolan, whose paltry response found John Bate dribbling to the Recreation lines. Vigorous attempts were made by the Warringtonians to evade a defence, but a lucky kick by Seddon cleared, Boscow responding with an excellent kick to the quarter flag. Warrington by the aid of the good combination of their forwards stilt attacked, and a chance by T. Jolley was ingloriously missed. Dolan threw across to Seddon, and a powerful punt caused an invasion into Warrington quarters. Webster, James Bate, Turner and Ashton tried hard to obtain their original position, and although the visitors managed to reach the quarter flag in one essay, it was not to be, for some fine play by Ellison and Pyke forced the game at the Warrington line. The defence was stubborn, Boscow repeatedly clearing. Turner and Holmes literally forced a way through the home backs, but the greasy nature of the ball, coupled with the state of the ground, wllich was an inch deep under water, prevented a splendid chance. So far Warrington had exhibited the better football, their footwork and short passing having been excellent, but it was now the homesters' turn, and Pyke and Sed- don exchanging kicks with Boscow and T. Jolley, ulti- mately ended in Jackson making his mark from a return by the Warrington custodian and Seddon with a brilli ant kick sent the oval sailing over the Warrington cross- bar. This was a staggerer to the 1,500 visitors' suppor- ters, who called not in vain at their team for renewed exertions. Turner again started from centre, and War- rington again showed remarkable dash. Each forward played brilliantly, and Berry from a line out:carried play to the home lines, the visiting centre missing a splendid opening from a line out. It was evidently not Warring- ton's day out, for St. Helen's changed the venue to the half way flag, Webster putting in a clever save. Bate stole away from a pack and evading Seddon, a brilliant passing movement by John Bate and T. Jolley was lost by the latter failing to hold the slippery oval. Not so with the Rec's., for fortune seemed to shine on them whatsoever they took in hand, and although Lawless, Webster, and James Bate each in turn tried hard to stave off a vigorous onslaught of the heavy home forwards, Boscow m his endeavour to clear had his kick charged and Ellison gained a some- what easy try. No sooner had Seddon missed at goal than his services were again required by Pyke, who from some loose play, notched a try near the posts, and Seddon this time placed a goal. The two Bates showed up on the restart with some beautiful transfers, and Thorniley and Holmes assisting the movement, the last named failed to hold the oval five yards from the line, and the chance was lost. Webster next put in a fine run to Jackson, who collared finely, and half time arrived with the score as :—St. Helens Recreasion, 2-1-0; War- rington, nil. With such a heavy score against them, Warrington entered on the second half with the hope that victory would yet be theirs, but the prospects of at- taining their desires received a severe check when Fildes, direct from the kick off, ran in near the corner flag, Sed- don almost landing a goal from the difficult place. The drop out was suppleinented by a long kick by Fair Turner, and Jackson being collared, for a few minutes play hovered dangerously near the St. Helens posts. Repeated endeavours to cross the line by the visitors' half backs were frustrated, and Pilkington and Ellison with well judged runs cleared, and half way was the scene of operations. Holmes put in a good run, and grand work

div.head: WARRINGTON ELECTIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON ELECTIONS.

ST. AUSTIN'S WARD.—MR. TITCHETT'S CANDIDATURE. There was a well attended meeting in the Working- men's Mission, Bank Quay, on Tuesday evening in support of Mr. Titchett, the Liberal candidate for St. Austin's Ward. Mr. Julian Winser presided, and amongst others present were the Rev. W. Graham, Councillor H. Roberts, Councillor Shaw-Green,Councillor T. Flood, Mr. J. Walker, Mr. Kiernan,Mr. W. Roberts, Mr. J. Hayward, Mr. J. Salt, Mr. S. Dunbobbin, and others. The CHAIRMAN said he hoped all there would make up their minds to give efficient help on the polling day. They were really most fortunate in their candidate. He had a good many special qualifications, amongst which was an intimate knowledge of house and other property, and also the great interest he took in sanitary matters. They also knew Mr. Titchett was in favour of temper- - ance and that was a great thing. (Applause.) It was a great wonder to him (the chairman) that members of Town Councils had consented to act so long without having control of the liquor traffic in any way. That traffic was the great disturbing element, and though the Town Council was reponsible for the good order of the borough yet they had not the slightest control over the number of public houses that might be thrust upon them. That seemed one of those strange anomalies one could scarcely understand. (Hear, hear.) The time of the police was largely taken up in looking after that traffic, and as the police were paid out of the rates that made the anomAly all the greater. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Titchett was a thoroughly practical business man and that was a qualification very necessary in a town councillor and the more they had of that element the better it would be for the Town Council. Referring to the public library the chairman added that he would be glad to see it opened on Sundays; it would be much better to have it open on Sunday than public houses. (Applause.) Touching upon the baths question he expressed the opinion that public wash-houses would be of advantage to the town (Applause.) Mr. Joirx WALKER remarked that the Chairman of the Conservative party (Mr. R. Pierpoint) had said that politics were introduced into those elections and they had to deal with the fact. He was glad that Mr. Pier- point had put himself in that clear position, because the Conservatives, when trying to arrange those compro- mises, which in his (Mr. Walker's) opinion had been so disastrous to the town as a whole, (hear, hear) said it was not a matter of politics at all. He asked them to go back to last year when the Tories, in face of an under- standing that had been come to, opposed two of the most useful members of the Town Council—Mr. F. A. Roberts and Mr. John Platt. He wanted them to say they accepted Mr. Pierpoint's challenge, and, having a good man, that they were willing to fight for that good man because he was a good Liberal. (Applause.) There was no escaping the fact that municipal politics were the politics of the poor, and the working classes who had votes and intelligence were letting it be seen that they intended to use their votes for their own advantage. (Applause.) In regard to this he called their attention to the treatment meted out by the Tory members of the Town Council to a resolution to be proposed by Council- lor Flood, a working-man and a representative of work- ing-men. The Tory members of the Town Council did not honestly face the issue raised by that resolution, but got up and walked out of the room to prevent it even being discussed. He asked if that was not an insult to every working-man in Warrington. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He was glad they recognised that fact, and he wanted them to act accordingly as far as that election was concerned. alluding to the intercepting depots, Mr. Walker said the time had come when they could be no longer ignored, and if the nuisance they caused could not be remedied they would have to be removed. (Hear, hear.) In regard to the scheme for improved baths, he said the halfpenny in the £ that had been saved on the proposed increase of id. in the £ on the library rate would in itself be sufficient to pay the way of the baths when the scheme was taken up. The libmry question itself was about settled, that was if the Library Com- mittee would act up to their engagements, and, he might say, up to their instructions. He had, however, heard that at least one member of the Library Committee had said that the additional halfpenny was not quite enough, that they did not know whether they would be able to free the library, but if the ratepayers made it quite clear that they were Hetermined the library should be absolutely free it would soon be made so. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Walker next referred to the undesirability of having men connected with the liquor trade on the Watch Com- mittee, and he added that by returning Mr. Titchett they would help towards getting a Watch 'Committee which was above reproach (Applause.) Mr. KIERNAN moved a resolution pledging the meeting to support the candidature of Mr. Titchett, and he said that he was quite willing to go with the Liberal party even if they shut up all the public houses in Warrington including his own. (Applause.) Mr. W. ROBERTS, in seconding the resolution, spoke highly of the qualifications of Mr. Titchett, and severely condemned the efforts of the Tories to blacken his charac- ter as a candidate. The Rev. W. GRAHAM also spoke highly of Mr. Titchett. He added that the manner in which some of the mem- bars of the Town Council had treated Councillor Flood's resolution was shameful, and he considered it was time a few inure working-men were lifted up to the honour- able position of Town Councillor. (Applause.) Councillor H. RonEaTs, in supporting the resolution, said that if they had had a few more strong men in the Town Council they should not have had ex-P.S. Shaw kicked oftt of the police force. (Hear, hear). The more he (Mr. Roberts) had thought about that, and the more fully he had gone into the details the more convinced he was that the treatment P.S. Shaw had received was simply disgraceful to all concerned. (Hear, hear, and applause.) From the way in which his efforts and the efforts of those who supported him in the matter had been received, he was convinced that, if a poll could possibly be taken on that one question in War- rington to-day, an over-whelming majority would denounce the action of the Watch Committee and those who instigated them. (Hear, hear). But the end was not yet. If they went back to the Town Council at all, they should ',o back reinforced by public opinion on that subject, and if it were possible to get any butter out of the dog's mouth, it should be got. (Applause.) Mr. Roberts next condemned the heavy expenditure on corporation deputations which he said had amounted to nearly £4OO between November last year and October this year, and he also alluded to a bill for £ll that had been passed by the Committee, £5 of which was for spirits, drinks, and cigars. (Laughter.) He held that a section of the Town Council which out of £ll required nearly £5 for liquors and sundries, was a section that ought to be eliminated from the Council at the earliest possible moment. (Applause.) Councillor SHAW-GREEN supported the resolution, and, speaking with regard to the cost of deputations, said this had had been unusually heavy during the past year in consequence of the passing of the Improvement Act. As for the bill of £ll that was incurred in connection with the recent visit of the Government Commissioner. Mr. TTTCHETT, on risin,g to address the meeting, was cordially received. With regard to sanitary matters he said that, even after the expenditure of some thousands of pounds. these were still in an unsatisfactory condition. He did not wish to gq back to the old system with all its disadvantages, but he thought there was still room for much improvement. (Hear, hear.) Speaking in reference to street making Mr. Titchett said he approved of a plan of deferred payments by the owners of houses for the making of the streets. He thought some discretionary , power should be left in the hands of the borough trea- surer so that a man who had perhaps built one or two houses might be able to turn his hand before having to meet the bill for making the street. On the baths ques- tion he was quite in accord with what had been said in

div.head: MR. S. B. STRINGER.
div.p: MR. S. B. STRINGER.

- - A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. S. B. Stringer, who is contesting this Ward in the Liberal in- terest was held in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, Knutsford-road, an Tuesday evening. Councillor Pier- point presided, and he was supported on the platform by the candidate, the R:V. C. Moore. Messrs. W Twiss, J. Walker, J. Strange, W. Gipaye, J. Clayton, and J. Gandy, (Liberal registration agent). There was a mod- erate attendance.

The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings,after refer- ring to the number of years which had elapsed without there having been a contest in that Ward, said so far as Mr. Ashton, who at present represented them, was con- cerned, he had not a word to say against him from a personal point of view. He had known him all his life, and he had always found him to be a true and honest Englishman. But they had then something more than personal matters to consider, and they were opposing him because they believed he did not represent them hi the manner they had a right to expect of their represen- tative. They were then met as Liberals, but Councillor Ashton was a Tory, and there was no disguising the fact that they were fighting politically—but this they could not help. Now there was a chance for victory in Latch- ford Ward, they had brought out a candidate whom they thought was better from every point of view than their present representative was. Mr. Ashton, as they knew, was a licensed victualler,and he thought the licensed vic- tuallers of Warrington had far more than their fair share of representation in the Town Council. He would like to see the workmen better represented, and some of the ! licensed victuallers' and brewers' interest transferred to the working-men. (Applause.) In their condidate they had a thoroughgood specimen of a working-man, 9. man who by his own efforts and handiwork had raised himself from the position of having to earn hisdaily bread to one in which he could enjoy the results of his labour, and on ! that account he (the speaker) could recommend him to the electors ot that Ward. (Applause.) Mr. Twiss then proposed a resolution to the effect that Mr. Stringer was a fit and proper person to represent Latchford Ward. In doing so he said he would not at- tempt to propose Mr. Stringer unless he had the greatest confidence in him. To him life was serious ; the business of life was serious, and they wanted serious men who took a serious view of the responsibilities of life in the ordinary concerns, and the municipal concerns, as well as the private concerns of individuals personally con- sidered to represent them. The change that would take place in the representation of the ward, if they returned Mr. Stringer, would entail neither suffering or loss. He had nothing to say personally against their present re- presentative ; but he had something to say against him as their representative in the Council Chamber. He thought he was neither qualified intellectually, morally, or physically for the position, for his days had gone by; and he would be much better fitted by a comfortable arm chair. (Laughter and applause.) The Rev. E. MOORE, in seconding the resolution, said he quite agreed with what was stated in the candidate's address that they had not regarded the present repre- sentative with anything like satisfaction ; and he felt disposed to congratulate himself somewhat that there was a prospect—and he had been a burgess of that ward for about nine years—of his being able to exercise his municipal right and show whom he would like to have as his representative in the Town Council. He under- stood that Latchford had three representatives in the Council, two of whom were directly occupied in the drink traffice, and the other was a tanner. Well, now, although he would not say for a moment that any trade that was considerable in the town ought not to have its proper representatives on the governing body of the town, yet he did say that two who were in the same business out of three in the same ward were two many • If he had his own way, he would object, like Mr. Twiss 1 to have any man engaged in the liquor traffic, as one o his rulers, whether in Municipal or Imperial affairs, and he congratulated himself that lie would have, on Satur- day an opportunity of showing—whether successfully or not—that he objected to be represented by two publi- cans nut of the three representatives of that ward. (Ap- plause.) Ho meant to say that tfie result of having per- sons ruling the town who were interested in the sale of drink must be disastrous. It was disastrous to Warring- ton ; it ruled the ToSim Council, and it ruled the com- mittees. Again, he averred that for a man to be on the Watch Committee—and tins Committee had the control of the police—who was. himself directly interested in the liquor traffic, was nothing short of a scandal ; because, as he said, the Watch Committee had the charge of the public looked to to public-houses It was a police,wat e h anda d it e wasal w with he thpeOlpiCuebltich viola- tion, of what was understood in all respectable councils, of a kind of law that all persons who were directly in- terested in the driTilc traffic ought not to have a place on the Watch Committee. After dwelling on the sanitary arrangements of the town, .in particular on the removal of refuse and the Intercepting Depots. Mr. GLEAVE supported the resolution, and spoke in eulogistic terms of. the candidate, and said he was fully qualified to be their representative. The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously.

Mr. STRINGER, who, on rising to address the meeting was received with prolonged applause, said he must first confine his remarks on his past life. He commenced work at nine years of age, and kept at it until 31 years ago, and he now found himself designated a gentleman. (Laughter.) Well, if he was a gentleman it was through his own industry for lie could not remember anyone ever having given him one sovereign, and if he was called a gentleman he wished to say that night that he hoped to sustain the designation throughout the campaign by every word he uttered and by all his actions. (Applause.) He did not say a word of disrespect about his opponent, for, like many of them, he did not know him. (Laugh- ter.) He (Mr. Stringer) had not thrust himself upon them as a candidate, and he had not sought the position in the slightest degree. Some of their leading men he might tell them, like David in olden times, laid violent hands upon him as David did with Uriah, and they had pushed him to the front of the battle. (Laughter.) He, however, did not think their leaders had the same object in view as David had; at tine same time he did not think they intended to put him to the front to be knocked down. But if he should be knocked down, if he had a spark of life left in him he would tell them that he would rise again ; he would get up, and perhaps face his opponents again with new energy and vigour. (Ap- plause.) He meant to say that a man who was sent to the Council should go there to work; and if they would not find him (Mr. Stringer) work to do, he would find it for himself in trying to lift those who were down in the world, and in endeavouring to lift the moral, spiritual. and physical condition of his surroundings to a higher level. iApplause.) He was not so narrow on things that some people called divine as some persons were. Thera were some who regarded things belonging to churches and chapels as sacred and divine; and who seemed to think the respensible part of their life should be spent in connection with spiritual matters. He was in much I sympathy with such persons, but he believed that those things which belonged to the welfare of the body, of the physical condition, were divine alse. Hewas a thorough neliever, and had been a -student for many years of the laws of health, and if they sent him to the Council he would do his utmost to improve the sanitary arrange- ments of the town. He thought a man who presented himself for their suffrages should be intelligent; and in the discharge of the duties of a councillor diligence and time were required—just as a man would give time and diligence to his own business if he wishes to succeed. With respect to the liquor traffic, being represented on the Watch Committee, he need not say very much to the intelligent men present. It was desirable that no person engaged in such a business should be on that Committee. Just fancy; policemen were but human beings, and if they were called upon to discharge their duties under the control of the men interested in the drink trade, could they expect them to discharge their duties with impartiality, as they would like the police to do? A publican who conducted his

house in a proper manner need have no fear of the magistrates or the police; but those who did not con duct their houses on this principle ought to be watched by the police and if they were not St persons to hold licenses, he (Mr. Stringer) would take the licenses from them. Now a word with respect to the library. They had had a library for a number of years, but it was not yet free. Warrington was behind with respect tehaving a free library. Widnes had had a Fplendid free library for a number of years ; and it would be a good thing for a town like Warrington if their's could be free. In brief- ly touching upon the question of the baths he said he believed that cleanliness waS next to godliness, and it was a capital thing for a person to plunge into a bath, and the exercise of swimming was very good indeed. If they sent him to the Council he would have ample time at his disposal and he would feel it his duty to face and to handle every subject brought beforebim in an intellig- ent manner. He would go to the Council, if returned, as a man and not as a tool. '(Hear, hear and applause.) After a few other observations, Mr. Knowles asked the candidate if he was in favour of the resolution passel by the trades Council of War- rington with regard to test questions put before candi- dates.

--Mr. Stringer in reply to this stated that he would send his answer direct to the proper quarter, but he could as- sure Mr. Knowles it was a favourable answer. On the motion of Mr. John Walker, seconded by Mr. J. Strange, a vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

LA.TCHFORD WARD. MR. ASHTON'S CANDIDATURE. A meeting in support of Councillor Ashton, the Con- servative candidate for this ward, was held on Thursday evening, in St. James' schoolroom, Latchford. Coun- cillor W. Tinsley presided, and he was supported by the candidate, Coucillors Taylor and Greenall, Messrs. John White, J. Hartley, J. Lee, and C. Chrimes. After the Chairman had commented upon Mr. Ashton's municipal experience, Mr. S. Reynolds moved a resolution to the effect that Mr. Ashton was a fit and proper person to represent that ward in the Town Council. Mr. John White seconded and criticised Mr. Stringer's address on Tuesday evening. He regretted that the Conservative candidate had been put to the trouble and expense of a contest, because the Liberals were well aware what the result would be. rhe resolution, having been carried, Mr. Ashton rose to give some account of his stewardship. He, however, had very little to say in this respect, and principally confined his remarks to sketch of his life, detailing the periods of love, courtship, and marriage. In his concluding remarks, he made a reference to the Watch Committee, and said publicans did more on that Committee than the teetotallers did. He trusted they would again return him if it was only for honour in his old age. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought th e meeting to a close. ST. JOHN'S WARD.—MEETING OF MR. HILL'S

div.head: SUPPORTERS:
div.p: SUPPORTERS:

A meeting in support of the--c;;;c" lidature of Mr. James Hill, who contesti this ward in the Conservative interest was held in St. Peters' schoolroom on Monday evening, the chair being occupied by Councillor Heaton' who was supported on the platform by the candidate, J. White, J.P., Dr. Cannel], Messrs. R. Heaton, John Roberts, W. Diggle, J. Banner, J. Hope, and H. J. Longton. There was a moderate attendance.

The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said they all knew Mr. Hill as well as he did. Personally, he had known Mr. Hill for five and twenty years. He was as one of themselves, a man who had worked for his daily bread, and knew, therefore, what work was. He had been careful, and industrious and he had attained a position of independence. He dared say that was a good recommendation that he would serve them well in the Council if he was returned. Mr. Hill was a straightfor- ward, and pugnacious man, and it was well known that he was a strong Conservative. On these grounds, and seeing that he was so largely interested in the ward, he asked them to support Mr. Hill on the polling day. (Applause>. Mr. J. ROBERTS then moved the following resolution, " That this meeting is of opinion that Mr. James Hill is a fit and proper person to represent St. John's Ward in the Warrington Town Council, and pledges itself to use every lagitimate means to secure his election on the Ist November. In a few remarks Mr. Robert's said they no doubt were aware that he (Mr. Roberts) was first ehosen the candidate to contest St. John's ward in the Conservative interest. He was exceedingly sorry, that getting rather out of sorts, he was prevented from stand- ' ing. But he could assure them they had a good candi- date before them whom he hoped they would support, and return at the head of the poll with a large majority. (Applause.) He had had the pleasure of knowing Mr. Hill for a many years, and he (the speaker) felt confident that they would not be in the least disappointed with him; but, on the other hand, he was sure they would I find him to be a straightforward man—a man who would speak his mind in the Council Chamber if he was returned. There had been a great deal said in respect to the Inteik- cepting Depots, and Mr. Hill, who had lived not far from one ef the depots, and who, consequently, knew of the unpleasant smell which issued therefrom would speak in confidence on them. and say that it was not right to build such places in the locality in which they stood. If he (Mr. Roberts) had been their candidate, he should have opposed the nuisance and done all in his power to get :rid of it; and if it was found that there was no remedy except by removing the depots, he would cer- tainly have been in favour of having them removed. He was sure the candidate would do what they required in this respect ; and he would also look well after the rates in the interest of the ratepayers. In Mr. Hill they had the right man in the right place, and he hoped they would do their best for him on Saturday. (Applause.) Dr. CANNELL seconded the resolution, and in doing so expressed his regret that Mr. Roberts, through ill-health, was not able to contest the ward; but the inevitable must take place. In Mr. Hill he thought they had a man who was well able to look after the interests of the borough, and no doubt would look after that ward in particular. *He after wardsreferred to the ratepayers as being partners in the Corporation, and as such they ought not to pay for their gasmeters. He also briefly touched on the question of the depots. The Quanta/4 then put the resolution to the meeting, and it was carried unanimously. . . . .

Mr. HILL, who was applauded on rising to speak, said it was with some reluctance that he consented to stand as a candidate for that ward,for Mr. Blackhurst had been a friend of his for a considerable time, and he had nothing to say against him personally. He would like to have seen Mr. Roberts contesting the ward ; but, when he knew he could not do so on account of his health, and after he had been pressed to stand, he con- sented. Since 1868 he had helped in election campaigns, both for their honourable member of Parliament and candidates for the Town Council, and he hoped others would now help him. In his address the condition of the streets was mentioned, as also the trade of the town. So far as the trade of Warrington was concerned, he was greatly interested, for he had investigated his worth in house property. He had spent thousands of pounds in that ward in putting up property, and he had always erected the best he could. He did not believe in building jerry property, but he endeavoured to make his houses as comfortable as possible, and fit for people to live in. (Applause.) Some people said he was not a workman, but if those persons had followed his heels during the last six months, they would say he was. The streets in the town were certainly in a disgraceful state. He had spent £2OO in improving a street, and when he had done so the assessment of the property was raised. He, however, appealed against this, and some consider- able time afterwards the assessment was reduced to what it was previously. After speaking of the insuffi- cient drainage in the streets, Mr. Hill said he thought he had done more for the ward than ever Mr. Blackhurst had, and he did not think Mr. Blackhurst had gone into that ward once in three years. He had not seen him at that end of the town at all • but he believed he did pay ' some attention to the market, for he was often moving 'about Sankey-st. He (Mr. Hill) thought that Mr. Black- hurst, representing St. John's Ward, ought to do some- thing for the benefit of the ward. The footpath in John- st. was as bad as any in the town, especially by the tan- nery, and if he was returned he would see that the condi- tion of the street was remedied, and would do plenty of other things. He believed the ratepayers paid too high a price for gas, and that they had not the quality of gas they should have. With regard to the Intercepting Depots, he told them in his address he would do all he could to dispose of them. If elected he would do his best for them, and any grievance in the town, he would always do his utmost to remedy. (Applause.) After Mr. LONGTON (the candidate for Fairfield Ward) had said a few words.

Mr. lonx WHITE also expressed the great respect he entertained for Mr. Hill. He had worked with him for many years in political matters, and if he was as good a candidate and friend of the ward as he had been a good friend to the Conservative party, he could assure the electors they would have no cause to regret electing him a member of the Town Council. (Applause.) The able and practical manner in which he had addressed them that evening was a sufficient proof that he would make a most efficient member of the Corporation. There was a great future for Warrington when the Ship Canal was finished and the docks open, and the time would come when they would require the best men they could get to look aftertheir interest. (Applause.) Mr. McCoLLost moved a vote of thanks to the Chair- man, and the vote, after having been seconded by Mr. DIGGLE, was put to the meeting, and carried. The proceedings then terminated: FAIRFIELD WARD.—MEETING OF MR. DIXON'S SUPPORTERS. Mr. F. Dixon, independent candidate in Fairfield Ward held a meeting in support of his candidature in the Cock. hedge Mission-room on Tuesday evening. There was a fair attendance. Mr. Dixon spokeat length upon the lead- ing questions of municipal interest, and proposed many radical reforms. With reference to the gas accounts, he said that if returned he would not be satisfied until they were published in such a form that they could be pro- perly understood. Touching upon the sanitary matters, Mr. Dixon said they might not all be aware that when the existing plant at Longford was purchased—it came from Nottingham—he was the only one who made any objection to it being laid, and his vote was the only one registered against the purchase of the works. The machinery was inadequate, and the smells that emanated from them were abominable. Mr. Dixon compared the

Longford works with those in existence, and which were working satisfactorily in other towns. From £30,000 to £31,000 had been spent on the works of Longford, and they, at the present time, were of little use to them. Ile contended that the plant which had been adopted could not be wonted satisfactorily. If elected he would not sanction any " tinkering " of the intercepting depots. Tlw must be entirely removed. TOWN HALL WIRD : MR. JAMES FAIRCLOITGE'3

CANDIDATURE. , A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. JameS Fairclough, Conservative candidate for the Town Hall Ward, was held on Thursday evening, in St. Paul's girls' schoolroom, Rolleston-st. Mr. James'Smethurstpre- sided and amongst those present were Mr. John White (chairman of the Conservative Association), Councillor E. Greenell, Mr. J. Hepherd, Mr. A. Jolley, Mr. T. Jones,, and Lieut.-Colonel Bolton, Mr. Nicholson, Sze. There' was a good attendance.—TheepAlßMAN said Mr. Fair- dough was a gentleman well-known in:the town,and waS a large ratepayer which ought to be one of the great- est qualifications for a candidate for municipal honours. They might be sure that in putting Mr. Fairclough st -the head of the poll they were returning a gentleman who would take care of his own money, and would there fore take care of their's. A resolution accepting Mr. Fairclough as a fit of proper person to represent the Ward was then moved by Mr. BANNER seconded by Mr. T. JONES, and carried unanimously.—Mr. FAIRCLOOOIt in reply, said if he was elected he could assure., them that he should do all ho could on the Count" to help on the prosperity of Warrington. (Hear, hear.> His firm were large ratepayers, and if they could get the rates reduced is. in the £ it would mean a saving of £5O to them. It as not likely, therefore, that he would be a party to increasing the rates it he could help it. (Hear, hear.) Warrington had been sadly handicapPed, in the past. In the first place the Gas Works belongeo to a private company. The town at last bought them,. and paid for them. Then they found they could net do without the water. The Waterworks Company hung on till they got to the top of the tree and they, too, get what they wanted. As for the baths, he quite agree",_ that they wanted new ones, for the present were deficient.—After Mr. IlEensun and Mr. Bormos had spoken in support of Mr. Faircleugh's candidature, Mr. White reminded the audience that Mr.Fairclough's familY had been connected with Warrington for many years. If they traced the history of Warrington for the past 20' years they would find very few movements for the good of Warrington in one direction or another' but what some member of the Fairclough family had been in it. That being the case,it was impossible for them as electors to find one who would serve their interests more faith- fully on the Council than Mr. Fairclough. (Hear, hear.) Why Mr. Fleming should come from another ward when ,- he was allocated by the Commissioner, to fight a man like Mr. Fairclough was one of "those things he could not. find out. Mr. Fairclough took the ward he was allocated to. He was not forcing himself upon them in any wal whatever. He came there because he was told to do sot and that was characteristic at the man. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the proceed' ings to a close. HOVVLEY WARD.—MR. PERCIVAL'S CANDIDATURE. A meeting was held in the National Schools on Thurs- day evening, in support of Mr. Percival's candidature for Howley Ward, Mr. J. Faircrough presided, and there were also on the platform Dr. Cannel, Councillor R. T. Fairclough, Councillor Hutchinson, Councillor Bolton, Mr. S. Davies, Mr. Dewhurst, &c. Mr. Dew' hurst moved and Mr. S. Davies seconded a resolution pledging the meeting to support Mr. Percival. This waS carried unanimously. Mr. Percival in his address re- ferred to the work of the Sanitary Committee and said there ought to be a Chairman at the head of the Colomittee that would listen to the Committee and not only to the Committee but to representatives in the Town Council and outsiders. He did not believe in being pre- judiced. If he were the chairman of a committee he, would listen to all grievances and enter into them gnu reply to every question put to him. (Hear, hear.) He was in favour of the entire removal of the Intercepting Depots unless the nuisance caused by them could be abated. (Applause.) With regard to the gas depart' ment he was of opinion that the price of gas in Warring' ton should be reduced to about 2s. 6d. per 1,000 feet. Speaking with respect to his opponent, Mr. Percival said they did not want boys in the Town Council but men of age and intellect and experience. When they had young men—juveniles he might say—gifted with the "gab" time was lost and not work done. They wanted men who spoke to the point • and did not want to make the Town Council into a debating society. Dr. Cannel', Councillor Bolton, Councillor R. T. Fairclough and others also spoke.

div.head: NOTES ON 'GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON 'GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
ASSOCIATION.

A vast amount of interest was shown in the return League fixture between the Rovers and North End at Blackburn on Saturday. Preparations had been com- pleted for accommodating a big crowd, and something like 20,000 were present. Some of the barricading gave way during the play but although a good many persons fell to the ground there was fortunately no serious injury. The game resolved itself early into a desperate struggle for mastery, in which the backs on each side were often seen to advantage. It was late on ere s goal was scored, and by this the Rovers won. With the exception of a benefit match, this is the first time the North End have been beaten at Blackburn. It speaks well for the Rovers that they should be able to beat the League champions twice in the same season, and on this form they should stand a good chance of winning the F.A. Cup once more:

Everton was defeated for the first time, and this, too, at Anfield-road, by West Ilromich Albion, who thus amply avenge themselves for their overthrow at Stoney - lane some weeks ago. The Albion forwards were exceedingly smart and tricky, and took advantaae of the absence of Hannah, the crack Everton back. Wolverhampton Wanderers are now again level with Everton. On Saturday they scored three goals to Burnley one, the latter thus adding another to their list of reverses.

Some association clubs have fine incomes. In the four League matches the Blackburn Rovers have played on their new ground the receipts have been—v. Accrington, £205: v. Wolverhampton Wanderers, £l5O ; v. Sunder- land, £180; and v. North End, £443, giving a total of £978.

One often hears of the great progress made by the Association code, but the splendid record of the Wigan Associationists reads like Julius Ciesar's triumphs. Al- though it is only two years since their establishment, yet they have so facinated the peorle of Wigan and their professional players, that the " pros." are on strike, because their munificent salaries of 2s. 6d. per match have not been paid up : the landlord is growling because they owe a couple of years rent ; the club has been dlB- - and re-organised as an amateur combination,rd last Saturday to fill the cup of bitterness up to the brim, the Associationists announced a sides game under Rugbi Rules.

FOOTBALL—Rt7GDY. Warrington are a trifle unfortunate this season, as four of their first team are now patients of Dr. Evan Thomas, the eminent surgeon of Liverpool The latest additbou to the noble army of cripples is Fair Turner.

Warrington have says the " Athletio News," unearthed a capital half-back in J. Bate. His play against St' Helens Recreation on Saturday was splendid for one viti,c; has not been used to good-class football, and he Iv" certainly prove an acquisition to the back division of the " Wirepullers." It is a rather singular fact that both of the Warrington half-backs are named J. T. Bate, arid they are not related.
J. B. Briggs, of Bramley, who has played so well at full-back in the Yorkshire county trials, is brother to the Lancashire cricketer, and this is his thirteenth season at at Rugby football.

The meeting of Runcorn and Wigan, after a lapSe of certain years, produced some excitement and a hard fought game. The struggle was very even throughout. and each side put in all they knew without having anY effect on the scoring board. Though the weather vrag humid the field did not show any great traces of the wet, and the "going "was not so heavy as was generally prognosticated. Runcorn seem to have the good luck to arop across fine players, and their latest recruit for the position of full back is as capable as any of his predeceS- sors. The absence of Hughie Hughes -from the field ou account of injuries is the only lament of the Runcogi people, and they won't be sorry when he returns.

div.head: _ ROYAL VISIT TO 'LIVERPOOL.
div.p: _ ROYAL VISIT TO 'LIVERPOOL.

The Duke of Clarence and Avondale, who arrived at Croxteth Hall, the seat of the Earl of Sefton, on Tues- day night, visited Liverpool on Wednesday for the pur- pose of opening the enlarged Royal Infirmary. Accom- panied by his host, the Earl of Lathom, and others, the Duke was first driven to the Town Hall, where he was welcomed by the the Mayor (Mr. Hughes) and heard an address read by the Recorder (Mr. C. H. Hopwood, Q.C.) His Royal Highness replied, expressing his extreme pleasure at visiting Liverpool to open an institution which was now undoubtedly one of of the most comPlete and perfect of the kind in the country, and that had been erected solely by , the liberality of the citizens- After luncheon at the Town Hall the Prince went to the Infirmary, which he opened, the ceremony including another brief speech. His Royal Highness was present in the evening at a ball given at St. George's Hall in aid of the Infirmary funds.

div.p: THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S ANNUAL REPORT.

The twenty-fifth annual report of the Chief Con- stable of Warrington was submitted to the Town Council on Tuesday night. SUMMARY CONVICTIONS, &C. It stated that during the year ended 29th September, 1890, the number of persons dealt with summarily dur- ing the year is 2,570, against 2,516 in 1889, being an in- crease of 54. 1,711 males and 435 females were con- victed, and 265 males and 159 females were discharged. The number of persons dealt with on indictment is 18, of whom 12 were committed for tidal, and 8 discharged for want of evidence or prosecution. Of these, 2 were sentenced to 5 years' penal servitude each, 3 sentenced to 12 months' hard labour, 1 to 9 months' hard labour, 2 to 8 months' hard labour, 1 to 1 month's hard labour, and 3 acquitted. TWO that were pending trial in 1889 have been sentenced this year, 1 to 5 years' penal servitude, and 1 to 20 months' hard labour. The indictable offences during the year were 2 for defilement of girls between the ages of 13 and 18 years, 1 abduction of girl under 18 years of age, 3 breaking into shops and warehouses, 3 Larceny to the value of £5 in dwelling-houses, 1 horse stealing, 13 simple larceny, 1 receiving stolen goods, 2 frauds or attempts to commit, 1 killing and maiming cattle, I uttering counterfeit coin, and one attempted suicide ; total 30 crimes.

DRUNKENNESS. The number of persons proceeded against for drunken- ness, &c., is 838, last year it was 840; assaults on police 23, last year 37 ; common assaults 175, last year 194 ; breaches of the peace 135, last year 213 • Elementary Education Acts 392, last year 308 again a large increase on the preceding year; Local Acts and Borough Bye- laws 308, last year 310; neglect of family 68, last year 34, an increase just double; simple larceny 162, last year 122 ; vagrancy 147, last year 134; 'other summary offences will be found accounted for in tbe tabulated forms appended.

div.head: MISCELLANEOLTS,
div.p: MISCELLANEOLTS,

The number 3f persons sent to gaol without the option of paying a fine is 335, the number tined 1,495, ordered to find sureties 103. deserters, &c., delivered to the Army, &c., 33, children whipped 38, sent to Reformatory Schools 7, to Industrial Schools 8, and persons subjected to other punishments 107 ; total convicted, 2,146. Four convicts on license have reported themselves at this office, 3 of whom have left for other districts ; and 1 still residing in the borough. Twelve persons under police supervision also reported themselves to the police, 10 of whom have left for other districts ; 1 continues to reside here, and the supervision of the other has expired. Ninty-eight prisoners have been received into custody and locked up for offences not connected with this Court. Ninety-seven deaths were reported to the Coroner from the Police Office, 39 of which were referred to the Registrar, and inquests were held on 58; the ver- dicts being—accidental deaths 30, natural causes 19, misadventure I,wilful murder I,and open verdict 7. One hundred and twenty-two pedlars' certificates and 10 chimney-sweepers' licenses have been issued during the year.

div.head: DOGS CASES.
div.p: DOGS CASES.

Seven persons have been summoned for keeping dogs without licenses all of whom were convicted and fined. Under the Rabies (Muzzling of Dogs) Order, 1889, since January Ist., 1890 the number of clogs dealt with is 405; viz., number seized by the police 152, number reported 253, 57 dogs were destroyed, 40 were sold, 272 were given up to owners on payment of detention fee, 24 were given up to the owners who were cautioned, and 1 dog escaped. Nineteen persons who did not pay detention fee were summoned, 18 being convicted, and fined by the magistrates; amount paid into court being £ll 4s. ed. The owners and purchasers of unclaimed dogs paid at the Police Office the sum of n 3 ss. ed. from January Ist, to September 29th, 1890, inclusive.

LICENSED PERSONS AND LICENSED HOUSES. There are 9 cabs and hackney carriage owners in the borough; 63 cab and omnibus drivers; 37 persons licensed to sell fireworks (6 of whom sell gunpowder), 12 amens store dealers, and 23 common lodging-house keepers. There are 87 public-houses,l4B beerhouses, and 70 off-licensed houses in the borough. Thiee persons are licensed game dealers, and 1 person holds a billiard license ; 2 licensed victuallers were summoned and cqn- victed, and 3 beerhouse keepers were summoned, but the cases against them were dismissed.

EIRES.-CHILDREN IN REFORMATORIES. Eight fires were reported during the year as having taken place in the borough. The damage done, so far as can be ascertained, amounted to about £1,200. Only 1 was uninsured. The warrants issued during the year were 165, executed 131. The number of children detained in Reformatory and Industrial Schools during the the year from this borough is 36. the parents of whom have paid through the Police Office tp the Home Office, London, for their part maintenance the sum of £7l 18s.

POPUIATION AND NUMBER OF CONSTABLES. The population of the borough is now estimated at something over 50,000, the present acreage is 1,442, and the valuation £47,844, but the new Borough Boundary Extension Scheme will come into force on October 30th 1890, when the population acreage, and valuation will be increased, find will necessitate another augmentation of the police force. It at present consists of 48 men, viz. : —1 chief constable, 3 inspectors, 4 sergeants, 1 detective, and 39 constables, and is complete. 'The variations dur- ing the year have been 1 resigned voluntarily, 1 through continued ill health, 1 compulsorily, 1 died after 4 day's illness, and 3 dismissed. The leave of absence to all ranks was 388 days.‘sickness 558 days, hurt upon dnty 21 days. Three of those who left the force were sick 145 days amongst them. LOST CHILDREN, &C. Windows and doors of 96 houses, shops, and ware- houses were found insecure at night by the policemen on duty, 48 lost children were found and restored to their homes, and 45 cattle found straying were placed in the pinfold until owned.

POLICE SUPERANNUATION AND COST OF POLICE. The value of the Police Superannuation Fund on March 25th, 1890, was £6,898 is. Bd., and being now free from charge is increasing satisfactorily. The cost of the police establishment for 1890 amounted to £4,344 Sc. 4d., as against £3,950 ss. 11d. in 1889. This increase is accounted for by the augmentation of the force by 6 men in the year ended September 29th, 1890. _

- . ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION CLASS. Number holding certificates :—Head constable 1 ; inapectors, 3 ; sergeants, 4 ; constables, 25 ; total 33: Valuable first aid has been given in 18 cases. cErmFmArg FROM THE HOME SECRETARY. The Right Hon. Henry Matthews, one of H. M. princi- pal Secretaries of State, has certified "That the Police of the Borough of Warrington has been maintained in a state of efficiency in point of numbers and discipline for the year ending the 29th of September, 1890."
POLICE CHANGES IN WARRINGTON. REPORT BY TRE CHIEF CONSTABLE.

The following report of the Chief Constable was I submitted to Warrington Town Council by the Watch Committee on Tuesday night, viz:—" In accordance with the instructions of the Watch ' committee I now submit for its consideration the , • following suggestions and recommendations which ' are rendered necessary by reason of the extension • of the Borough boundaries, and the consequent ad- dition to the population and area to be covered by police patrols. The population is now reckoned at , 51,977 (say 52,000), the strength of the force, there- ' fore, should be 52 men ; as the present strength is 48 men I recommend an augmentation of four men, and, as the added acreage is 562' it will take at : least three out of the four to patrol same. The cab, hackney carriage, omnibus, and other veld- ' cular traffic having now assumed very large proportions, and is almost daily increasing, I would suggest that an old and experienced police officer, in addition to other ' duties which he will have to perform, be specially ap- pointed to regulate such vehicular traffic; for this duty I recommend Police Sergeant John Bowen, who joined the force on December 15th, 1870 (nearly 20 years ago), he having taken Ids full share of night duty during the whole of that period, but will be placed permanently on days should this recommendation be adopted. Owing to the making ,of the Manchester Ship Canal, the influx of great numbers of strangers, many of whom are suspicious characters, requiring a large amount of attention by the police, I recommend P.C. 11—Patrick Monaghan—who joined the force February 19th, 1878 (over 10 years ago), and who is a zealous, hardworking, and therefore a successful detective officer, to be pro- moted to Detective Sergeant, with either more pay or extra allowance for plain clothes ; the object of this pro- motion is to give him power on emergencies to command the assistance of the police constables, who, as it now is, do not take kindly to instructions given by one of their own rank. And, as the extended area of the Borough will make the duties of P.C. Chantler, who is Police Messenger and Summons Server, more arduous and tiring, I recommend that he also be appointed Sergeant, to enable him too to command the assistance of a constable when circum- stances require it. P.C. Chantler was appointed on April 9th, 1870, and has therefore done over 20 years' service; he has been a steady, well-conducted, and able officer, and the best we have for the conveyance of pri- soners to gaol, which is a responsible and dangerous duty. Ile has, however, been reported once within the last ten years, when he was cautioned by the Watch , Committee. Having recommended that Sergeant Bowen be placed permanently on day duty for certain fixed purposes, it becomes necessary to appoint from the constables one to take his place as sergeant on day and night patrol duty. At the proper time I shall call the attention of the Corn- rniteee to the fact that although the constables are as well paid as in any other forces of similar strength, the sergeants and inspectors are not, and I shall, therefore, recommend a slightly increased scale so far as they are concerned. Having been instructed to put tiny sugges- tions and recommendations into form, I now willingly leave them for your consideration and shall be glad to give you any explanations you may require to assist you in either adopting or modifying them, and shall fall in With any decision you may come to on anything above set forth.
accordance with the above report the Watch Corn-

mittee submitted the following resolutions for adoption to the Council :-1. That the police force be augmented by the appointment of four additional constables. 2. That Sergeant Bowen be appointed inspector of hackney car- riages with the duties above assigned to him. 3. That P.C. Monaghan be promoted to the rank of detective sergeant -with the duties above assigned to him. 4. That P.C. Chantler be promoted to the rank of Sergeant, with the duties above assigned to him. The rasolutions were adopted.

div.head: LAC ROSSE.
div.p: LAC ROSSE.
WARRINGTON v. OVVENS COLLEGE IST.

Warrington opened the season on their own ground at Arpley, on Saturday, with a match against the ex-flag, holders, who were captained by Mr. Norman Me!land, the international cover-point. The visitors turned up one short, so it was agreed to play eleven a-side. For- tunately, the rain held off while the game was being played, though the ground was very wet and slippery. Bennett and Dutton faced about 3.30, and far the first quarter of an hour the game was very even, the War- rington attacks playing up grandly, but Norman Mel- land and Zimmermann were in excellent form and re- I sisted all attempts at scoring. At last the Warrington centre got in a good shot from the wing, and drew first blood for the home team. After this Owens wakened up their attacks. All worked hard, and the home custodian was called upon to save several hot shots, and after a I bit of good passing, the visitors soon equalised. The I play was now very even, when Norman MeHand getting I possesdon from a long throw of the home defence ran right down centre field, and was, unfortunately, allowed a clear run, and scored goal No. 2 for Owens, and at half time the game was in faveur of the visitors by 3to 1. After the face the superior condition of the College men told considerably, this being their fifth match this season. Their attacks played a splendid pas- sing game, and scored two more goals. This put the Warringtonians on their mettle, and by a bit of good play they scored again, this being the last point of the match. The Owens College team were thus victorious by five to two. On the victorious side Norman Melland and Zimmermann were in their best form, and their sharp passing was a treat to witness. On the attacks, Duttcn and Macbeth worked hard. Barker, in goal for the horre team played an admirable game, and no doubt the War- ringtonians would have suffered a heavier defeat but for his services. Remembering who their opponents were, the Warringtonians are to be congratulated upon the form they displayed, and if they will practise there is nothing to prevent them developing into a good team.

div.head: INFIRMARY CONCERT.
div.p: THE INFIRMARY CONCERT.

That the Warrington Infirmary is recognised t deserving of support was again amply demonstrated on Saturday evening by the large number who at- tended the tenth annual carmen, arranged by the Working-men's Committee, in the Public Hall. The higher priced seats were nearly all occuliied, whilst the gallery was filled to its utmost capacity. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and in a few remarks at the opening of the concert, said Mr. Roberts bed placed in his hands two letters of apology for non-attendance. One was from Alderman Davies which was worded as follows:—" I quite looked forward to coming to your concert to-night, but I am laid up with a bad cold, and shall not ven- ture out before Monday. I heartily wish you will have a good concert." The other letter was from Mrs. J. Reynolds, which read :—" I am sorry we shall not be with you to-night ; but when! tell you we have just received news of my brother-in-law's death, you,will understand the reason. You remem- ber him, I am sure, for just a year to-night you gave him such an enthusiastic welcome; and I should not be able to sit in the same place, knowing that I should not see his face again." In presenting an account of the subscriptions collected by the Working-men's Committee, the Mayor said that in 1880 that Committee first came into existence, and previous to that year there were very small sums collected indeed. In 1881 the Committee man- aged to get together £165 9s. :311th ; and they had gone on increasing the amount, year by year, the result being that last year £489 Os. Old. was received, making the grand total from 1880 to 1888 of £3,444 Ils. lid. (Applause.) The concerts were started in 1881, the first of which gave the Committee a surplus of £29 Gs. Bd.; and the last concert enabled them to hand over to the funds of the Infirmary £6O 12s. 3id., or a grand total from the commencement of the concerts in 1881 of £417 79. Od. (Applause.) He was quite sure they would all say with him that the workmen deserved every support. They had taken a proper course in trying to help themselves, and it there was an institution in the town that should be helped by everyone, it was thei Infirmary. lie quite understood that the homes of ' working-men were not suited for the treatment of cases of severe accidents; and they knew it was utterly impos- sible for even the best people in the town to have the care and attention bestowed on them at their homes like they could have at the Infirmary. At that place, night and day, ,nurses and doctors were at their disposal, and especially was this so in cases of accidents. Where there were a large number of men, as in Warrington, who worked at the forge, they were obliged to hear of numerous accidents, and he was quite certain that those who knew most about the work of the Infirmary, would be most anxious to help it. lie thought that that large audience was ample proof to the Working Men's Com- mittee, that the labouring classin Warrington thoroughly appreciated their efforts. (Applause.) The following programme was then proceeded with:—

Miss Florence Dick is titled "the eminent soprano," and this is justified, judging from the excellent manner in 'which she acquitted herself on Saturday. She was very successful in "The nightingale's her warbling being specially commendable. Her rendering of "Scenes that are brightest" was very effective, and brought forth an encore, for which she substituted "Home sweet home." This latter, however, was not sung so nicely as it might have been, but still it was warmly appreciated. Miss Bessie Fanshawe possesses a capital contralto voice, but she would be heard to much better advantage if she could control her bold delivery. She was less successful with" In old Madrid," than with the droll song "To- morrow will do," which was enamouring, and so loud was the applause that a re-appearance was demanded, when she effectively sang "The minstrel boy." Mr. Ben Roberts has an excellent tenor voice, and ht well merited the rounds of applause with which his efforts were received. "The anchor's weighed" always goes well on account of its popularity, but its effec- tiveness was considerably enhanced by the precision and pathos with which Mr. Roberts rendered it. The same remarks may be applied to his singing of "When other lips," which brought an encore, when he sang" The death of Nelson." Mr. Paul Conway, bari- tone, met with a hearty reception in his song " The Toreador." This composition is by no means a simple one, and its efficient accomplishment necessitates a versatile voice ; but, notwithstanding this Mr. Conway gave an admirable rendering. He also sang "Anchored," in a brilliant manner. It was loudly applauded, and the approval of the audience was acknowledged by him. Mr. R. D. Rodgers' humourous songs and recitations had a very enlivening influence, and produced much laugh- ter. He is very clever with his witticisms, and his per- formances came as a relief, they being interspersed in convenient parts of the programme. Mr. T. J. Down's Military Band, consisting of 45 performers, was a great attraction, and it is no more than merited praise to say that Mr. Down has worked the band up to an enviable pitch. The overtures were classic, and were gone through in a brisk style, while the other pieces played, especially the last selection, were at once conclusive of the com- bined assiduousness of the performers to attain, as near as possilde, the acme of perfection. Mr. George Riley, who accompanied at the piano the greater part of the evening, displayed his musical abilities, and acquitted himself as usual in a praiseworthy manner. Mr. Arthur Miller also acted as pianist in one or two songs. To Mr. Thomas Roberts, the hon. sec, of the Working-men's Committee, and, coupled with him all who gave a helping hand in the arrangement of the concert are to be congratulated on the:success of their efforts. During the vote of thanks to the Mayor, the artistes, band, and workers, at the close, it was stated that the attendance was greater than was expected, and that the result of the concert, financially, was highly satisfactory.
