TORY SLANDER REFUTED.
Sir,—The Tory party are seeking to damage my per- sonal character by means of a gross misstatement of facts.

About three years ago, owing to the death by drown- ing of my youngest brother, my mother became depen- dent for support upon her children. At that time, and frequently since, I have done my utmost to induce my mother to come and reside permanently in my own home, where she would have all the comforts which are enjoyed by my own family ; but although, fully appreciating my offer, she preferred to keep to her own house, and con- sequently I have always ccntributed towards her expen- diture what she considered far more than my share. On many occasions she has returned to me money that I had sent her in addition to the regular weekly sum.

My mother's only object in applying, in the first instance, for extra help on the Union, was in order that her other two sons might be called upon to contribute their fair share of the cost of her maintenance. I need hardly say that both my mother and myself are deeply grieved at the unjust attempt which has been i made n so cowardly a manner to blacken my character. I have the utmost confidence that, with the truth before you, your readers will see that the Tories have resorted —not for the first time—to unfounded accusations in order to injure a political opponent.—Yours truly, JOSEPH TITCHETT.

CHURCH PARADE AND FRIENDLY SOCIETIES. Sir,—l was pleased to see in your last issue that arrangements are being made for a church parade of the Warrington Friendly Societies. The dark days when members of the affiliated societies looked with envy, hatred and malice upon each other, have passed away and have given place to brighter days. Now the Odd- fellows vie with the Foresters, the Foresters with the Druids, the Druids with the Shepherds, and the Shep- herds with the Gardeners iu making their Society finan- cially sound,so that when the day of sickness comes, each member may receive the benefit promised at the time of his initiation. These thrift societies, these modern com- pulsory savings banks, have done more towards educa- ting the working classes than all the claptrap one hears

from itinerant politicans. Aa a move in the right direction has taken place,might I suggest that, in addition to going to church onca a year, the officers of the various societies form a cons- injae,e p meet once amonth (oftener if required) to dis-

cuss friendly society subjects, e.g.—What is there to prevent such a body deciding upon an equalized scale of contribution for the whole of the Warrington district ? Then again, there is the so-called, " rent of room" which is still a vexed question, and only requires the heads of the friendly societies to take a firm and res(alute step and the question would be settled once for all. I only mention these things as examples; they are not the whole of the subjects, by any means, that require the cool heads of the leaders; but I think it is sufficient to show that there is plenty of room for such a committee, and at the same time I feel confident they would be the means of doing a large amount of goad. I hope the members will turn out in large numbers and give liberally to the collection that will be made", at the close of the service, in aid of the Infirmary. A cause like ' • Friendly Societies" with their millions of members, and millions of capital, and probably nine out of every ten of your readers directly or indirectly interested in them, hardly requires an apology for trespassing upon your space.—l am, dear sir, yours faithfully, J. G.
Warrington, Oct. 28th, 1890.

MR. ASHTON'S CANDIDATURE. Sir,—Having seen in your Tory contemporary. and heard from seveial individuals, that Councillor Ashton, who is contesting Latchford Ward in the Conservative interest, in opposition to Mr. Stringer, was in every way qualified to satisfactorily discharge the duties ap- pertaining to the work of the Council, I thought I would judge, by attending his meeting at St. James, School, on Thursday. Mr. John White having delivered himself, all interest was centred upon the candidate, Mr. Ashton, who is represented by his supporters as having most efficiently done his duty during the 22 years that he has served in the Town Council. From my observations of him, lam at a loss to see what the Consuvatives of Latchford Ward can see in him as their representative, and it is surprising after the ludicrous speech which he delivered on Thursday that they cannot per- ceive h:s unsuitability to act as one of their rulers- I attended the meeting for the purpose of hearing him give an account of his stewardship, but imagine my. surprise when I was under the necessity of listening to a most uninteresting, desultory, and unimpressive sketch of his life from youth upwards. He pursued in a bold manner the event which led to his being enamoured of a fair damsel; related the many pleasant walks which he enjoyed with the " light of his life,"demonstrated how profound his courtship grew, and then gave a short his- tory of his connubial bliss. What I, amongst others, went for was to hear something that would materially add to my knowledge of the town's affairs, and hear his remarks cn the work he had himself performed. Love tales, surely do not constitute a Councillor's stewardship! Then why was Mr. Ashton not told he was speaking in an absurd fashion? Why was he not reminded of the prime object of the meeting, viz. : that the burgesses wanted to know how he had acted in their interests dur- ing the many years that he has represented them. In my opinion, Mr. Stringer is far the better man of the two. He is intelligent, observant, and will make an accomplished member of the governing body. Under these circumstances, it behoves the electors to poll early for Mr. Stringer, for if he is returned he will be a credit to the Council, and a worthy representative. Yours !cc.,
PRACTICAL.

FEASTING RUNCORN OFFICIALS. Sir,—Having read the letters of your correspondents Messrs. Ratepayer and Marshall, I thought the rate- payers of Runcorn were entitled to further explanations respecting the expenses incurred by the Returning Officers, at the annual electim of the Improvement Com- missioners during the past six years. If the statement given by Mr. Marshall be correct, that the expenses in- curred by Mr. Shaw in conducting the election on Sep- tember 3, 1885 were £l4 Os. id., it certainly appears very strange,that the following resolution should be passed at the next monthly meeting of the Commissioners : "That a cheque be drawn on the Treasurer in favour of Mr. Shaw, to reimburse him for the expenses incurred by him in conducting the election on the 3rd of September, 1885, amounting to £6 45.," he having at the said elec- tion dispensed with the services of the Law Clerk whose fee was £2 25.; also the dinner usually given to the officials. . .

The following year Mr. Dobson was appointed Return- ing Officer. At the next monthly meeting of the Com- missioners held September 8, 1886, it was resolved : " That a cheque be drawn on the Treasurer in his favour, to reimburse him for the expenses incurred by him in conducting the election on the 2nd day of September, 1886, amounting to £8 95." The next year Mr. Dobson was again appointed Return- ing Officer. At the next monthly meeting of the Com- missioners, held September 8, 1887, it was resalved "That a cheque be drawn on the Treasurer in his favour, to reimburse him for the expenses incurred by him in conducting the election on the Ist day of September, 1887, amounting to £8 10s. 6d." The following year Mr. Fisher was appointed Return- ing Officer. At the next monthly meeting of the Com- missioners, it was resolved :—" That a cheque be drawn on the Treasurer in his favour, to reimburse him for the expenses incurred by him in conducting the election on the 6th day of september, 1888, amounting to £l3 2s. 3d." Mr. Manhall states in his letter that the expenses in- curred by Mr. Lightburn in conducting the election in September, 1889, were £l2 7s. Mr. Lightburn also sub- mitted an account of the expenses as Returning Officer at the recent election, amounting to £l7 95., which in- cludes £5 14s. for refreshments. Hoping this statement of the facts will be a satisfac- tory explanation to all parties concerned; also trusting that the 7s. dinners will, at the ratepayers' expense, at future elections, only be known by their absence from the Returning Officers report,—l am, sir, yours Sm.. JUSTICE.

div.p: LONDON.
SHOCKING DOMESTIC TRAGEDY NEAR

The quiet village of Hanworth, near Twickenham, was on Monday night the scene of a shocking tragedy. A labourer named Edward Hedges, aged about 50, who for some time past has been unable to follow his employment in consequence of illness, lett his home in the afternoon, and upon returning between five and six o'clock,savaE,rely attacked his wife with a hammer. He inflicted three severe wounds on the woman's head, fracturing the skull. In an exhausted condition and with blood stream- ing from her wounds, Mrs. Hedges crawled to the house of a neighbour. Immediately after the attack upon his wife Hodges went into his bedroom, and, seizing a razor, cut his ttiroat from ear to ear, death being almost instantaneous. Mrs. Hedges lies at her neighbour's house in a precarious condition. She is a sober, industrious woman, and as a family of ten children. It is said that Hedges was jealous of his wife.

div.head: MR.. BALFOUR'S TOUR IN IRELA.ND.
div.p: MR.. BALFOUR'S TOUR IN IRELA.ND.

The "Freeman's Journal" Westport correspondent states: Mr. Balfour with his sister and Sir J. Ridgeway , and Mr. Wyndham, left Belmullet on Wednesday morn- ing in very inclement weather for Achill. At Ballycroy, after luncheon, General Clive provided a carriage in which the party drove to Cluggan Ferry, crossed in a boat, went on to Achill Viaduct on an outside car, and after thirty miles drive through wild country reached the Island. There was no demonstration. The Chief Secre- tary stayed the night with the parish priest. Mr. Balfour and party left Kylemore on Wednesday morning and drove rid Cleggan and Cloddogh Duff to Clifden, where the Chief Secretary had a long conversa- tion with Father Lynsky as to the means required to prevent the impending distress. Mr. Balfour agreed that a first seed supply was needed. He obtained reports and Union statistics from Major D'Arcy, clerk of the Union. Mr. Balfour afterwards inspected the Industrial School, conducted by the Sisters of Mercy, returning to Kyle- more Castle in the evening.

div.head: TIPPERARY TRIALS.
div.p: THE TIPPERARY TRIALS.

The opening of Wednesday's proceedings in the Tipper- ary Courthouse seemed to arouse a good deal of interest on account of the presence of two persons who were required as witnesses for the Crown and had no intention of giving evidence. One of these,a shopkeeper's assistant named Gleeson, was produced in custody, a warrant having been issued against him after his failure to appear at a previous stage. The other was a woman named Alice Sadler, a relative of a witness already heard. Both refused to be sworn, and were ordered to be kept in custody until next day. Head Constable Jennings was afterwards examined with regard to various phases of the alleged conspiracy, and gave evidence as to speeches delivered by Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., and Father Humphreys, directed against Mr. Smith-Barry. On Thursday, Mr. Ronan, Q.C., on behalf of the Crown, made an application that the recognizances of Mr. Dillon, M.P., and Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., should not be estreated until the conspiracy trials had termi- nated. The application was agreed to, as also was one for the further adjournment a the police summonses in connection with the disturbar.ce on September 25. The chief witness produced at the further hearing of the con- spiracy charges was Mr. G. Caldwell, manager of Mr. Smith-Barry's rent office. After a stormy scene between counsel following an application by Mr. Redmond that the crown should furnish him with copies of certain documents produced by the witness, the Court ad- journed.

THE ROYAL EXCHANGE LICENSE. TIIE APPEAL AT LIVERPOOL SESSIONS. SETTLED BY AGREEMENT. The appeal of William Bolton and Edward Bul- lock, owner and tenant respectively of the Royal Exchange public-house. Warrington, against the refusal of Warrington magistrates to renew the license was heard yesterday at Liverpool County Quarter Sessions, before Mr. Hugh Perkins (in the chair) supported by Sir W. B. Forwood, Mr. S. Rig- by, Mr. R. Tomlinson, Mr. James Tinsley, Captain Withington,Mr. F. Stapleton-Bre th erton, and Mr. W. Li. Tate. Mr. Segar (instructed by Mr. Well- head, of Warrington) appeared for Mr. Bolton ; Mr. McKeand (instructed by Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw, Warrington) appeared for Mr. Bullock; and the magistrates were represented by Mr. W. Swift, who had been instructed by the magistrates' clerk (Mr. H. B. White). The grounds of the appeal were as follows:- 1. That the said premises are fit and proper for licensed premises and that you refused such license without any sufficient reason for so doing; 2. That the renewing of such license would have been a convenience to the public and an accommodation to the neighbourhood; 3. That there was no sufficient cause arising from the conduct or character of me the said Edward Bullock or any other sufficient or just reason why such license should not have been renewed; 4. That supposing (which is not ad- mitted) that there was any valid reason for objecting to the character of the license, the interest of the owner should not have been under the circumstances prejudiced, and upon his undertaking, if you the said justices disap- proved of the tenant to cause the license to be without delay transferred to some other tenant, who should be a fit and proper person to receive a license or to use hisbest endeavours in that behalf you the said justices should in the exercise of your discretion have renewed the said license; 5. That the said refusal to renew the said license was inequitable and was unjust to me, the said owner of the said licensed premises. Mr. Swift, in opening, said in that appeal of Edward Bullock and William Bolton were the appellants, and Richard Walker Francomb and fourteen other justices of the borough of Warrington were the respondents. Bullock had been the tenant and occupier of the Royal Exchange for about three years, having entered into occupation of the premises in August, 1887. The general annual licens- ing meetint, of Warrington in the present year was held, as required by law, in the month ot August, and at that meeting some of the inhabitants ratepayers of the borough, attended in person and also by a solicitor made objections to the renewal of that particular license. There were four objections alleged against the renewal of the license, and it was only the third that was material. The first objection was that the license was not required for the necessity of the neighbourhood ; the second that the premises were not structurally adapted for the purpose of a license, and the fourth that the pre- mises were used for the purpose of betting. Theseobjec- tions were not material for their consideration, and he should deal only with the third because it was upon that that the magistrates acted, and it was upon the third that the magistrates refused to grant the renewal of the license. The third objection was" That you (that is Bullock) are not afit and proper person to hold a license for the sale of intoxicating liquors." He thought there could not and would not be any doubt or any suggestion that the ground, as it existed in fact, was anabundantly sufficient ground for the refusal to renew, because, as had been put beyond all questions recently, the power and the dis- cretion of the licensing bench was precisely with regard to renewal as it was with regard to the original grant of a new license, provided that in the case of a renewal ob- jections were properly lodged and made in due time; that was to say when a new license was applied for the magis- strates had, of course, the right, and it was their duty to consider the character of the applicant. They never dreamed of granting a licence to a man unless he was a person of good character, and when a license was asked for by way of renewal,and it was suggested to the bench by way, of a proper objection laid in due time that a person was not a fit and proper person, then they had the same discretion precisely upon the hearing of that objection that they would have had if it had been a new application. Having quoted in favour of this conten- tion, Mr. Swift went on to say that Warrington justices considered the objection and found that the applicant Bullock was not a fit and proper person to keep a public house, and they accordingly, in the exercise of their discretion, and, he might say, in the execution of their duty, refused to grant any renewal of the license. The question that day was whether or not the magistrates of Warrington came to a wrong conclusion in refusing to give Bullock a license. That was the only question, be- cause the appellant there that day was Edward Bullock was the only person that they could law- fully and properly consider. If they came to the con- clusion that he was not a fit and proper person thed they would not grant the license to him, and then could not, however much theypight wish, assist the land- lord ; they could not grant the license to any- body else. Edward Bullock was the only person in the world who could that day receive the license from that court. He thought he might say at once that, as a matter of law, if the magistrates at Warring- ton had thought fit to grant the license to the landlord, or to any other nominee of the landlord, they would have had power to do it. They could have done it, but that Court could not do. The time for that had passed away. When the renewal of a license is applied for, there is no need to give any notice whatever in regard to that to the licensing justices, and any person of respectable charac- ter which was the occupier of the premises at the time might go to the licensing meeting and say "The old licen- see is gone; I am the new occupier and a person of fit and proper character, and I ask you to renew this license in my name," and the licensing justices at the licensing meeting or at the adjournment of it had abundant power to do that if they chose. That was fully conceded. The magistrates did not do that, and now it was too late for the license to be renewed in any name but that of Bul- lock. With regard to the facts, the magistrates below had evidence before them to show that Bullock was ad- dicted to betting, and he (Mr. Swift) thought he should, if necessary, satisfy them that Bullock did absent him- self from his licensed premises and from Warrington and attended racing meetings as a betting man, and that as a betting man he kept a booking clerk. Perhaps some of the magistrates might think that a person who occupied a considerable time in that way was not a suitable person to be entrusted with a license in Warrington or in any other borough, but in addition to that the mag- istrates below had evidence before of what he ven- tured to think some gross misconduct. When the gentle- men who conducted the objection at Warrington pro- posed to call the evidence to which he now referred his learned friends who then represented, as they did now, the two appellants, objected to the admission of that evidence from the mouths of the parties, or in anything like detail, and, yielding perhaps a little weakly to that objection, the magistrates did not hear the evidence in detail, but they heard the substance of it from the police. That day he should tender that evidence, and he did not know whether his friends would have the boldness to say that it was not admissible there. There they were engaged in a judicial inquiry, and there was no limit to the scone of their inquiry, excepting that it should be relevant to the issue, and the issue was : Is this man a fit and proper person to be entrusted with a license to keep a public-house,as a man of good character ? Mr. McKeand, interrupting, said as he understood Mr. Swift was going to call one or two girls in respect to that matter, it would be better if they went out of court. The Bench, agreeing to this suggestion, the two girls, Harriet Bailey and Annie Mansell, went out of Court. Mr. Swift said it was no use arguing a point until it arose, and he thought his friends could not by any pos- sibility have any successful objection to the reception of that evidence. Mr. Swift then alluded to the allegations that Bullock and his clerk, Smith,went from Warrington to Wolverhampton Races with the two girls named above. In addition to this, there would be evidence given that, at the Warrington Football Club Sports on August Bank Holiday, Bullock had been seen making bets in the football field. He (Mr. Swift) should also mention as it was part of his case, and part of his in- structions that Bullock had had notice from the 26th August down to the 23rd September, that his license was going to be objected to upon various grounds, and one of the grounds distinctly was that he was not a fit and proper person, and, although he had that month's notice given to him he never attempted at Warringtan to go in- the box to justify his own conduct, nor did he call any evidence whatever to say that he was a fit and proper person. In fact he seemed by his conduct to accept the position. Mr. Segar said he wished to ask his friend whether he, on behalf of the justices of Warrington,desired to oppose the renewal of that license if the landlord was now in a position, which he (Mr. Segar) could prove he was, to present to the court a tenant who would give satisfaction to the Chief Constable and to their worships. If the magistrates had not instructed Mr. Swift to oppose the renewal on that ground he (Mr. Segar) suggested that that would be a short way of dialing with the matter. He should call a gentleman whom the magistrates would undoubtedly approve, and the license could be renewed upon the terms that the license should be at once trans- ferred to such person. Mr. Swift said the third ob- jection was the only one that was material, and with regard to Bullock's character he had never been sum- moned and there had been no conviction against him, but it was all in consequence of that unfortunate busi- ness at Wolverhampton. At Warrington the magistrate's were anxious to preserve the rights of Mr. Bolton, the landlord, and they proposed to adjourn the case to do what they could to preserve those rights, but they were advised they had no power to do so. Mr. McKeand and Mr. Swift, who was at the time engaged for some other brewers, got up and advised the magistrate they had the power to renew the license in the name of somebody else, but notwithstanding this they were mistakenly advised by their clerk that they had not. He (Mr. Segar) had the Mayor of Warrington there to explain the circumstances, and he would say that they had intended, as far as possible, to assist Mr. Bolton. Mr. Swift admitted that the Warrington magistrates could have transferred the license to anyone they thought fit and that was undoubted law, as his friend (Mr. Swift)

TIIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 1• . 1890 • had said to the magistrates at that time, but they would THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. not be advised by him and took the view of their properly authorised adviser. The Chairman asked if Mr. Segar said that Bench had INPENDING KEEN CONTEST. power to transfer the license. Mr. Segar said they might renew the license to Mr. Bullock on the understanding that it be transferred from him at the earliest possible moment. The Chairman said the question was whether they had the right to transfer the license ; it was not a question of what the right was below but what it was there. Mr. Seger said there was no case in point, but he said they could renew, placing upon the renewal the condi- dition that the license must be transferred to somebody else, and of course if the license went on in Bullock's name, and there was no excuse for his not turning out, the license would not be renewed. That was the only way they could enforce a condition of that sort, but the brewer in this case was a gentleman who was perfectly reliable. He owned several licensed victuallers houses and had done for many years, and there had never been a single charge against any of the houses. The Chairman said they mnst be guided by the law. If they could not transfer to the landlord, they could not transfer to anybody else. Mr. Segar was not going to ask them to transfer, but to renew on the condition that the license was to be transferred to some gentleman. He had there a gentle- man who was approved by the Chief Constable, and the transfer could be carried out at the next transfer Sessions. He had there a blank transfer signed by Mr. Bullock, and he had also an agreement which was in- tended to be read to the Court signed by Mr. Bullock and Mr. Bolton. He then read the agreement as follows : "1. The said Edward Bullock hereby agrees that, in case the magistrates who shall hear his appeal, shall decline to renew his license except upon the terms that lie quits and gives up possession of the Royal Exchange premises, add transfers the license to a respectable tenant to be approved of by the Chief Constable of Warrington, or upon any terms requiring him to quit and give up possessionof the said premises, that he will quit and deliver up immediate possession, and will transfer such license as aforesaid. 2. The said William Bolton hereby agrees for the consideration aforesaid to pay the said Edward Bullock for his tenant's fixtures, and the un- expired term of his license. 3. The said Mr., Bolton to be at liberty, if necessary, to use and read this agree- ment on the hearing of the said appeal." He (Mr. Seger) thought Mr. Bullock had been painted a good deal blacker than was justifiable, but if the justices were of opinion he was not a fit and proper person, there was more than sufficient evidence to satisfy them that he would be turned out at once and that a proper tenant would be put in. They had got a man there named Bolton—a cousin ef the proprietor—a man of high respectability and approved of by the Chief Constable. Mr. Segar then read from a shorthand note what had been said at the Warrington Licensing Sessions on the occasion of the refusal of the license, in order to show that the magis- trates had no wish to injure Mr. Bolton, as the landlord of the Royal Exchange. He asked the magistrates there to do to Mr. Bolton what the magistrates at War- rington would have desired to do if they had known they had the power to do it. He thought it had been held that they could not grant a license conditionally, but they could so grant a license that if a condition was not carried out it would not be renewed. The Chairman; That must be a condition. Mr. McKeand said he appeared for Mr. Bullock who said he was a fit and proper person, and he (Mr. McKeand) must protect him. After it was ilhown he was not a fit and proper person, it would be time to consider whether they should grant him the license subject to a condition. The Chairman : That is what I say; it is like put- ting the cart before the horse. Mr. Swift said it appeared to him that if Mr. Segar's statement meant to anything at all it meant first of all that there was not any authority for their granting the license to anyone but Bullock, and, secondly, Mr. Segar showed that there was not any authority for granting a license on appeal with a con- dition inserted for the transfer to somebody else. It appeared to him in reality that, whatever his friend Mr. McKeand might say, his friend, Mr. Segar, Mr. Segar's client and Mr. Bullock himself had all given Mr. Bullock away, because it was quite clear that the agree- ments which had been read and the undertaking all went to shqw that it was confessed that Mr. Bullock could not maintain his title. Their worships had now learned that he (Mr. Swift happened to be present to watch the inter- ests of other people at Warrington, and as a friend of the Court he did intervene to prevent an adjourn- ment taking place to an unlawful day, and then after- wards he did suggest to the magistrates exactly what he said to them in his opening that morning, that if the magistrates had so dispised they could then and there have renewed the license under another name. There could be no doubt whatever that the magistrates at Warrington were dominated by the feeling that they did not want to jeopardise Mr. Bolton. They did not want to disfranchise his house, but they could not grant the license to Bullock, and therefore they refused to renew to him and they wished to adjourn the further consider- ation Of the matter till the 9th October. The obvious interpretation of that was that the renewal having been I absolutely and definitely refused so far as ISullock was concerned, the magistrates were wishful to give time and opportunity to get Bullock out and to get a suitable person in. Be therefore felt that in arguing against Mr. Bolton he was arguing in truth against the justices and against the deliberate wish and intention of the magistrates at the Licensing Court, and it had led him to consider his position. He felt that as counsel in that I case he was responsible for the correct representation before that court of the feelings of the respondent justices, and lie felt that the respondent justices 1 would at Warrington have granted the license in the name of some other fit and preper per- ' son, if they could have seen their way to do it. They did not see their way to do it, and he did not think there was any blame to be attached to them for not seeing it, but their worships that day might think he should not be wrong in endeavouring to give force and effect to the justice of the case as representing the wishes of the magistrates at Warrington. The question that agitated his mind was whether he should be justified, and he almost thought he should,but he would not with- out some sign from their worships, in saying that that case having now been very fully ventilated, and the magistrates at Warrington having had a manifest and express desire to save the license for Mr.Bolton,he would be justified as their counsel, and in order to carry out their predominant intention, that he would not offer any evidence, but let the license be renewed in point of law and in point of form to Bullock, knowing as he did that Bullock would not be allowed to act upon it, but that he would be got out of the premises, and a new tenant put in his place. He thought himself that the ends of justice would be fully and entirely met by that course. The Chairman said it was a pity that did not come before the case as they should then not have been asked to make a sort of arrangement which undoubtedly they had no right to make. The Bench would take no responsibility whatever. If they chose to give no evidence, and the case dropped the responsibility would be with them. Mr. Segar said they were quite agreeable to that. (Laughter.) They would consent to carry out their agreement. and put in a responsible tenant. Mr. McKeand : We simply say we allow this appeal, and ttpe rest remains with us. ThT Chairman : Yes ; We are parties to no arrange- ment whatever. Mr. Swift represents the justices, and the responsibility will be on his shoulders. Mr. McKeand consulted with his client, Mr. Bullock, and then said he was afraid they could not come to the suggested arrangement. Mr. Bullock was anxious to have his character cleared and he said " I will either have it cleared here or the decision of the justices." Mr. Swift; Then what is the meaning of this agree- ment. Ido not understand this. Mr. McKeand said that, supposing the magistrates came to the condusion,that Mr. Bullock was not a fit and proper person, they could then come to the arrangement. I The Chairman : It would be too late then. 1 Mr. McKeand: I must protect the interest of my client. 1 The Chairman; Yes, of course you must. Mr. Swift then called Inspector SpinkS. but the witness had only entered upon his evidence when some further consultation took place amongst the counsel andtheir clients, after which Mr. Swift said he was now in a position to say that their worships ought not to be troubled further with that appeal. He believed that in taking that course he was I doing his utmost to carry out the wishes and intentions 1 of the licensing meeting, namely, that the license was not intended to be confiscated or forfeited altogether but that it was intended to be preserved for the appellant, Mr. Bolton, as the owner. Mr. Bullock had now con- sented that if the license be renewed— The Chairman did not think that should be gone into. Mr. Swift added that he could only say that, by his not offering any further evidence upon that appeal, the wishes of the magistrates would be entirely—not only in the spirit but to the very letter—carried out, and there- fore he submitted to have that appeal allowed. The Magistrates' Clerk asked what about costs? Mr. Swift said they did not ask for any costs. The Chairman; The appeal is allowed without costs. The Chairman added that he wished the reporters to understand that the magistrates were in no way respon- sible for the decision. They were powerless to do any- thing but what they did. They did not sanction anything.

There has been considerable activity and excite- I ment during the week, consequent upon the pre- parations made for the municipal elections in War- rington, which take place to-day. Canvassers on both sides have been busy in every Ward, except Bewsey Ward, which is the only one in which there is no contest. There have been public meetings in most ot the Wards in support of the various candi- dates, and good feeling has, on the whole, been maintained. Hand-bills and circulars have been plentifully circulated, and, if the electors are not tolerably well informed as to the issues pending, it is not because they have not been plentifully sup- plied with literature. The Liberals are hopeful of winning one or more of the seats held by the Con- servatives, and their success is undoubted if all the electors who have promised are careful to redeem their pledges at the polling booths. It is to be hoped that no Liberal will fail to record his vote because of any inconvenience he may be put to through tip contest taking place on a Saturday,as it may happen 'that a single vote will determine an election. We give particulars below as to the various candidates and their prospects, and we . would ask our readers, and especially all Liberals to—

The Countess of Jersey had a good night on Tuesday, and continues to progress satisfactorily. The Countess of Rosebery is also making progress, though slowly, to- wards recovery. Mr. Fenwick, M.P., the Parliamentary secretary to the Trades tinionCongress, proposes to revive the ques- tion of payment of members of Parliament by introducing a Bill next session to enact that every member of the House of Commons should be required to accept a salary of about £3OO for his public service. A remarkable discovery has been made at Birkenhe td. While a cellar on the premises of a plumber in the Hay- market was being dug a vein of gravel containing large grains of a yellow metal was revealed, and these have been found by the ordinary chemical tests to consist of gold.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

COLLISION AT SEA. 61 LIVES LOST. NEW YORE, FRIDAY.—A collision took place yester- day, off Barugatt, between a schooner and the Spanish steamer Viz Caya bound for Havana. The latter foundered, and 61 persons, passengers and crew, were drowned.
WRECK OF A STEAMER.-10 SEAMEN DROWNED.
BERLIN, FRIDAY EVENING.—The British Erik Berentsen has been wrecked at Westerland. The captain and 10 seamen were drowned. NEW BISHOP OF. WORCESTER.
Dr. Perow—n—ew,Dean of Peterborough, yesterday morn- ing accepted the bishopric of Worcester. _ .
A BARRISTER KILLED.
Mr. E. F. Ashworth Briggs, barrister, of Daventry. was killed yesterday morning by the express, whilst crossing the railway at Bliswerth Station.
LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR NORFOLK. It is announced that Mr. Robert Price, barrister, Lon- don, has been selected as the Liberal candidate for the East division of Norfolk, to oppose Sir Edward Birkbeck.
MR. GLADSTONE IN SCOTLAND.

Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone spent Thursday at Fasque, the residence of their nephew, Sir John Gladstone. He will remain at Fasque until Monday morning. FOUR INTENDING EMIGRANTS SHOT DEAD. BERLIN, FRIDAY.—The " Vossische Zedung " reports that a Russian guard on the Prussian frontier, near Slupeaf recently shot dead four persons who were about to emigrate to Brazil. THE CHESHIRE MURDER CONFESSION. Yesterday, Mr. H. Churton, the South Cheshire coroner, received from New Orleans the full written con- fession of the Cheshire murder, 35 years ago. The state- ment is of an incoherent and extraordinary character, and Mr. Sawers, who first drew attention to the matter, writes declaring his conviction that the whole story is pure rubbish and merely the reminiscence of a drunken creature.

FIRE AT BRIGHTLINGSEA : TWO LIVES LOST. A Colchester correspondent telegraphs that a destruc- tive fire broke out yesterday morning on the premises of Mrs. Lord, tailoress, at Brightlingsea, Essex. At the time of the outbreak the whole of the inmates, namely, Mrs. Lord, her eight children, a sea captain named Had- lei, and a servant, were asleep. A ladder was procured, and all the occupants escaped, except Will Lord and Clara Lord aged nine and seven years respectively, whose charred remains were afterwards found in the debris.
THE HAMPSTEAD TRAGEDY.-FEMALE SEARCHER'S STATEMENT. . .

The Press Association says :—We learn that Mrs. Piercey on the day of her arrest admitted to the female searcher, who examined her clothing in the cell at Holloway, that she sent the invitation to Mrs. Hogg. She said, "I invited Mrs. Hogg to my house. We had a few words. One word led to another. But there, I had not better say anything more about it." The searcher, who comes from Holloway Gaol, was taken to the Treasury this morning. She did not say any- thing to the authorities about the matter uatil 'Thurs- day evening.

MURDER OF ANOTHER ENGLISHMEN IN AMERICA. NEW YORK, TEURSDAY.—The dead body of Mr. Norris Watts, son of Mr. Edward Hannay Watts, a wealthy Londoner, has been found at Cumberland Gap, Tenessee. Death had been caused by bullet wounds, and it is obvious that these must have been fired by another per- son. There are no circumstances to indicate who com- mitted the murdsr. A fire broke out on Wednesday night in a building at Trinity wharf, Woolwich, containing 450 tons of cpm belonging to Messrs. Lee and Co. The conflagration illuminated the whole of South London, and raged for several hours in spite of the immense quantity of water available from the River and shore. Adjoining property was also greatly endangered, and the rigging of the brigantine Ann Isabella and barge August took fire. The building and contents were insured.

The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) attended at the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon to receive and con- sider any objections that might be made to the nomina- tions of any of the candidates. There were also present the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), Councillor Henry Roberts. Mr. A. Browne, Mr. Clayton (Liberal Agent), and Mr. F. Dixon, jun. The proceedings were entirely formal and only lasted a few minutes, the Town Clerk informing the Mayor that each of the candidaies seemed to be validly nominated, and that there were no objec- tions.

STRINGER'S CANDIDATURE.—MEE riNG LAST

div.head: NIGHT.
div.p: NIGHT.

A meeting in support of Mr. Stringer, the Liberal can- didate for Latchford Ward, was held last evening in the Temperance Hall, Latchford. Mr. L. Ellison pre- sided, and atnongst others present, besides the candidate, were the Rev. E. Moore, Mr. W. Weave, Mr. J. Strange, and Mr. W. Twiss. There was a fair atten- dance. The Chairman said that many of them had been very dissatisfied with their present repre- sentation, and they felt that they needed a change. If they all worked together, he believed they should be able to put in their friend Mr. Stringer. (Applause.) He believed that it was not only one side that was tired of the present representation, but that there were others also. If they could not put in their candidate they should make the other side see that they must put better candidates in the field, if they wished to hold their seats. (Hear, hear.)—The Rev. E. Moore moved a resolution in favour of Mr. Stringer. He referred to the fact that Mr. Ashton as well as another representative of Latchford were engaged in the liquor trade, and he added that any town that was mainly ruled by those who were directly interested in the liquor traffic was a town that was sure by that very fact to be hindered and impeded in its best and truest welfare. There was a temptation to make all things subservient to the interests of that particular trade, and when it was the case it was an evil thing for any town. (Applause.) —Mr. (*leave seconded and Mr. Twiss supported the resolution. The latter gentleman spoke strongly against people engaged in the liquor trade being on the Watch Committee, which had: in a sense, the care of the morals of the town—Mr.Stringer, the candidate, next spoke. He deprecated the, introduction of politics at municipal elections, ashe believed they would otherwise get better men to represerlt them, but politics having been intro- duced they as Liberals would have to make the best of it. He then proceeded to give his views as reported in another column. :The resolution was afterwards unani- mously passed with ac,damation, and the meeting was soon afterwards brought to a close.

THE WARRINGTON TRADES' COUNCIL AND THE ELECTIONS. As intimated in our last issue, several questions, framed by the Warrington United Trades Council, have been sent to all the candidates with the re- quest that they would favour the Council with re- plies. A meeting of the Council to receive these replies was held on Wednesday evening, and, after considering them, it was resolved that the follow- ing candidates should receive their support :—Mr. Titchett (L), Mr. Fleming (L), Mr. Woods (C), Mr. Bolton (C), Mr. Dixon (I), Mr. Percival (C). and Mr. Ashton (C). Nothing was decided as to the candi- dates in St. John's Ward, which was understood to be "left open." From what we can'gather, there were no more than a dozen members of the Council present, and there is reason to believe that some members who do not usually attend were present in order to help their party interest. The decision to support the various candidates was not taken in all cases on the merits of the replies, for it is stated that Mr. Bolton answered one question only, entirely ignoring the others; whilst Mr. James Walker, his opponent, not only answered that question unreservedly in the affirmative; but promised what was regarded as a favourable consideration of the others. And yet Mr. Bolton was the accepted of the :Council ! Mr. Ashton was accepted as a sitting member, although it was admitted that his reply to the questions was not more favourable than that sent in by Mr. Stringer. Mr. Alfred Woods,Conservative candidate forWhite- cross Ward, answered" Yes," to every question, but in this connection it is worthy of note that Alder- man Sutton, in presiding at a meeting in support of Mr. Hepherd, the Conservative candidate for St. Austin's Ward, said the questions were " an insult to the intelligence and common-sense of the Con- servative canditates " ; and Mr. Ilepherd expressed himself as agreeing with Alderman Sutton that it was an insult to send such questions. These expres- sions of opinion put Mr. Woods, or the Tory party, in a corner, and they may be left to fight it out amongst themselves. A hand-bill on behalf of the candidature of Mr. Henry Roberts for the White- cross Ward has been issused, signed by Messrs. G. Legge, S. J. Beaman, J. W. Hayward, J. Hayward, T. Flood, J. Salt, J. Crowther, and R. Roscoe, which affirms that the answers given by Mr. Roberts are "fair, reasonable and honest." The following are the questions with the answers given by Mr. Roberts:— Question.-1. Will you, if elected Member of the Town Council, promise to Vote that all Corporation work and contracts be given only to those firms who pay the recog- nised rate of wages to their workmen? Answer.—l am quite in accord with the question in- volved in your proposition. Question. —2. Will you vote that the workmen in the employ of our Corporation shall receive the recognised rate of wages ?

div.head: BALACLAVA VETERANS.
div.p: THE BALACLAVA VETERANS.

Over a thousand pounds was realised by the perform- ance at the Empire Theatre in aid of the Balaclava— veterans. The house was packed from floor to ceiling, despite the charging of double prices. The enthusiasm was unbounded. It was positively thrilling when to the peal of Trumpeter Landfried's trumpet the surviving ' heroes of the glorious tradgedy of war filed on to the stage, and Mr. Charles Warren recited Tennyson 0• famous lines. It was a sight to stir a Stoic.
The Liberal delegates of the Ayr Burghs:on 'Wednesday night adopted Mr. William Berkmyre, merchant, of Greenock, as their candidate at the next election.

MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, 180. To um BURGESSES OF TOWN HALL WARD. LL'DIES AND GENTLEMEN,—AS the term for which I was elected a Member of theWarrington Town Council is about to expire, I offer myself as a candidate for your Ward at the pressing request of an influential body of ratepayers. During the six years I have had a seat in the Council, I have made it my duty to promote those measures which had far their object the economical and better government of the town. If again returned I need hardly say that it will stil be my object to faithfully serve the ratepayers as a whole. •I trust that the Public Health Amendment Act, which hate just been adopted, will be drought into operation, and thu, be the means of improving or removing insanitary pro- petty, while ridding us at the same time of the Black Spots .et Warrington. I am in favour of an immediate inquiry being instituted as to the effect of the Intercepting Depots upon the health and "comfort of the inhabitants, and shall 'vote for their being sclosed, or removed, if they cannot be made inoffensive. Having supported the movement for freeing the Library, I -shall vote, if returned, for the Lending ,Department being made free to the public as soon as itican be done in the coming year. I think the time has arrived when new baths should be provided, and every facility Offered for boys to learn to swim. These and other matters shall receive my careful consideration if you return mete the Town Council. Hoping to have your support on theday of election. I remain, Ladies and Gentleman. Your obedient Servant, 'JOHN 11. FLEMING. Winmarleigh Lodge, October 24th, 1890.

MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, 1890. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE ORFORD WARD. LADIES ADD GENTLEISEEN.-I have been waited upon by a deputation asking my consent to .-contest your Ward as a Candidate for the Town Council. After giving the matter very or.reful consideration, I hays decided to place my services at your disposal. As a large employer of labour in the town, I shall at all times endeavour to keep down tile 'Borough expenditure, and so lessen the rates, in order to induce other manufacturers to open out new industries in oursiaidst. The question of a Free Library which is practically settled) and the proposed new Baths wiih have my hearty support. With regard to the Intercepting Depots, I regret that serious complaints ass made as to the nuisance arising from them. I shall do my utmost to-secure the abatement of this nuisance, and, if that is impracticable, I shall be prepared to vote for the closing of the Depfits, rather than inflict upou my friends and neighbours anything which interferes with their health and the comfort ef• their homes. All other matters of local interest, which may come before the Council shall have my beet .etteution, and, should you honour me by election, rely upon it, I shall do my best to deserve your confidence and approval. lam, Ladies and•Gontlemen, Your. obedient Servant. JAMES WALKER. Dallam-lane Foundry, Warrington, October 24th. 1 MOO.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. ST. JOHN'S WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.-At the , request of a large and influential body of the Ratepayers of Me Ward, I have much , pleasure in offering myself as a candidate for election on the let November next, as your representative q the Town Council. Should you do me the honour to,,elect me, my constant object in the Council will be to do alldn my power for the , Improvement of the Town and its Trade, so as to create Labour and Wages for the Working Classes, and Business for the Shopkeepers and Commercial Interest. My best attention will be given to the.limprovement of your Streets, Workingmen's Houses, the supply of good Gas at as low a rate as possible, the 'lmprovement of the Sanitary , Arrangements of the Town, and to full efficiency with due economy in all matters ‘connected with the Ward and I Borough. As regards the Intereeptiing Depot so cruelly planted in your midst. I shall do all in my power tod:ave it swept away and 'entirely removed. I am also strongly in favour of the nightsoil being removed during the night, and thus do away with the nuisance of having to meet bad smelling carts in the streets at all hours of the day. I am a resident in your Ward, your intesests and mine are identical, and I shall at all times be at hands and ready to hear the grievance of any Burgess, and so far as it lies in my power I shall endeavour to have such grievance rewedied. Having lived amongst you ;far many years and being well known to a very large number ..sf you. I feeli,hat I may with great comiSdence ask your votesand active support on the Pol- ling Day. I am, Ladiesamli Gentlemeß, ours faithfdßy, JAMES HILL. 24. Ashtesi-street, October 23rd, 1890.

WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTION. 'TO THE BURGESSES OF LATCHFORD WARD. 1_ LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—My term of office having expired, I again offer myself to the Electors of Latchford Ward, and seek their suffrages for re-election. My line of action in the past, extending over 22 years, has been faithfully devoted to the interest of the ratepayers in general, performing my duties on the various committees fearlessly and conscientiously to the'best of my judgment and ability. I can only add, should you again place your confi- dence in me, that nothing shall te wanting on my part to serve you as earnestly in the future as ift the past. I remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JOSEPH ASHTON. Bridge Inn, Wilderspool Causeway, October 24th. 1890.

For fond hearts laugh at sternest foe, Say to great Marquisses ";stand down " ; Lords' S. and H. it is "no go" Upon the happy pair to frown. How crowded will be all the church To witness marriage rite divine, No scene more grand although we search Through all the County Palatine. JUDEX.

WHY DOES A woman's health so often breaks down at an early age? Put a man at a washing tub ; let him get heated with the hot suds until every pore is opened ; then let him stand over the filthy steam that comes from scalding and boiling clothes, and his health certainly would break down before long. And yet this terrible ordeal is exactly what A WOMAN Has to go through on washing days ; and besides, while over-heated at the Lot work, she has to risk her life by going out into the open air to hang up the clothes. Answer.—l will support the payment to Corporation Workmen of an equal rate of Wages to what is paid for similar work in other Boroughs of a similar size to Warrington. Question.-3. Will you vote for an advance of wages to able-bodied Corporation Workmen, who receive less than 20s. per week ? 4. Will you record your vote in favour of the Workmen of the Corporation being allowed holi- days every year, and receive wages for the same, the number of holidays to be the same as allowed to the higher officials of the Corporation ? Answer. —ln regard to these two questions, I will, when I have been able to ascertain the facts, give the matters referred to my careful consideration. Mr Arthur Browne, candidate for Howley Ward had the same questions put to him, and his answers were as follows :- Ist. I am quite in accord with the resolution that was intended to be proposed by Mr. Flood, at the last Council meeting in September, and I am quite agreeable that all workmen in the employ of the Corporation should received the recognised rate of wages. 2nd. lam quite agreeable, if elected, to give all able-bodied Corporation workmen, who receive less than 20s. per week, the average rate of wages paid by other Corporations of a similar size to our own, for a similar class of work. 3rd. As this is the first time I have heard that the lower officials of a Corporation should have similar holidays to those holding highet\ offices, I can only say, if I am elected, and the matter comes before the Council, I shall give it my best consideration on its merits. These answers were admitted to be more favour- able than those sent in by his opponent, Councillor Percival, and yet Mr. Percival is the accepted candidate of the Trades' Council! It was suggested that the whole of the answers should be published by the Council, but this was not done, on account of expense. Let them be published and we venture to say they will confirm our statement. However, seeing that there was a small meeting of the Council and the decisions were not given solely on the merits of the answers, it is not likely that the result will h ave any great influence with the electors either one way or the other.
